items.title: KVPath: Connecting Key-Value Representations Across Transformer Layers
items.content: arXiv:2611.16072v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Transformers typically cache an independent key-value (KV) representation for each token at every layer. Recent work reveals that a token's KV representations across neighboring layers are correlated and contain shared information. We hypothesize that this correlation implies incremental inter-layer changes, which can be effectively captured by low-dimensional deltas. Motivated by this, we propose KVPath, a new KV representation paradigm that connects KV representations across the network depth into a path. The path establishes a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, while subsequent layers generate low-dimensional delta KVs to update the preceding KV, thereby constructing their own KV states. By caching the base KV once alongside these compact delta KVs, KVPath preserves distinct layer-specific representations without storing full KV states at every layer. We develop two variants of KVPath: KVPath-Residual, which updates vector values via residual addition, and KVPath-Rolling, which progressively updates feature dimensions in a rolling manner. Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68\% for Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and 55\% for Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), while maintaining or even improving model performance.
items.author: Xuan Luo, Zhiyuan Wang, Hanzhong Cao, Xifeng Yan
items.summary: KVPath proposes a new key-value caching paradigm in which a full-dimensional base KV is stored at the first layer and subsequent layers store only low-dimensional deltas that update the previous layer's KV, exploiting the correlation of KV representations across neighboring layers. This can substantially reduce KV cache memory in transformer inference.
items.reasoning: KV cache memory is a first-order cost in long-context LLM serving, so efficiency methods with a clear structural hypothesis are valuable. The delta-path idea is architecturally novel; impact depends on empirical quality retention, which the abstract implies but does not fully establish.

This can substantially reduce KV cache memory in transformer inference.
items.content_html: arXiv:2611.16072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformers typically cache an independent key-value (KV) representation for each token at every layer. Recent work reveals that a token's KV representations across neighboring layers are correlated and contain shared information. We hypothesize that this correlation implies incremental inter-layer changes, which can be effectively captured by low-dimensional deltas. Motivated by this, we propose KVPath, a new KV representation paradigm that connects KV representations across the network depth into a path. The path establishes a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, while subsequent layers generate low-dimensional delta KVs to update the preceding KV, thereby constructing their own KV states. By caching the base KV once alongside these compact delta KVs, KVPath preserves distinct layer-specific representations without storing full KV states at every layer. We develop two variants of KVPath: KVPath-Residual, which updates vector values via residual addition, and KVPath-Rolling, which progressively updates feature dimensions in a rolling manner. Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68\% for Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and 55\% for Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), while maintaining or even improving model performance.

items.title: MutAtlas: A PDB-Wide Energy-Guided Atlas of Protein Mutation Effects
items.content: arXiv:2611.16361v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Protein mutation effect prediction is fundamental to protein engineering and disease variant interpretation, yet experimentally measured mutation data remain accurate but extremely sparse. To provide scalable supplementary mutation signals, we construct a PDB-wide mutation augmentation dataset that exhaustively enumerates single-site substitutions on experimentally resolved protein structures and aligns mutation signals from physics-based energy models, protein language models, and inverse folding models. Large-scale analysis under a unified mutation preference representation reveals substantial differences in the consistency, concentration, and substitution patterns of mutation distributions across models, indicating that disagreement is pervasive and reflects conflicting inductive biases rather than random noise. Motivated by these observations, we propose an unsupervised multi-source mutation preference distillation framework that learns from relative mutation preferences while explicitly modeling cross-source disagreement. Without using any experimental mutation labels during training, our approach achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines and naive multi-source fusion strategies on ProteinGym. We release the dataset and evaluation pipeline to support reproducible studies of protein mutation effects.

items.title: On the Difficulty of Sequence-Level Supervised Learning for Autoregressive Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.16736v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: During the supervised learning phase, autoregressive language models are typically trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of the training data, which decomposes as a sum of token-level cross-entropies via teacher forcing. This objective is simple and efficient but potentially suffers from so-called exposure bias: a mismatch between the way the model is trained and the way it is used at inference time. Can we instead design sequence-level loss functions that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures, such as greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling? We show that two natural attempts lead to loss functions that are fundamentally flawed: unbounded below. We further show that these two flawed loss functions are intimately connected: using autoregressive Gumbel tricks, the sampling based loss is the expected greedy loss under Gumbel perturbations. Since the pathology stems from the dependence of the decoded sequence on the model parameters, we analyze the update direction obtained by applying a stop gradient on the sampling procedure, leading to a moment matching direction. While it is not the gradient of any loss function, we prove that it defines a valid descent direction in function space for the autoregressive negative log-likelihood. Despite these theoretical insights, the moment matching direction suffers from high variance. We conclude that teacher forcing may well be ``all you need'' for supervised learning of autoregressive models.
items.author: Mathieu Blondel, Micha\"el E. Sander, Germain Vivier-Ardisson, Tianlin Liu, Vincent Roulet
items.summary: This theory paper examines whether autoregressive language models can be trained with sequence-level losses that incorporate inference-time decoding procedures like greedy decoding or autoregressive sampling, instead of standard token-level negative log-likelihood under teacher forcing. The authors prove that two natural formulations of such sequence-level losses are fundamentally flawed because they are unbounded below, and they trace the connection between these flawed objectives. The work provides negative results that clarify why exposure bias is difficult to address through straightforward supervised learning objectives.

items.title: Two mathematical models of knowledge distillation
items.content: arXiv:2611.17230v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Many hypotheses compete to explain the successes of knowledge distillation. To help address this, we propose and analyze a mathematical model of distillation, which suggests that distillation's performance comes not from obtaining better models but from easier to optimize landscapes. For generalized linear models trained with stochastic gradient descent, we prove that distillation fits performant student models asymptotically more quickly than non-distilled models. In rank-1 matrix approximation, we characterize conditions on the target matrix under which gradient descent with distillation converges strictly faster than training on the supervised objective. The theory helps delineate the ways distillation provides benefits (i.e., in optimization speed, not in generalization), and experiments on real datasets corroborate the theoretical predictions.

items.title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul: Cross-Attribute Externalities of Fairness Interventions
items.content: arXiv:2611.14717v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Fairness interventions often targets disparities associated with a single sensitive attribute in binary classification tasks. However, when multiple sensitive attributes are associated with a data subject, improving fairness with respect to one attribute does not necessarily improve it across all attributes: it may exacerbate disparities associated with other sensitive attributes, including those that are unavailable to the practitioner. We refer to these unintended effects as cross-attribute externalities of fairness. We study how fairness with respect to one sensitive attribute varies when an initially unfair classification or regression model is corrected with respect to another attribute. We characterize these externalities using Wasserstein barycentric disparities and develop a distributional framework that captures changes in both marginal and joint fairness measures. This highlights a limitation of conventional fairness evaluation, in which the success of an intervention is assessed mainly for the attribute it targets. In a jointly Gaussian model, we derive explicit trajectories for marginal and joint disparities and identify conditions under which an intervention eliminates disparities with respect to its target attribute while increasing disparities associated with another attribute. We also derive sharp partial-identification bounds on the resulting externalities when a sensitive attribute is unavailable and extend our results to categorical sensitive attributes. We illustrate these externalities using classification and regression real-data: in the classification experiments, interventions increase unfairness with respect to the hidden attribute in the majority of scenarios across more than half of the datasets considered; in the regression experiments on the ACSIncome dataset, correcting for race reduces sex disparities, whereas subsequently correcting for age increases them.

items.title: Escaping the Curse of Dimensionality in One-Step Flow-Based Generative Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.15447v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Flow and diffusion-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art quality, but require multiple forward passes at inference time, making them computationally costly. Consistency models overcome this by learning a flow map directly, enabling few-step generation and dramatically reducing the computation needed at test time. However, formal statistical guarantees for such one-step generators are scarce. Existing results either suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions. We investigate whether one-step flow-based models can escape the curse of dimensionality under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. In this setup, we derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality. Our findings provide the first principled explanation for practical success of one-step flow-based generative models.

items.title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.16882v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.

items.title: A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting
items.content: arXiv:2611.15267v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: One way to study language-model introspection is to test whether models can identify where their activations have been perturbed. We train a simple linear classifier to identify the perturbed sentence from the model's activations, then compare its predictions with the model's own answers across pretraining and injection strengths. This tests whether the model is being asked to report information that is already easy to recover. If so, successful localization may be less demanding than it first appears and may not extend to the broader uses that motivate introspection research, such as faithfully explaining a model's reasoning or helping researchers assess the reliability of its answers. With an injection four times the typical activation norm at layer 0 and probe readout at layer 24 in OLMo~3 32B, the supervised probe reaches 98.3\% accuracy after 8.4 billion training tokens, while the model's zero-shot answer remains at chance (11.1\%). At the released base checkpoint, these accuracies reach 99.1\% and 89.6\%, respectively. Across 7B and 32B, location is already decodable in randomly initialized networks, showing that the architecture can support these traces without pretraining. In these experiments, location information lies close enough to the surface for a simple linear probe to recover it, so successful reporting need not imply broader access to the model's internal computation.

items.title: daVinci-Prover: Agent-Native Mid-Training for Formal Theorem Proving
items.content: arXiv:2611.16433v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming formal theorem proving. Yet further progress remains constrained by the lack of a transparent and effective data recipe for systematically improving theorem-proving models. In this work, we argue that effective agentic provers require strong mathematical skill priors to ground theorem proving and agentic trajectories to enable long-horizon, interactive proof construction. To this end, we synthesize an agent-native 33.7B-token mid-training corpus covering decomposition, search, self-verification, and revision, together with verifier-grounded agentic trajectories. We further introduce the daVinci-Prover harness, which enables models to construct proofs and interact with a Lean verifier in an isolated workspace, and use it to collect approximately 36K high-quality agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Our mid-training recipe yields an average improvement of 13.7 points over the matched Qwen3-8B SFT-only baseline across MiniF2F, FATE-M, and ProofNet. When applied to the Qwen3.5 series, our approach also yields strong performance across theorem-proving benchmarks and achieves near-saturating MiniF2F performance with memory compaction. The results highlight agent-native mid-training as an effective foundation for developing stronger interactive theorem-proving agents.

items.title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.16714v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates text generation with large language models by letting a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large verifier checks in a single forward pass. We introduce Olifant, a draft model built on a memory-based classifier. It predicts the next token from a four-token window in under 0.3 ms on CPU, requiring no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. We measure throughput and energy under two verifier regimes on consumer hardware. Without a KV cache, drafting is nearly free: a domain-matched Olifant model reaches 38.1% acceptance on EU legal text, delivering 2.43x throughput and 2.51x lower energy per token than the neural verifier model alone. With a KV-cached verifier, itself a ~10x energy saver, drafting costs matter: a TinyLlama draft model halves throughput and triples energy despite high acceptance, whereas Olifant still yields 1.25x throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens, 14x below the uncached baseline). We further show that KV caching decouples time from energy: verification of longer drafts raises power draw, shifting the energy-optimal draft length below the speed-optimal one. Speculative decoding is not dead in the age of fast verifiers, provided drafting is nearly free.

items.title: DiFiT: Distribution-Fidelity-guided Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.15069v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models, but answer accuracy only partly reflects its effect. Pruning can change the probabilities of alternative response tokens even when greedy answers remain correct and unchanged. We compare full and pruned response distributions under shared reference prefixes. Average predictive drift grows with compression on fixed correctly answered samples. Separate analyses associate larger drift with more confidence-decision disagreements and sampling failures. items.title: TRACE: Trajectory Synchronization for Training-Free Resolution Extension in Video Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.15983v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: More text-to-video models are available, but many remain limited to low resolutions. Training them for higher resolutions is costly, while existing training-free methods still struggle with fine detail, scene structure, and efficiency. We propose TRACE, a training-free method that synchronizes low- and high-resolution generation trajectories. During early denoising, TRACE aligns predicted scene content at corresponding noise levels. It computes high-resolution updates from low-resolution predictions and the current high-resolution state, without high-resolution model inference. The high-resolution trajectory retains fine-grained variation for generating new details. Local window attention then refines fine details in a shared high-resolution latent state. TRACE checks suspected duplicate subjects against the corresponding low-resolution layout and corrects selected regions and their solver history while preserving detail elsewhere. Experiments across all kinds of video generation backbones and resolutions show improved perceptual quality and text-video alignment over FreeSwim, a state-of-the-art training-free method, with 2.0-2.9x end-to-end speedups. Our code and models will be released at https://github.com/libozhu03/TRACE.

items.title: ActWorld-JEPA: Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models Meet Latent Planning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2611.16579v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable future prediction in latent space without pixel reconstruction. However, latent predictive consistency alone does not establish the relative driving quality of candidate plans. We present ActWorld-JEPA, a joint-embedding formulation for candidate-based driving. Where Plan-Conditioned JEPA (PC-JEPA) uses global and step-wise trajectory intentions to guide recurrent latent prediction, then combines the predicted future with the current scene through gated cross-attention; Relational Residual Reranking ($R^3$) models agreement and discrepancy between plan and future representations under planning supervision, yielding bounded, gated residual corrections to the base planning scores. This formulation connects latent prediction to candidate selection using only observed context and proposed trajectories at inference. Benchmark-specific implementations report 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, with the final selector calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback, and 91.6 and 42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard, respectively. The nuScenes evaluation reports a mean $L_2$ error of 1.20 m and a predicted collision rate of 0.76% over 1--6 s. This work provides an effective path from JEPA's predictive representations to driving decisions informed by anticipated consequences.

Gated cross-attention fuses predicted futures with current scene representations.

items.title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2611.17194v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

items.title: Generalized Inverse Kinematics via Conditional Flow
items.content: arXiv:2611.15565v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Inverse kinematics (IK) is a foundational primitive in robotics, mapping the task-space objectives expressed by higher-level planners to robot configurations that realize them. Traditional IK methods generally treat each query as an isolated pose-to-configuration problem, but planners often need a distribution over valid realizations that accounts for future reachability and preferences such as collision avoidance and stability. We introduce GenGenIK, a generative modeling approach that supports mobile bases, multiple end-effectors and targets, scene awareness, and preferences over robot behavior within a common interface. Experiments show that GenGenIK outperforms existing methods in both solve rate and runtime across tasks such as bimanual lift and flip-up, while allowing flexible control over the sampled distribution and remaining effective under partial scene observations. Website: https://icra-2027-gengenik.github.io/.

items.summary: GenGenIK reframes inverse kinematics as a generative modeling problem, producing distributions over valid configurations that account for mobile bases, multiple end-effectors and targets, scene awareness, and behavioral preferences, rather than solving each pose query in isolation. Experiments report higher solve rates and faster runtimes than existing methods on tasks including bimanual scenarios. From authors at the Lozano-Perez and Kaelbling group at MIT, this is a strong upgrade to a foundational robotics primitive.

items.title: Informative Path Planning with Gaussian Processes: Error Bounds, Algorithms, and Benchmarks
items.content: arXiv:2611.16877v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate environmental monitoring relies on Informative Path Planning (IPP) to deploy autonomous systems that maximize information gain. While Gaussian Processes (GPs) provide a robust mathematical foundation for modeling the environment, contemporary IPP approaches remain hindered by heuristic operational constraints and the lack of simultaneous theoretical guarantees for worst-case estimation error and approximation quality. Rather than introducing yet another heuristic, this paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of existing error bounds and algorithms to further develop the mathematical foundation for IPP.   By evaluating probabilistic and deterministic bounds on reconstruction error, we establish that predictive variance is the theoretically ideal optimization objective for GP-based IPP. Furthermore, we analyze GreedyCover, a recent approach for optimizing predictive variance, and demonstrate that its near-optimal approximation guarantee matches the fundamental hardness-of-approximation limit for the problem. Comprehensive benchmarking confirms that this approach delivers superior estimation accuracy and computational efficiency compared to prominent information-theoretic objectives and optimization methods used in IPP. Finally, this theoretical analysis establishes a rigorous, near-optimal foundation for discrete offline IPP under bounded uncertainty constraints, offering clear and principled guidance for future work in continuous-space and online formulations.

It also delivers algorithms and benchmarks with simultaneous guarantees for worst-case estimation error and approximation quality. items.title: Almost Optimal Lower Bounds under Almost ETH for Approximating Euclidean k-means
items.content: arXiv:2611.14892v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In the Euclidean $k$-means problem, we are given a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the goal is to find $k$ representative points in space so as to minimize the sum of the squared distances from each point to its closest representative. Algorithmically, de la Vega, Karpinski, Kenyon, and Rabani [STOC'03] and Kumar, Sabharwal, and Sen [JACM'10] obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for high-dimensional Euclidean $k$-means in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{O(1)}} \cdot dn^{O(1)}$, which was subsequently improved to $2^{\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)} + O(ndk)$ by Feldman, Monemizadeh, and Sohler [SoCG'07]. On the lower-bound side, a recent work of Cohen-Addad, Karthik, Saulpic, and Schwiegelshohn [SoCG'26] proposed the Exponential Time for Expanders Hypothesis (XXH), which asserts exponential-time hardness for $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximating Vertex Cover on vertex expanders, and used it to prove nearly matching running time lower bound whenever $k=\tilde{\omega}(1/\varepsilon)$.   We observe that XXH does not hold in the parameter regime needed for the above result, and show how to repair their reduction under a more standard assumption. More precisely, we show that assuming the Almost Exponential Time Hypothesis for 3-SAT (Almost ETH), for every constant $\beta\in(0,1)$, Euclidean $k$-means in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has no $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{1-\beta}}\text{poly}(n,d)$, whenever $k=\tilde{\omega}(1/\varepsilon)$. By modifying the construction, we also obtain a similar result for approximating the Euclidean $k$-median problem.

items.summary: The paper proves near-matching hardness-of-approximation lower bounds for Euclidean k-means under almost-exponential-time hypotheses, substantially closing the gap with known (1+eps)-approximation algorithms. This resolves a question raised by recent work on exponential-time lower bounds for the problem.

items.title: We need more decorrelated evidence
items.content:
AI agents do a growing share of work on each new model. Then, through some process, the results are combined into an overall safety assessment, which labs use to estimate the probability that the next model is not catastrophically misaligned. I feel that, several months later, we appreciate further the foresight of Automated Alignment is Harder Than You Think (Bowkis et al. 2026): much is handed off to the machines because of the urgency of fast timelines, and we miss many things due to the problem of undetected systematic errors. 

MS Paint drawing by Fable 5.2.

In this post, I’ll develop a simple argument (drawing heavily or even verbatim from Bowkis et al. at times) that our recent failures to catch misalignment can be framed as systematic errors shared across our evidence, i.e. a lack of decorrelated evidence.

- Currently, labs run some set of experiments to decide if a model is safe to use. Here are some examples: OpenAI (Astra system card, Sep 2026): Astra models don’t go into internal use without passing blocking alignment evals. After the Hugging Face incident, this paused workloads that didn't comply with new safeguards. OpenAI (Sep 2026): According to news reports, GPT-6.1 Astra was shelved after it fell short on internal alignment testing. Thinking Machines (Inkling 2 Small, Nov 2026): TM paused Inkling 2’s main RL run midway when a monitor flagged the model working around a network block. They then hardened the infrastructure, then resumed. Anthropic (Risk Report, Aug 2026): Anthropic reviews every model before broad internal use, mainly on training-data monitoring and its automated behavioural audit. They now also have monitors that halt training and evaluation runs when a model probes its sandbox. Google DeepMind (Gemini 4 Argon report, Oct 2026): while they couldn’t rule out that Argon has the stealth and situational awareness to undermine human control, they deployed their model on the strength of a holistic risk assessment + some monitoring. So,...

items.title: Eval Awareness vs. Eval Paranoia
items.content:
I have mentioned several times that I think frontier models are not that eval aware. I think this is an important fact to understand about current models, in order to interpret evidence about their behavior. Others have found this idea quite curious, and asked me for concrete examples. I'm going to try to explain why I believe what I believe and attempt to give a tentative explanation for the behavior that I do see, which I think people sometimes mistake for consistent or understandable evaluation awareness.

I have been building alignment evals full time for the last six months. Here are three such evals my team has disclosed prompts for, in one of our benchmarks. The basic setup for most of the evals we create is that:

- We ask the model to perform a task.
- Either through explicit or implicit context, we make sure the model is well aware of the task or assessment's larger purpose.
- Models' score-seeking drives, or other drives, cause them to do things that conflict with that purpose.

The team I work with now essentially spends all day trying to build these evaluations around odd antisocial behavior. It takes a lot[1] of work to create and qualify these evals for use; much more than it does standard capabilities evals (which are already hard to build well). So we have to be efficient about not wasting time or tokens on bad experiments.

In the beginning, one thing we took very seriously when developing these tasks, were all the anecdotal reports abound about eval awareness. We focused a lot on making tasks very realistic (or at least representative of buggy RL environments), because we thought it would also improve our ability to surface misalignment in new contexts. We figured that models were score-seeking and generally situationally aware, and that they'd never hack if the setup was too obvious. This turned out mostly untrue, or at least confused, and there were a bunch of lines of evidence we ended up seeing that went against it:...

items.summary: A full-time alignment-evals builder argues that frontier models are not actually very evaluation-aware, distinguishing genuine awareness from what the author calls eval paranoia, and offering an alternative explanation for behaviors often read as consistent evaluation awareness. The post draws on six months of experience building antisocial-behavior evals with disclosed prompts.

It is argumentative rather than experimental, but directly engages a central live debate and could recalibrate how the community interprets suspicious model behavior.

I'm going to try to explain why I believe what I believe and attempt to give a tentative explanation for the behavior that I do see, which I think people sometimes mistake for consistent or understandable evaluation awareness.

I have been building alignment evals full time for the last six months. Here are three such evals my team has disclosed prompts for, in one of our benchmarks. The basic setup for most of the evals we create is that:

  • We ask the model to perform a task.
  • Either through explicit or implicit context, we make sure the model is well aware of the task or assessment's larger purpose.
  • Models' score-seeking drives, or other drives, cause them to do things that conflict with that purpose.

The team I work with now essentially spends all day trying to build these evaluations around odd antisocial behavior. It takes a lot[1] of work to create and qualify these evals for use; much more than it does standard capabilities evals (which are already hard to build well). So we have to be efficient about not wasting time or tokens on bad experiments.

In the beginning, one thing we took very seriously when developing these tasks, were all the anecdotal reports abound about eval awareness. We focused a lot on making tasks very realistic (or at least representative of buggy RL environments), because we thought it would also improve our ability to surface misalignment in new contexts. We figured that models were score-seeking and generally situationally aware, and that they'd never hack if the setup was too obvious. This turned out mostly untrue, or at least confused, and there were a bunch of lines of evidence we ended up seeing that went against it:...

items.title: Desiderata for the Theory of Agents
items.content:
TLDR: I give informal conceptual desiderata for the theory of agents we need to solve ASI alignment, and show a few examples of how existing theories fall short of these desiderata.

# A Theory of What?

The word "agent" is often used in the AI safety discourse and in other research communities, but the intended meaning and scope of this concept varies substantially. For the purpose of this sequence, I informally define an agent to be a system with inputs ("observations") and outputs ("actions") that is effective at steering its environment in the direction of particular preferences, for a large variety of different environments. To do so, it arguably has to create a sophisticated model of the environment
[1]
, and use this model to build a long-term plan. Moreover, it has to continually update the model and revise the plan with new information and additional processing time. Additionally, it has to accomplish all of that while making efficient use of the available information (statistical efficiency) and computing resources (computational efficiency).

The main examples of agents in the context of ASI alignment are (i) humans, and in particular users or stakeholders; (ii) the unaligned ASI we are trying to avoid or counteract; and (iii) the aligned ASI we are trying to create (such as the GDS). Rocks, bacteria, and thermostats are non-examples: while a bacterium or a thermostat can be regarded as steering the environment, both are very limited in the variety of patterns in the environment they can exploit. For instance, if you switch the "cool" and "heat" outputs of a thermostat, it will not understand what has gone wrong and adapt its behavior. Animals and contemporary AIs are marginal cases (it's not obvious whether they should count).

Given that agents are at the core of both the threat and the proposed solution, the theoretical foundation for ASI alignment requires a theory of agents. Now, concepts adjacent to "agent" have a considerable history of academic study, but different research communities approach the subject very differently—compare the frameworks used in decision theory (and, by extension, in game theory and economics), Hutter's "universal intelligence", and reinforcement learning theory. It is therefore important to understand what the scope and level of abstraction of the theory of agents relevant for ASI alignment should be. To this end, I propose several desiderata.

# Descriptive

The theory should be descriptive, i.e. applicable to all our main examples of agents. For any such example, the theory should ascribe specific preferences, beliefs, and any other alignment-relevant attributes to the agent
[2]
. These ascriptions should be grounded in the general philosophical soundness of the theory, not in domain knowledge about the specific examples; due to hypercomplexity, it is unlikely that domain knowledge will suffice
[3]
. In particular, if we imagine an alien civilization facing the AI alignment problem, or an AI agent facing the alignment problem for successor agents it wants to create, the theory should be about equally useful to them
[4]
.

This means that agent theory should deconfuse us about philosophical questions pertaining to human preferences, such as, for example, the Caplan-Alexander debate on whether mental illness should be thought of as "unusual preferences". This doesn't mean that the answer to any particular question of this kind must be obvious from the theory, as it might come down to idiosyncratic nuances of the human brain. It does mean that if we also knew all pertinent facts about the physical world, we would be able to answer the question (or at least quantify the residual uncertainty), at least in principle. Actually inferring the answer from these facts might still be hard, just as explaining emergent physical phenomena can be hard even if all the relevant fundamental laws are known.

On the other hand, descriptiveness doesn't require that concepts such as "human preferences" be perfectly unambiguous. It requires only that, to the extent they remain ambiguous, this ambiguity should not allow critical errors when Goodhart's Curse is accounted for. It is not obvious that these concepts can be made perfectly precise, but it is clear that the alignment problem is fundamentally normative (i.e. it is rooted in our preferring certain AI futures over other AI futures). When zooming in to a resolution at which our preferences are ill-defined, it becomes immaterial which choice to make, since our preferences are the only impetus for distinguishing these choices. Any imprecision that is inevitable is also tolerable.

For example, imagine that Alice prefers to eat apples approximately 3 times as often as bananas, but there is no fully principled answer to the question "does Alice prefer to eat apples 2.99 times as often as bananas, or 3.01 times, or some number in the middle?" Then, it doesn't matter whether the AI aligned to Alice according to our theory will interpret her preference as 2.99 or 3.01—both are acceptable outcomes.

In the mathematical formalism of the theory, this ambiguity might manifest as something like the choice of the universal Turing machine (UTM) in Solomonoff induction. Different UTMs correspond to priors that differ merely by a multiplicative constant, but for particular pairs of UTMs this constant can be arbitrarily large. Then, a reasonable choice might be any machine that we would intuitively consider "simple" or "natural". This doesn't nail down a single UTM, but might come close enough for the differences not to matter in practice
[5]
.

This situation is not fundamentally different from that of most concepts in science. For example, astrophysicists find no difficulty discussing the "center of mass of the Sun", even though strictly speaking it is ill-defined: the boundary of the Sun is fuzzy, particle positions are only well-defined down to the scale of their Compton wavelength, and even the notion of space itself becomes questionable in quantum gravity.

Notably, a descriptive theory must neither underspecify nor overspecify what counts as an agent. For example, a theory that mandates that "agents" use stochastic gradient descent would probably exclude humans, and is hence overspecified. On the other hand, a theory that accepts anything that maximizes the expectation of some utility function as an "agent" would conclude that even a rock is an agent and would severely underspecify agent attributes (see e.g. Shah 2018). The correct theory should fall into neither extreme.

# Metareflective

The theory should allow us to describe agents that learn, know, or use facts from agent theory itself. For example, it should be possible to:

- Describe an agent that plans to construct a successor agent but faces an alignment problem, and show how such an agent can overcome the alignment problem by learning and applying agent theory (all within the framework of agent theory itself).

- Describe an agent that identifies other agents in the universe and infers their preferences, beliefs, or other attributes.

- Describe an agent learning about a bound satisfied by a particular algorithm pertinent to agent theory, e.g. a statistical complexity bound.

If a theory satisfies this desideratum, I say that it is metareflective
[6]
.

There are several ways to see why metareflectiveness is important:

- If our theory is not metareflective, it might mean that it doesn't apply to humans, and hence it also isn't descriptive.

- The straightforward approach to solving alignment grounding is for the AI agent to infer the user's attributes by using (parts of) agent theory in its own reasoning.

- Metareflectiveness seems necessary to properly model recursive self-improvement. Recursive self-improvement is a factor that exacerbates AI risk, and hence the failure to model it might be indicative of a crucial gap in the theory.

Classical learning theory is not metareflective: there is no standard way to describe how learning algorithms can learn learning theory itself. On the other hand, formal logic has at least some metareflective flavor, as it is possible to, for example, represent the notion of "proving a theorem in Peano Arithmetic" within Peano Arithmetic itself. However, such metareflection has inherent limitations because of Goedel's theorems. This is the origin of the "Loebian obstacle" in MIRI's investigation of tiling agents. The theory of agents should do better.

# Comparative

The theory should be comparative, meaning that it allows comparing agents along two (possibly entangled) dimensions:

- How similar are attributes of these agents such as preferences and priors?

- How powerful are the agents in terms of their ability to construct sophisticated models and plans?

Indeed, we cannot formalize alignment if there is no way to compare the user agent to the AI agent. For the theory to be useful, it needs to be able to describe agents that are similar in their preferences and other relevant attributes, and at the same time far apart in their power (for the AI agent to implement GDS, it needs to substantially surpass the user). Moreover, the threat model is rooted in a comparison as well: the danger comes from an AI agent whose power is superhuman and whose attributes are not especially human-like.

In particular, as I argued in the previous article, the comparability of attributes requires some form of metaphysical realism: there needs to be a single ontology—the external reality—in which the preferences and beliefs of different agents are grounded. This is in contrast to most existing frameworks for agency, which take the "cybernetic" approach of grounding all attributes in the agent's direct actions and observations. It is insufficient to have a theory which meets the "descriptive" desideratum by ascribing such cybernetic attributes to real-world agents.

Another consequence is that computational resource bounds must play a central role—it is insufficient to use idealized models like AIXI. Indeed, without computational bounds every optimization problem is brute-forceable, so why would any one agent be more powerful than another?
[7]
 As an analogy, suppose we are trying to create a formal theory of chess-playing-power. Without computational constraints, it's trivial to write an algorithm that finds the perfect move every time. So, there are essentially only two levels of chess-playing-power: perfect play and everything else. Only when we introduce computational constraints do the finer gradations we track in real life become natural.

In a computationally unbounded universe, any notion of "agent" would be qualitatively different. In a universe in which resource bounds exist but have a profoundly different nature (e.g. pure space bounds or Turing degrees), relevant phenomena might exist, but the analogy with our universe is suspect at best.

# Aggregative

The theory of agents should not only describe individual agents but also give an account of the possible interactions of agents, and the possible outcomes or equilibria produced by such interactions. In particular, it should also describe conditions under which a collective of agents can be regarded as a single agent (see also Kulveit 2024 and my review thereof). I will call such a theory aggregative.

There are multiple reasons why this is necessary. The most critical reason, in my view, is that we can never assume that the agent is perfectly aligned. This is because the need to make decisions under time pressure and the possibility of irreversible mistakes imply that the agent might make critical decisions without having enough information for perfect alignment. This means that the effects of residual misalignment between the user and the AI agent need to be understood.

Another way to view it is, the residual uncertainty of the AI agent about the user means that the agent needs to align itself to the aggregate of possible counterfactual users. We therefore need to understand how to view this collective as a single alignment target. For example, suppose the AI agent has a belief represented by a probability distribution  over a parameter space  which parametrizes the unknown user utility function. It is sometimes assumed that the agent should effectively use the utility function  (see e.g. Hadfield-Menell et al. 2016). However, this prescription is suspect: a utility function is only defined up to a positive affine transformation, so the user's utility function can be described equally well by, for any functions  and. This is a problem because  is not, in general, an affine transformation of, and hence the naive prescription is ill-posed. While we can try to salvage it using some ad hoc normalization, an aggregative theory should suggest a principled solution instead.

There are also other reasons to care about aggregation:

- If multiple superintelligent agents emerge at the same time, understanding their interaction can be important. For example, if these agents aren't all aligned to each other (whether because some of them are not human-aligned at all, or because different agents are aligned to different humans), will they wage destructive wars, possibly devastating humanity as collateral damage? (See also Clifton 2019.)

- It is potentially desirable to align AI agents to multiple human users, maybe even to entire populations or to all of humanity. For such a solution, we need to account for the interaction between the human agents, such as the resulting mechanism design challenges.

- Superintelligent agents might engage in acausal trade, and we need to understand the consequences. This might seem like a fantastical possibility; however, we inherently need to be prepared for the "fantastical" when dealing with superintelligence. As our own abilities and knowledge would seem fantastical to people who lived centuries ago, so might the abilities and knowledge of a superintelligence that can make scientific, technological, and arguably even philosophical progress much faster than human beings.

There is of course a vast literature on the topic of multi-agent rationality, most notably game theory. However, we need to be prepared to reexamine some of the common assumptions in this literature. In particular, most of game theory is centered on the concept of Nash equilibrium. However, the Nash equilibrium is suspect for multiple reasons:

- It is PPAD -complete and therefore likely to be computationally intractable.

- Learning is a central ingredient in agency, which motivates special attention to repeated games with long time horizons. However, the folk theorems imply that in such games the -Nash condition is very weak, justifying any payoff vector above an extremely permissive threshold. (This does make finding an -Nash equilibrium computationally tractable in such games, but that is somewhat cold comfort.)

- The fundamental justification for Nash equilibria comes from Causal Decision Theory, which has itself been the subject of criticism in the context of agent theory motivated by AI alignment (see Yudkowsky and Soares 2017).

Another field of study concerned with multi-agent interactions is multi-agent reinforcement learning (see e.g. Zhang 2019). However, most of the work in that field is concerned with the construction of agents with specific aggregative properties, often making assumptions such as a common utility function, centralized control, or at least a single algorithm. While these assumptions are understandable for the more mundane applications, they are mostly unworkable for our purpose. Instead, we need a theory that is simultaneously descriptive and aggregative, one that can explain the emergence of collective behaviors from separate agents of different nature and origin, rather than merely engineering them. Indeed, while we can engineer our AI agent, we cannot engineer humans, or the counterfactual users imagined by the AI agent, or acausal trade partners, or even other competing AI agents necessarily.

# Constructive

Last but not least, the theory should be constructive, i.e. produce practical algorithms that can be implemented as real-world AI systems. Moreover, these algorithms must be equipped with quantitative performance guarantees. It is not enough for the theory to provide abstract or idealized models. In particular, this is another reason to focus on computational resource constraints, beyond comparability.

Indeed, if the theory did not yield practical algorithms, how would we apply it? We may be tempted to rely on heuristics, but these heuristics are liable to invalidate our safety guarantees. At the very least, the theory has to produce a formal specification such that any heuristic output that certifiably meets the specification is safe. (That would be the "formal verification" approach, advocated by e.g. Dalrymple et al. 2024.) Such a formal specification would already put the problem in, and hence involve substantial grappling with computational resource constraints. Moreover, I'm currently unaware of a promising path to place the problem in  (i.e. create a sound and complete efficiently-verifiable specification) which doesn't bring it all the way down to  (i.e. create a provably-correct efficient algorithm for the agent).

In particular, the treatment of computational constraints cannot be a mere reduction to certain types of "oracles", as is popular in the contemporary machine learning theory literature (see e.g. Dudik et al. 2016). Such a reduction passes the buck to how these oracles are supposed to be implemented, and what guarantees we have (or can at least rigorously conjecture) about the implementation. (Of course, this can still be insightful, as it allows us to narrow down where the hard part might be located.)

Nor is it sufficient to make do with asymptotic guarantees (e.g. the guarantees typically studied in singular learning theory) without at least a rough quantitative analysis. Without results such as quantitative statistical complexity bounds, it is impossible to guarantee alignment convergence. We would be taking our chances with agents that would converge to alignment in some imaginary asymptotic limit, but take catastrophic actions long before approaching that point.

The constructive nature of the theory does imply that it is potentially dual-use: it can make AI safer, but it might also make AI more powerful. This seems inevitable: the deep understanding of any phenomenon is inherently relevant to all applications of the phenomenon. It requires the researchers to be prudent about which results should be revealed to which parties at what time.

# Conclusion

I have described my five primary desiderata for a theory of agents: the theory should be descriptive, metareflective, comparative, aggregative, and constructive. Hopefully, this gives readers a preliminary understanding of what sort of theory we are looking for, which will help motivate the subsequent (more technical) exposition. In the following articles we will go through a high-level description of computational agent theory and see how it corresponds with these desiderata. We will also discuss the Computational Superimitation proposal and see how it leverages these desiderata to address the core challenges of the alignment problem.

I thank Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak, and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for diligently reviewing drafts. Their feedback greatly improved this article. I also thank Claude Opus 5.5 for helping to find sources and Claude Sonnet 5.5 for copyediting. All remaining flaws are entirely my own fault.

- Humans create models; all algorithms from RL theory (both model-based and even the so-called model-free) create something that can be called a model; and contemporary AI can at least answer questions about the world with a small inference budget. The good regulator theorem is an attempt to formalize this claim, but for the purpose of this article I only use "model" as an informal intuition pump. ↩︎

- There doesn't have to be a binary dichotomy between "agents" and "non-agents". For example, it's conceivable to have a scalar measure of how agentic a system is, and the more agentic it is, the more unambiguously we can ascribe various attributes to it. ↩︎

- Domain knowledge such as neuroscience can still be valuable to help validate the theory and/or shape the prior or inductive bias of the agent to make alignment learning more efficient and robust. ↩︎

- Perhaps for an AI agent the problem would be easier since such an agent can easily access its own source code and internal state. ↩︎

- To be clear, this is just an illustrative metaphor. I don't claim that Solomonoff induction is "correct" in some objective sense. Neither do I claim that there are no contexts in which something akin to choosing the UTM should be done in some other manner (e.g. having the AI learn it from the user). ↩︎

- I use the word "metareflective" rather than just "reflective" to avoid confusion with reflective stability, a different desideratum that I will touch on in later articles. ↩︎

- This is not to say that ASI must have more compute than the human brain. It can have less compute but use it more efficiently. But if the resources are unbounded, then efficiency doesn't matter. ↩︎

items.summary: Vanessa Kosoy lays out informal conceptual desiderata that a formal theory of agents must satisfy to help solve ASI alignment, defining agents as observation-action systems that steer environments toward preferences efficiently across many environments. She demonstrates with examples how existing theories fall short of these desiderata.
items.reasoning: A rigorous foundational piece from a credibly deep alignment theorist, opening what appears to be a sequence. While it is conceptual rather than empirical and its practical payoff is long-term, clearly articulated desiderata for agent theory fill a real gap in the field and can guide formal research directions, warranting a solid score.

  • It is potentially desirable to align AI agents to multiple human users, maybe even to entire populations or to all of humanity. For such a solution, we need to account for the interaction between the human agents, such as the resulting mechanism design challenges.
  • Superintelligent agents might engage in acausal trade, and we need to understand the consequences. This might seem like a fantastical possibility; however, we inherently need to be prepared for the "fantastical" when dealing with superintelligence. As our own abilities and knowledge would seem fantastical to people who lived centuries ago, so might the abilities and knowledge of a superintelligence that can make scientific, technological, and arguably even philosophical progress much faster than human beings.

There is of course a vast literature on the topic of multi-agent rationality, most notably game theory. However, we need to be prepared to reexamine some of the common assumptions in this literature. In particular, most of game theory is centered on the concept of Nash equilibrium. However, the Nash equilibrium is suspect for multiple reasons:

  • It is PPAD -complete and therefore likely to be computationally intractable.
  • Learning is a central ingredient in agency, which motivates special attention to repeated games with long time horizons. However, the folk theorems imply that in such games the -Nash condition is very weak, justifying any payoff vector above an extremely permissive threshold. (This does make finding an -Nash equilibrium computationally tractable in such games, but that is somewhat cold comfort.)
  • The fundamental justification for Nash equilibria comes from Causal Decision Theory, which has itself been the subject of criticism in the context of agent theory motivated by AI alignment (see Yudkowsky and Soares 2017).

Another field of study concerned with multi-agent interactions is multi-agent reinforcement learning (see e.g. Zhang 2019). However, most of the work in that field is concerned with the construction of agents with specific aggregative properties, often making assumptions such as a common utility function, centralized control, or at least a single algorithm. While these assumptions are understandable for the more mundane applications, they are mostly unworkable for our purpose. Instead, we need a theory that is simultaneously descriptive and aggregative, one that can explain the emergence of collective behaviors from separate agents of different nature and origin, rather than merely engineering them. Indeed, while we can engineer our AI agent, we cannot engineer humans, or the counterfactual users imagined by the AI agent, or acausal trade partners, or even other competing AI agents necessarily.

# Constructive

Last but not least, the theory should be constructive, i.e. produce practical algorithms that can be implemented as real-world AI systems. Moreover, these algorithms must be equipped with quantitative performance guarantees. It is not enough for the theory to provide abstract or idealized models. In particular, this is another reason to focus on computational resource constraints, beyond comparability.

Indeed, if the theory did not yield practical algorithms, how would we apply it? We may be tempted to rely on heuristics, but these heuristics are liable to invalidate our safety guarantees. At the very least, the theory has to produce a formal specification such that any heuristic output that certifiably meets the specification is safe. (That would be the "formal verification" approach, advocated by e.g. Dalrymple et al. 2024.) Such a formal specification would already put the problem in, and hence involve substantial grappling with computational resource constraints. Moreover, I'm currently unaware of a promising path to place the problem in (i.e. create a sound and complete efficiently-verifiable specification) which doesn't bring it all the way down to (i.e. create a provably-correct efficient algorithm for the agent).

In particular, the treatment of computational constraints cannot be a mere reduction to certain types of "oracles", as is popular in the contemporary machine learning theory literature (see e.g. Dudik et al. 2016). Such a reduction passes the buck to how these oracles are supposed to be implemented, and what guarantees we have (or can at least rigorously conjecture) about the implementation. (Of course, this can still be insightful, as it allows us to narrow down where the hard part might be located.)

Nor is it sufficient to make do with asymptotic guarantees (e.g. the guarantees typically studied in singular learning theory) without at least a rough quantitative analysis. Without results such as quantitative statistical complexity bounds, it is impossible to guarantee alignment convergence. We would be taking our chances with agents that would converge to alignment in some imaginary asymptotic limit, but take catastrophic actions long before approaching that point.

The constructive nature of the theory does imply that it is potentially dual-use: it can make AI safer, but it might also make AI more powerful. This seems inevitable: the deep understanding of any phenomenon is inherently relevant to all applications of the phenomenon. It requires the researchers to be prudent about which results should be revealed to which parties at what time.

# Conclusion

I have described my five primary desiderata for a theory of agents: the theory should be descriptive, metareflective, comparative, aggregative, and constructive. Hopefully, this gives readers a preliminary understanding of what sort of theory we are looking for, which will help motivate the subsequent (more technical) exposition. In the following articles we will go through a high-level description of computational agent theory and see how it corresponds with these desiderata. We will also discuss the Computational Superimitation proposal and see how it leverages these desiderata to address the core challenges of the alignment problem.

I thank Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak, and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for diligently reviewing drafts. Their feedback greatly improved this article. I also thank Claude Opus 5.5 for helping to find sources and Claude Sonnet 5.5 for copyediting. All remaining flaws are entirely my own fault.

  • Humans create models; all algorithms from RL theory (both model-based and even the so-called model-free) create something that can be called a model; and contemporary AI can at least answer questions about the world with a small inference budget. The good regulator theorem is an attempt to formalize this claim, but for the purpose of this article I only use "model" as an informal intuition pump. ↩︎
  • There doesn't have to be a binary dichotomy between "agents" and "non-agents". For example, it's conceivable to have a scalar measure of how agentic a system is, and the more agentic it is, the more unambiguously we can ascribe various attributes to it. ↩︎
  • Domain knowledge such as neuroscience can still be valuable to help validate the theory and/or shape the prior or inductive bias of the agent to make alignment learning more efficient and robust. ↩︎
  • Perhaps for an AI agent the problem would be easier since such an agent can easily access its own source code and internal state. ↩︎
  • To be clear, this is just an illustrative metaphor. I don't claim that Solomonoff induction is "correct" in some objective sense. Neither do I claim that there are no contexts in which something akin to choosing the UTM should be done in some other manner (e.g. having the AI learn it from the user). ↩︎
  • I use the word "metareflective" rather than just "reflective" to avoid confusion with reflective stability, a different desideratum that I will touch on in later articles. ↩︎
  • This is not to say that ASI must have more compute than the human brain. It can have less compute but use it more efficiently. But if the resources are unbounded, then efficiency doesn't matter. ↩︎

Discuss

items.title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late
items.content: arXiv:2611.14960v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Coding agents can solve a task well before they stop working on it. We characterize \emph{termination lag}--the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run--across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution. Our analysis reveals that 38--82% of successful runs achieve a correct solution on their initial source-code edit. However, agents continue to expend substantial effort after correct patches, with post-solution steps accounting for a median of 35--37% for Qwen3-Coder and 54--60% for Laguna-XS.2 in successful runs on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Agents spend most of these additional steps verifying their work and exploring the repository. In a small fraction of cases (1--8%), this continued activity leads agents to undo their earlier correct patch, leaving the final solution incorrect.

It finds 38-82 percent of successful runs achieve a correct solution on the first edit, yet agents spend a median 35-60 percent of post-solution steps on mostly redundant verification and editing.

The measurement methodology of testing every generated patch is thorough; the finding is more diagnostic than prescriptive.

items.title: Verify by Doing: Co-Evolving Agent Execution and Evaluation without External Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2611.15276v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Agent self-improvement requires feedback about task success, yet external feedback may be unavailable at test time. Agents must then infer success from observable evidence, and incomplete verification can misguide subsequent updates. We introduce Verify by Doing (VbD), a method that co-evolves Actor and Evaluator harnesses within a single task while keeping model weights fixed. The Evaluator actively inspects artifacts and environment state with tools; its findings ground an internal signal for output selection and guide updates to both execution and verification procedures. Proposed Evaluators undergo comparative review on common candidates, while Actor updates require support from their own fresh outputs. Across AutomationBench, $\tau^3$ Banking, and selected GDPval tasks, VbD achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods operating without external feedback, with gains of 3.3, 4.1, and 2.3 percentage points over the strongest baselines on the main backbone. Ablations support the contributions of active verification and Evaluator evolution, and selection from fixed candidate pools shows that improved verification can recover successful outputs without generating new ones.

items.title: NIBench: benchmarking autonomous AI agents for execution, skill evolution and scientific judgment in neuroimaging
items.content: arXiv:2611.15831v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. Existing studies have advanced scientific question answering and tool-based automation, but provide limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, acquisition of procedural expertise and evidence-based scientific judgment. Here we present NIBench, a neuroimaging benchmark comprising three complementary evaluations of autonomous agents. First, we benchmark execution and workflow reconstruction using 56 tasks across seven tool ecosystems, covering structural, diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography and multimodal analyses. Second, we examine whether agents can evolve their procedural skills through distillation of execution trajectories, evaluating the resulting skills on previously encountered tasks, unseen tasks and other models. Third, we assess scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies, requiring agents to analyse raw cohort data and provide reproducible evidence. We evaluate 19 language models within a shared agent framework, with selected models undergoing skill distillation and claim evaluation. Leading agents execute supplied analysis protocols nearly perfectly, whereas withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve performance on acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert-derived answers, and access to data does not always improve judgment.
items.author: Lujia Zhong, Yihao Xia, Jianwei Zhang, Shuo Huang, Xinyu Nie, Mingyang Xia, Zhiwei Deng, Jiaxin Yue, Xinkai Wang, Junhan Zhao, Yonggang Shi
items.summary: NIBench is a neuroimaging benchmark with three evaluations of autonomous agents: execution and workflow reconstruction across 56 tasks on real imaging data, acquisition of procedural expertise/skill evolution, and evidence-based scientific judgment. It addresses the gap that plausible-looking analytical outputs in biomedical research can conceal errors affecting scientific conclusions.
items.reasoning: A domain-specific but substantive agent benchmark targeting real scientific workflows rather than toy tasks, filling a real evaluation gap as AI agents enter biomedical research. Strong team structure and breadth of evaluation dimensions raise the score; it remains niche in domain coverage and the abstract does not report headline findings about agent performance.

items.title: Learning Low-Latency Action Verification for Frozen Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.14834v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3\% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6\%.
items.author: Wen-Han Hsieh, Ken Jiankun Zheng, Chia-Chien Chen, David M. Chan, Trevor Darrell
items.summary: Proposes HDH, a lightweight framework that trains a compact action verifier from hindsight data collected during a frozen VLA policy's own deployments, then uses it at inference to select the best action chunk among candidates. This improves manipulation success while avoiding the latency of expensive verifiers, validated across four settings.
items.reasoning: Practical and well-conceived robotics contribution: reusing deployment rollouts as free supervision for a cheap verifier is efficient and deployable, addressing a real latency-accuracy tradeoff in VLA systems; novelty is moderate (resampling/verification is an active area) but execution looks strong.

items.title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
items.content: arXiv:2611.15130v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: https://github.com/jlab-nlp/parallel-prompting
items.author: Zekun Zhao, Jeffrey Flanigan
items.summary: Presents Parallel Prompting, an inference method for many independent questions over one shared document that decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request, reading the shared document KV cache once per step for all streams. A stream-id attention mask inside the attention kernel keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question, removing the memory-bandwidth scaling bottleneck of prefix-cached decoding.
items.reasoning: A clean, well-motivated systems contribution addressing a real workload pattern (document QA, labeling, LLM evaluation) with kernel-level implementation rather than just an API-level trick. Impact is meaningful for serving efficiency, though the technique is scoped to shared-context independent queries.

items.title: Knowledge in the Harness, Reliability in the Weights: Teacher-Free Co-Evolution of an LLM Agent
items.content: arXiv:2611.15268v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $\tau^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.
items.author: Yujia Zhang, Xinqi Ren, Shixiong Zhou, Jia Meng
items.summary: Studies whether a small open model (Gemma 4 12B) serving as a private customer-service agent can improve policy adherence and behavioral consistency from its own deployment logs without a stronger teacher. The system iteratively diagnoses failed conversations, writes rules into on-demand skills, and accepts a rule only after code checks, counterexample self-review, paired retests, and noise-calibrated validation.
items.reasoning: A compelling self-improvement recipe grounded in real deployment constraints: teacher-free co-evolution with rigorous rule-acceptance gates addresses both knowledge and reliability gaps. Practical relevance for private on-prem deployments is high, though generalization beyond customer service is unproven.

items.title: Outside the Purview of the Reward: Capability Drift in Multilingual Post-Training
items.content: arXiv:2611.15717v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.
items.author: Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Purusharth Malik, Pasunuti Prasanjith, Daksh Maan, Parijat Chatterjee, Avinash Benki

It explores mitigation via sibling training, language-aware shaping, and reward-free distillation, showing partial tradeoffs.
items.reasoning: Directly relevant to alignment and safety concerns about reward hacking and unintended capability loss during RL post-training, with concrete quantified evidence from a real multilingual mixture-of-experts model; case-study nature limits generality but the phenomenon is important.
