items.title: When Does Causality Help in Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection?
items.content: arXiv:2611.15073v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Causality-aware scoring is common in multivariate time-series anomaly detection, yet the literature rarely states when it helps. Holding one causality-guided autoencoder (DeCauAE) fixed, we vary graph quality, anomaly type and protocol against ground truth. Graph quality fixes the payoff: on a twenty-variable DAG the gain over a graph-free autoencoder decays as the graph is corrupted. Anomaly type fixes the target: the structural factor lifts window F1 from 0.800 to 0.976 where anomalies break conditional structure, and its advantage vanishes below a break severity s 0.3. Protocol fixes the ranking: point-adjusted F1 lets a random score match the full model, while range-aware VUS separates the autoencoder family from the classical baselines. On real benchmarks the causal module pays only where density makes a system eligible and cross-subsample reproducibility selects entities inside it; enabling it everywhere costs 0.012 VUS-ROC. The structural factor also transfers to classical detectors .
items.author: Long Zhang, Wei Huang, Aishui Rao, Jian Hu, Binxiang Wu, Jie Li, Chen Gong, Linxi Feng
items.summary: Provides a controlled analysis of when causality-aware scoring helps in multivariate time-series anomaly detection, varying causal-graph quality, anomaly type, and evaluation protocol while holding a causality-guided autoencoder fixed. Results show gains decay with graph corruption, depend on structural break severity, and that point-adjusted F1 can mask differences that range-aware VUS reveals.
items.reasoning: Valuable clarifying study in a noisy literature: it states precise conditions under which a popular technique helps and exposes protocol artifacts (point-adjusted F1 inflation). Rigorous empirical design, though scoped to one model family.

items.title: Regret Bounds for Quantum Linear Bandits
items.content: arXiv:2611.15237v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study $d$-dimensional quantum linear bandits with bounded rewards, where the learner selects an action and queries its quantum reward oracle or its inverse in each round. For general action sets, existing algorithms achieve regret $O(d^{3/2}\operatorname{polylog}(T))$ over $T$ rounds. Prior work established a lower bound of $\Omega(d\log(1+T/d))$, leaving open whether the $d^{3/2}$ dependence in the upper bound is necessary. We resolve this question by proving a minimax lower bound of $\Omega(d^{3/2}\log(1+T/d^{3/2}))$. To prove this result, we construct a family of hard instances in which the reward gap of each action is proportional to its squared distance from the optimal action. We establish a posterior Fisher information bound for adaptive quantum queries with quantum memory, relating the information acquired about the optimal direction to the regret incurred. Viewing each selected action as an estimate of the optimal direction, we use a matrix Cram\'er--Rao argument to derive a lower bound on expected regret. When the action set is fixed and has size $K$, we propose two phased elimination algorithms, Soft-G-Elim and QG-Elim. We adapt quantum phase estimation to construct SoftQME, a mean estimator with small bias and controlled tails. Soft-G-Elim estimates the mean reward of every surviving action from independent SoftQME outputs on the support of an experimental design. Controlling the bias and fluctuations of these estimates yields regret $O(d\log T\log(dT)\sqrt{\log(KT)})$, reducing the $\log(KT)\log\log(dT)$ factor in the previous regret bound to $\sqrt{\log(KT)}$. QG-Elim further reduces this factor to $\min\{\sqrt{\log(KT)},\sqrt d\}$.
items.author: Maoli Liu, Zhuohua Li, John C. S. Lui
items.summary: Resolves an open question in quantum linear bandits by proving a minimax lower bound of Omega(d^1.5 log T), matching existing upper bounds, via a construction of hard instances with gap proportional to squared distance from the optimal action. This shows the d^1.5 dependence is unavoidable, closing the gap between known lower and upper bounds.
items.reasoning: Clean theoretical contribution that settles an open problem with matching minimax bounds; strong rigor and novelty, but relevance is confined to the quantum bandits theory community.

items.title: Overcoming the Resolution Limit: Significance-Aware Regularization for Intersectional Fairness
items.content: arXiv:2611.15427v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Intersectional fairness requires evaluating models across fine-grained subgroups. However, as group definitions become more granular, the sample size per subgroup shrinks, causing fairness estimates to become increasingly unstable. Existing in-processing methods are certainty-blind: they penalize observed disparities without distinguishing statistically certified unfairness from sampling noise. This leads to fairness overfitting, where models sacrifice utility to "fix" spurious disparities in sparse regimes. To address this, we introduce the significant-excess metric family, a continuous, uncertainty-aware fairness score that measures only the portion of a subgroup's disparity exceeding what sampling variation can explain at a specific confidence level. Building on this metric, we propose SAFER (Significance-Aware Fairness Regularizer), a differentiable in-processing method that gates fairness penalties using a soft-count likelihood-ratio evidence statistic. SAFER satisfies a provable safety property: when every subgroup disparity lies well below the gate threshold, the unconstrained optimum is nearly stationary for SAFER. At that optimum, the back-propagated contribution of its significance-gated component is exponentially small, and the additional fairness contribution comes from a small ungated term with a fixed weight. Mechanism ablations across three benchmark datasets and purpose-built stress variants show that removing any component of SAFER (threshold smoothing, the significance gate, or a dense-tail term) produces the failure the theory predicts on at least one stress variant. In sparse intersectional settings, SAFER achieves a better fairness-utility Pareto frontier than the baseline methods, and it preserves utility when certified unfairness is absent.
items.author: Antonio Ferrara, Andr\'e Panisson, Francesco Cozzi, Alan Perotti, Francesco Bonchi
items.summary: Identifies fairness overfitting in intersectional fairness: fine-grained subgroup estimates become unstable at small sample sizes, and certainty-blind in-processing methods penalize sampling noise. It introduces a significant-excess metric family that measures only disparity exceeding sampling variation at a given confidence level, and builds a regularization scheme around it.
items.reasoning: Statistically principled fix to a real and recognized problem in intersectional fairness; conceptually clean contribution with relevance to fairness-aware ML practice.

items.title: Continual Event Recognition for Autonomous Optical Network Monitoring
items.content: arXiv:2611.16038v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autonomous optical networks require monitoring systems capable of adapting to evolving disturbances without repeated retraining or service interruption. We propose a continual event recognition framework for state-of-polarization (SOP)-based optical monitoring based on prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot prototype registration. The framework supports recognition of known disturbances, detection and integration of novel events, and investigates whether overlapping disturbances can be inferred through compositional reasoning from existing prototypes. Experimental validation on a 2600-km ROADM-based optical testbed demonstrates 99.82% closed-set recognition accuracy, successful adaptation to novel disturbances without encoder retraining, and reveals that overlapping optical disturbances exhibit varying degrees of latent compositionality. While some overlaps can be recognized in a zero-shot manner through prototype composition, others require explicit few-shot registration. These results establish continual event recognition as a promising paradigm for future autonomous optical network monitoring systems.
items.author: Khouloud Abdelli
items.summary: This paper proposes a continual learning framework for recognizing disturbances in polarization-based optical network monitoring, combining prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot registration of new event classes. items.reasoning: Solid domain-specific contribution with real hardware testbed validation, which is rarer than simulation-only work. The continual/open-set combination is sensible but the impact is largely confined to optical networking and applied ML rather than general machine learning.

items.title: Manifold Attracting Flow Matching: Physics-Constrained Sampling via Continuous Geometric Dynamics
items.content: arXiv:2611.16677v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generating scientific data under previously unseen equality constraints requires satisfying the prescribed constraints without destroying the physical structure learned from data. Existing inference-time approaches often enforce physical constraints by repeatedly correcting predicted endpoints, but such discrete corrections can distort learned generative structure and introduce unstable feedback. In this work, we propose Manifold Attracting Flow Matching (MAFM), which continuously evolves a persistent anchor through an ODE whose dynamics drive it analytically toward the constraint manifold. Specifically, its geometric correction preserves model-guided tangent motion while prescribing the normal motion to contract constraint violations toward the manifold. This construction separates model tracking from constraint attraction and provides theoretical guarantees for residual contraction and local feedback stabilization. Experiments across geometric and partial differential equation benchmarks demonstrate improved generation quality over variant constraint-guided baselines while maintaining low constraint residuals. MAFM provides a flexible framework for coordinating learned physical structure and explicit constraints through controllable sampling dynamics, without retraining the underlying generative model.
items.author: Guanyu Chen, Jinchen Wang, Shengze Xu, Xingyu Ren, Tieyong Zeng, Antonios Armaou, Dong Ni
items.summary: MAFM enforces equality constraints in scientific data generation by continuously evolving a persistent anchor through an ODE that drives samples toward the constraint manifold, rather than repeatedly correcting endpoints discretely. The geometric correction preserves model-guided tangent motion while contracting constraint violations.
items.reasoning: A principled and technically elegant way to inject physical constraints into flow matching at inference time, avoiding the instability of discrete projection; relevant to the growing intersection of generative models and scientific simulation.

items.title: Near-Optimal Regret for Oracle-Efficient Adversarial Contextual Bandits
items.content: arXiv:2611.17109v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study contextual bandits with $K$ actions, a class of $N$ policies, and i.i.d.\ contexts from a distribution that the learner can sample. For any sequence of loss functions fixed before play, we give an oracle-efficient algorithm with expected regret $O(\sqrt{KT\log(2N)}\,\log(2KT))$ against the best policy in hindsight on the realized contexts. This improves the $T^{2/3}$ dependence on the horizon in prior oracle-efficient bounds and achieves the optimal regret rate in this setting up to logarithmic factors.   Our algorithm perturbs policy scores using a Poisson sample of auxiliary contexts. At each sampled context, the perturbation assigned to an action is a Laplace noise draw multiplied by a scale specific to that context and action. We show that choosing these scales to minimize a convex objective determined by past observations yields the stated regret bound. We further approximate the minimizing scales by projected stochastic gradient descent using only an exact offline cost-sensitive optimization oracle that returns the optimum value. Since the table of scales can be large, the algorithm represents the SGD iterates implicitly by storing the random draws that determine each update and evaluates the scales only at queried contexts. items.title: Physically Interpretable Basin Selection in Discrete-Variable Origami Design
items.content: arXiv:2611.17196v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Automatic differentiation has enabled rapid progress on continuous-variable mechanical design problems, but gradient-based optimization still struggles with discrete variables. The standard approach is to optimize using a continuous relaxation of the choices, then commit to the nearest discrete design at the end. Why this procedure selects unfavorable basins is poorly understood. Here, we introduce a practical, interpretable design problem inspired by origami, in which automatic differentiation is used to design shapes with a target functional behavior. Each origami sheet has a fixed geometry, and a bilevel optimization framework tunes which one of four discrete hinge types to place at each fold. Baseline gradient-based design settles into basins with a large discretization gap: relaxed optimization solves 97% of runs, but the final, discrete solutions succeed only half the time. We find that the gap can be relieved with a surprisingly simple modification. An initialization prior uniformly biased toward the stiff, flat hinge option boosts the final solve fraction from 49% to 69%. Applying the prior adds no additional compute and leaves the optimization process unchanged. Compared to the baseline, sheets produced with the prior have greater geometric compatibility and mechanical stiffness. Directly penalizing frustration and floppiness in the outer loss function produces an even greater improvement than the prior does, raising the solve fraction to 78% and indicating that these properties help distinguish the unfavorable basins. Our results demonstrate that loss landscapes for mechanical design can have physically meaningful basins that are not robust to discretization and cause solves to fail. Targeting these basins' physical signatures, even with just an initialization bias, helps avoid them.

items.title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
items.content: arXiv:2611.17329v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.

This matters because deep RL for finance typically ignores rule compliance, limiting real-world deployment under formal investment policy statements.

items.title: Arbor: When Labels Are Not Coarsened at Random
items.content: arXiv:2611.15311v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Merging datasets labelled at different levels of a taxonomy leaves some images with only a coarse label, and some classes with no fine-grained label at all. Standard training scores a coarse label by the total probability of the classes under it. Coarse labels name superclasses, and the standard objective is exact only when every class within a superclass is equally likely to receive a coarse label. We call a class novel if it is never labelled finely, and known otherwise. A novel class violates the assumption, and the classifier assigns its images to a known sibling. We propose Arbor, which models how labels become coarse. In each superclass with a novel class, Arbor adds a virtual novel class, and a logistic gate divides the superclass's probability between it and the known classes. The gate is trained with the likelihood of the observed labels under this model, the coarsening likelihood. We prove that at its population optimum the gate equals the Elkan-Noto correction of positive-unlabelled learning, and show that training the correction into the classifier improves on applying it after training. Across Cars, CUB and Aircraft with 90% coarse labels, Arbor correctly assigns 76-85% of novel-class images to their superclass, more than hierarchical classifiers, hierarchical novelty detection and the Elkan-Noto correction. Its top-1 accuracy over the leaf classes on known-class images is within 1.6 points of the best baseline, although its final predictions return the superclass more often. On the more challenging iNaturalist-2019 benchmark, Arbor improves novel-class accuracy from 46% (uniform target, the strongest baseline) to 68%.

items.summary: Arbor addresses dataset merging across taxonomy levels where coarse labels are not assigned at random, showing that standard superclass-probability objectives fail for classes that never receive fine labels. The method models the coarsening process with virtual novel classes and a logistic gate, improving classification when some classes are only coarsely labelled.

items.title: Smart Model Routing for Order-of-Magnitude LLM Cost Reduction
items.content: arXiv:2611.15911v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) deliver the strongest response quality but carry per-token prices often more than an order of magnitude above those of smaller, task-adequate models. Smart model routing addresses this mismatch by assigning each query to the cheapest model expected to answer it adequately, rather than sending every request to the most capable, most expensive endpoint. This paper develops a formal cost-quality optimization framework for routing -- including a derived optimal threshold-policy structure, a calibration-versus-discrimination distinction, a cascade breakeven condition, and a sensitivity analysis over price ratio and traffic skew -- situates that framework against the principal routing architectures and the signals used to estimate query difficulty, and works through a numerical example showing how a calibrated router can reduce blended inference cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an always-frontier deployment under specific, stated pricing and traffic assumptions, reporting both the gross reduction from routing policy alone and the net figure with the router's own overhead priced in. We situate this figure against the range reported by published routing systems (roughly 2x to frontier-level accuracy at one-fifth the cost), and close with the practical risks -- under- and over-routing, aggregate quality constraints masking segment-level harm, calibration without discrimination, calibration drift, prompt injection into routing signals, and operational failures such as tier outages and multi-provider price variation -- that determine whether the savings materialize in production. The analysis is primarily analytical, complemented by a GSM8K evaluation of the cascade framework (Section 5), validated (Section 5.2); extending the evaluation across tasks and model families is future work.

items.title: DexRemo: A Force-Sensing Hand Platform and Task Suite for Contact-Rich Removal Manipulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.15981v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Many manipulation tasks require separating adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained targets. We study this setting as removal manipulation, where progress depends on evolving contact states that are only partially observable from vision and kinematics. We introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. To make multi-finger force observations easier to fuse, we express fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, giving force components consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time. Using an Action Chunking Transformer backbone, policies fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force observations to predict closed-loop action chunks from demonstrations. Evaluation uses six core benchmark tasks for controlled fingertip-input and force-frame ablations, plus three extension scenarios for additional held-out coverage. Across these evaluations, the learned policies achieve consistent removal performance, and ablations show that wrist-frame forces, especially with fingertip pose, improve stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs and no-force baselines. Project website: https://dexremo.github.io

items.title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
items.content: arXiv:2611.16219v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

It uses a swap-AB warp-level FP8/FP4 block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights and FP8 activations, plus SM120-specific optimizations, to overlap token dispatch, grouped GEMM, and combine phases.

items.title: Joint Null-Space Projection for Data-Free Model Merging
items.content: arXiv:2611.17103v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Merging independently fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model requires no data, no labels, and no gradient steps. In practice the task vectors of different tasks interfere, and the standard remedies--averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election--operate entry by entry, ignoring that each delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon. We recast merging as a subspace interference problem. For every two-dimensional weight tensor we take the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta--the input directions along which that task moves the representation most--and remove from each task vector the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces. The resulting Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set. On eight CLIP image-classification tasks JNSP merges ViT-B/16 experts to 89.45% average accuracy without using a single image, 11.88 points above the strongest parameter-wise training-free baseline (TIES-Merging, 77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic, and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). The gain holds across three backbones on the independently trained TALL release (+10.8, +12.6, +9.1 over TIES for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) and replicates there at 89.20%; controls confirm the source--a single shared subspace instead of per-task ones loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the same projection underperforms plain task arithmetic, which we report rather than hide. Code is available at https://github.com.

items.title: FIBER: Bayesian Fusion of Fast-DetectGPT and IRT-Informed Detector Evidence for LLM-Generated Text Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.15058v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Detecting large language model (LLM)-generated text remains challenging under domain and generator shifts. Supervised detectors may generalize poorly, while zero-shot methods often rely on individual statistical signals without leveraging historical detector behavior. We propose FIBER (Fast-DetectGPT with IRT-informed Bayesian Evidence Recalibration), which integrates continuous Fast-DetectGPT scores with auxiliary detector outputs through Bayesian evidence fusion. Item response theory (IRT) models historical detector-correctness patterns, providing class-conditional detector-output likelihoods through marginalization over latent text representations. These likelihoods are combined with Fast-DetectGPT score densities and a historical class prior for prediction. When historical Fast-DetectGPT scores are unavailable, a variant called FIBER-Stream estimates class-specific score distributions from an unlabeled batch. On a 32,000-text multi-domain benchmark, FIBER achieves the highest accuracy (0.620) and improves mean AUC over Fast-DetectGPT (0.664 versus 0.600) under five-fold cross-validation. FIBER also consistently improves AUC across four individual domains. Under out-of-distribution transfer, FIBER-Stream achieved an AUC of 0.911, compared with 0.889 for FIBER and 0.922 for Fast-DetectGPT alone. These results demonstrate the potential of integrating complementary detector evidence and historical information to improve detection performance across heterogeneous settings.

Under out-of-distribution transfer, FIBER-Stream achieved an AUC of 0.911, compared with 0.889 for FIBER and 0.922 for Fast-DetectGPT alone. These results demonstrate the potential of integrating complementary detector evidence and historical information to improve detection performance across heterogeneous settings.

items.title: Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text
items.content: arXiv:2611.16260v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.

items.title: Neural Compression for Scientific Particle Data: Perspectives on How Learning Can Help
items.content: arXiv:2611.14832v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As particle-based simulations grow in scale, efficient compression of scientific data becomes critical. Neural point cloud compression (PCC) methods excel on computer vision (CV) benchmarks, but do they transfer to scientific particle data? We highlight that scientific particles differ from CV point clouds in fractal dimension: CV point clouds are locally planar, but particles are not. This key difference limits the effectiveness of the octree data structure that underpins most PCC methods. Neural codecs achieve only marginal bitrate reductions over the traditional G-PCC baseline on scientific data, revealing a significant performance gap. Supported by an evaluation spanning domains of cosmology, molecular dynamics, and plasma physics, we outline where the structure of scientific data limits current neural approaches and where learning can help in the future.

The work charts where learning-based compression could genuinely help scientific data.

items.title: PCLSegNet: Anatomy-Aware Deep Learning Framework for MRI-based Pancreatic Cyst Segmentation and Size Assessment
items.content: arXiv:2611.15278v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Early detection and follow-up of pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are crucial, as some of their subtypes, such as mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms, carry a significant risk of malignant transformation. Although most AI studies investigating PCLs rely on computed tomography (CT) scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers superior soft tissue contrast, making it highly suitable for PCLs assessment. In this work, we propose an anatomy-aware two-stage deep learning framework for automated PCLs segmentation on abdominal MRI scans. First, a publicly available pancreas segmentation model is used to localize the pancreas. Then, we introduce the anatomyaware PCLSegNet, which incorporates anatomical priors as guidance for pancreas and PCLs segmentation. To address the class imbalance problem, we develop a Class-Specific ErrorWeighted (CSEW) loss function. Postprocessing is applied through anatomical constraints.Our proposed method outperforms multi-organ segmentation models such as TotalSegmentator, achieving substantially higher Dice scores for pancreas segmentation. Moreover, it also achieves a superior normalized surface Dice (NSD) and recall for PCLs segmentationcompared to other state-of-the-art models like nnU-Net, while also notably reducing the false negative rate, facilitating the automatic early detection and the noninvasive imaging-based assessment of PCLs.

items.title: AcrossPlace: Do Vision--Language Models Recognize Places Beyond Their Source Views? A Comprehensive Benchmark
items.content: arXiv:2611.15314v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Language-guided place recognition requires recovering geographic identity across visual observations beyond the image from which a description originates. However, aggregate retrieval scores often entangle observation transfer, gallery competition, and linguistic evidence, obscuring the underlying recognition capability. We introduce AcrossPlace, a provenance-aware benchmark establishing a systematic evaluation standard for bidirectional language--vision place recognition. Built upon GSV-Cities, AcrossPlace comprises 56,726 places across 23 cities, 156,800 automatically generated, rule-filtered descriptions, and 113,404 target images. Each description retains its source-image provenance, while retrieval operates on disjoint target observations. Text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) retrieval share a unified place-identity relevance criterion supporting multiple valid matches. Two geographic protocols evaluate unseen places within represented cities (P0) and generalization to held-out cities (P1). Paired observation comparisons, gallery-controlled evaluations, fixed-query scaling, and blinded annotation auditing systematically characterize retrieval performance. Across three training seeds, place-supervised SigLIP2 T2I Recall@1 decreases from 19.69% on source images to 12.31% on independent targets under P0. For fixed P1 queries, expanding the gallery from 500 to 8,425 places reduces Recall@1 from 14.67% to 2.87%. A 240-description audit further reveals discrepancies between automated acceptance and factual evidence. These findings establish AcrossPlace as a reproducible evaluation standard for assessing transferable place identity across visual observations and geographic environments.

items.title: Sub-actions in Action: Text-Guided Hand-Role Alignment for Sub-Action Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.16056v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding. Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.

It defines sub-action detection as a new task for fine-grained egocentric action understanding.

items.title: Selective Generative Restoration for Video Deraining via Uncertainty-Aware Diffusion
items.content: arXiv:2611.16310v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video deraining is challenging due to rain streaks, occlusions, and atmospheric effects. Existing methods mainly follow a deterministic restoration paradigm, assuming that clean scenes can be uniquely recovered from rainy observations. However, rain degradation is spatially heterogeneous. Reliable regions require faithful reconstruction, whereas severely occluded regions contain ambiguous content that require stronger prior-driven inference. Therefore, conventional deterministic restoration often produces over-smoothed results, while global generative restoration may introduce unnecessary hallucinations. We introduce a Selective Generative Restoration paradigm for video deraining, where generative priors are adaptively activated according to restoration uncertainty. Based on this principle, we propose Selective Generative Video Deraining (SGVD), an uncertainty-aware diffusion framework that enables adaptive fidelity preservation and generative recovery. Specifically, SGVD exploits stochastic diversity between dual one-step diffusion predictions to estimate region-level restoration uncertainty, which determines where observation fidelity should be preserved and where generative inference should be activated. Furthermore, an anchor-guided trajectory consistency mechanism is proposed to regularize stochastic diffusion evolution across frames, reducing temporal generation drift and improving video coherence. To achieve practical efficiency, SGVD adopts one-step diffusion inference while maintaining uncertainty-aware generative capability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVD achieves superior restoration performance, perceptual quality, and temporal consistency compared with state-of-the-art video deraining methods.

items.summary: This paper proposes a selective generative restoration paradigm for video deraining that adaptively activates diffusion-based generative priors depending on the spatial heterogeneity of rain degradation. Reliable regions receive faithful deterministic reconstruction while severely occluded regions get stronger prior-driven generation, avoiding both over-smoothed outputs and unnecessary hallucinations. The work matters because it reframes video restoration as a hybrid deterministic-generative problem rather than choosing one paradigm globally.
items.reasoning: The core idea of uncertainty-aware selective activation of generative priors is a sensible and novel contribution to video restoration, addressing a real limitation of purely deterministic or purely generative approaches. However, video deraining is a niche task with limited downstream impact, the abstract does not report state-of-the-art benchmark results, and the authors are not from a major AI lab. Solid, well-motivated incremental research rather than a field-shifting result.

items.title: Model Distribution-Aware Multimodal Dataset Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2611.16418v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal dataset distillation (MDD) aims to reduce the cost of vision-language pre-training by synthesizing compact image-text datasets. Although recent feature-matching methods have improved distillation efficiency, synthetic data may become specialized to the model representations encountered during optimization, limiting generalization to unseen model states. We propose Model Distribution-Aware Multimodal Dataset Distillation (MDA-DD), which leverages supervision from a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages. We further introduce asymmetric dual projection for complementary alignment in visual and linguistic spaces and an uncentered second-order moment objective that retains mean-related cross-modal information. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO demonstrate consistent retrieval improvements over existing methods across synthetic-data budgets. With only 100 synthetic pairs, MDA-DD improves IR@1 and TR@1 on Flickr30K by 12.9 and 18.2 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baseline at the same budget, outperforming all compared methods using 500 pairs on both datasets across all six retrieval metrics.

It adds asymmetric dual projection for visual-linguistic alignment and an uncentered second-order moment objective preserving mean-related cross-modal information.

items.title: HIFC-IQA: Train-Free Cross-Domain Image Quality Assessment via Dual-Process Cognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.16451v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The gap between controlled synthetic distortions and complex real-world degradations introduces a critical domain shift challenge for No-Reference Image Quality Assessment. Although Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) approaches attempt to address this issue, they remain constrained by substantial retraining overhead and cumulative error propagation inherent in iterative pseudo-labeling. Inspired by the dual-process theory of human cognition for remarkable generalization ability, we propose Hierarchical Intuitive and Fuzzy Consensus (HIFC), a completely train-free Cross-Domain IQA framework. HIFC employs asymmetric perceptual decomposition to disentangle semantic content from distortion-sensitive representations. The final quality score is fused through the synergy of two complementary branches: a memory consensus branch that retrieves a stable Fuzzy Quality Centroid from a synthetic reference gallery, and an intuitive branch that captures aesthetic polarization via zero-shot vision-language alignment. Extensive experiments show that HIFC achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, attaining the highest average SRCC and PLCC among competing UDA methods. Most notably, in the challenging synthetic-to-authentic cross-domain setting, HIFC achieves a substantial performance margin over competing methods, demonstrating remarkable robustness and generalization.

items.summary: This paper introduces HIFC, a training-free framework for no-reference image quality assessment that handles the domain shift between synthetic distortions and real-world degradations. It uses asymmetric perceptual decomposition to separate semantic content from distortion-sensitive features and draws inspiration from dual-process human cognition, avoiding the retraining overhead and pseudo-label error propagation of unsupervised domain adaptation approaches.
items.reasoning: A train-free approach to a practical domain-shift problem is appealing for deployment, and the cognitive framing is creative. However, it is an incremental application area (IQA) without evidence of a new architectural paradigm, so impact is moderate.

Extensive experiments show that HIFC achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, attaining the highest average SRCC and PLCC among competing UDA methods. Most notably, in the challenging synthetic-to-authentic cross-domain setting, HIFC achieves a substantial performance margin over competing methods, demonstrating remarkable robustness and generalization.

items.title: TuMAP: A Dual-View, Morphotype-Aware Pathomics Pipeline for Quantifying Renal Tubular Remodeling
items.content: arXiv:2611.17104v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Quantifying disease-associated renal tubular remodeling is challenging because tubular appearances are heterogeneous. We introduce TuMAP (Tubular Morphotype-Aware Pathomics), a pipeline combining (1) dual-view foundation-model representations and provisional morphotype annotation, (2) compositional and within-morphotype pathomics, and (3) patient-level statistical inference. From 456,158 tubules in 358 PAS-stained kidney biopsy slides, TuMAP identified eight image-based morphotypes, seven of which showed stable subsampling assignments. Across 219 patients in six diagnostic groups, diabetic nephropathy (DN) and tubulointerstitial nephritis/acute tubular injury (TIN/ATI) each differed from minimal change disease in seven morphotype proportions, while IgA nephropathy differed in six. DN showed reduced nuclear solidity and increased eccentricity across all eight morphotypes. Area-normalized nuclear density exposed additional within-morphotype differences. TuMAP provides a framework for separating changes in tubular morphotype composition from phenotypic differences within morphotypes.

items.title: Neural Render Proxies for Interactive and Differentiable Lighting
items.content: arXiv:2611.17185v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.

items.title: DeNA-SGN: Deterministic Neighborhood Aggregation for Verified Spiking Graph Inference
items.content: arXiv:2611.14775v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Graph learning on neuromorphic substrates requires an explicit spiking realization of neighborhood aggregation, supporting control and classification. We propose DeNA-SGN, which combines fixed OR and tie-inclusive Majority aggregation of binary node features with a learned signed-weight threshold classifier. A degree-dependent inhibitory construction implements Majority through shared control neurons, enabling a complete circuit compilation into SuperNeuroMAT. Across seven datasets and 41 mapped classifiers, native simulation matches the exported ANN on every evaluated class decision and output-spike pattern. On the new confirmatory Amazon Photo dataset, DeNA-SGN achieves 83.93+-0.93% current-readout accuracy and 71.61+-2.22% strict output-spike accuracy; Wiki-CS reaches 75.99+-0.54% over 20 public masks. In the matched Cora study, we achieve 74.90+-2.67% on current-readout and 68.57+-2.94% strict spike accuracy. Complete circuit and activity accounting supports analytical energy comparisons and identifies the cost of clocking inactive neurons in large deployments. Current argmax is decoded on the host, and energy is modeled rather than measured on hardware. These findings establish a reproducible route to useful graph classification with decision-matched spiking execution and explicit implementation costs.

items.title: SunLightBots: Turning sunlight into self-sustained, high-power motion in soft robots
items.content: arXiv:2611.14729v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Soft robots built from active materials can directly convert environmental stimuli into motion, offering a route to energy autonomy and embodied control. However, environmental energy is generally harvested at low power, whereas rapid, mechanically demanding actions require high mechanical output power. Reconciling this mismatch while sustaining self-regulated cyclic actuation is challenging, particularly at the subgram scale, where limited payload capacity constrains the integration of conventional power and control hardware. Here, we present SunLightBots, a class of subgram, sunlight-powered, untethered soft robots that achieve autonomous locomotion under continuous illumination near 1 Sun (100 mW/cm2). Their operation is enabled by a self-resetting snapping (SRS) mechanism that integrates liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) with snap-through instability to accumulate solar energy supplied at low power, release it as rapid, high-power motion, and reset through photothermal-mechanical feedback. Through coordinated optimization of the LCE actuation temperature, photothermal conversion, actuation stress, and structural energy barrier, the system operates near 1 Sun and achieves a peak mass-specific mechanical power of 89 W/kg. At this irradiance, the optimized LCE generates an actuation stress of 0.1 MPa at approximately 60 deg C. SunLightBots demonstrate sustained swimming, crawling, and repeated impulsive jumping. Under 1.5 Suns, the swimmer advances more than three body lengths per cycle. This work provides a materials-mechanics route toward autonomous soft robots powered entirely by the environment.

The work addresses the core mismatch between low-power environmental energy harvesting and the high mechanical output power needed for rapid, cyclic actuation, without conventional onboard power or control hardware. It matters because it demonstrates a pathway to energy-autonomous embodied systems at scales where batteries and electronics are impractical.

However, it is a niche robotics/materials contribution without direct relevance to mainstream AI, and the abstract does not indicate immediate broad deployment impact.

items.title: Recover, Don't Just Continue: Learning from Feedback for Physical Failure Understanding and Correction
items.content: arXiv:2611.15651v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.

The authors build failure-recovery training data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, teaching models to understand why execution deviates and how to revise plans. This addresses a real gap between planning from instructions and reliable physical execution.

items.title: MotionSkill: From Bipedal Motion Video to Control across Embodiments
items.content: arXiv:2611.16346v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reusing a demonstrated gait can reduce the work of specifying the same motion for each biped. A video captures the timing of a step, but each robot must execute it with its own limbs and actuators. MotionSkill recovers a timed reference once from monocular video and adapts it to each target in simulation. It aligns root motion and body landmarks in a common frame and records which landmarks are available at each instant. At each source timestamp, the mapper preserves limb directions, uses the target segment lengths, and solves inverse kinematics under joint limits and closure constraints. In MuJoCo, we train a separate residual policy for each of ten bipeds on its mapped reference from one four-second walking clip. Each policy uses the measured robot state to correct joint commands during contact. From initial states held out during training, MotionSkill completed 98% of trials on the original video and 26% with the upper body occluded for one second.

Each embodiment then trains a residual policy on the mapped reference in MuJoCo. The approach enables cross-embodiment motion reuse from casually captured video.

items.title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction
items.content: arXiv:2611.17160v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker--Talker--Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.

This targets socially capable embodied agents that communicate intentions multimodally.

items.title: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving
items.content: arXiv:2611.08631v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.
items.author: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Zixuan Wang, Weisong Shi
items.summary: BEVCast is a two-stage bird's-eye-view representation for camera-based end-to-end autonomous driving that allocates high resolution only to cells predicted to lie on the vehicle's future path, keeping the rest of the scene at coarse resolution under a fixed compute budget. The approach removes the need for HD maps or navigation commands while improving efficiency relative to uniformly fine BEV grids.

items.title: Post-Glasswing cybersecurity projects
items.content:
When Claude Mythos was announced, many people said that we had about six months before open-weights AIs could hack everything, using advanced exploitation and vulnerability-finding capabilities. This timeline for capabilities was correct, and open-weights models have about the same scary capabilities as Mythos did. However, things are not as bad as "everything connected to the internet is probably hacked", and even PHP2Shell seems to not have had especially bad consequences. I think we remain relatively unhacked because exploitation is still difficult and annoying and there's general "inertia", but the situation is likely not sustainable.

Glasswing and similar projects were meant to patch important software, but left large gaps. OpenAI found 948 local privilege escalation exploits in a Linux environment recently. This does not suggest a mature, secured software environment.

In security, doubling down on the same process/design (identifying vulnerabilities and submitting them to maintainers to fix) when it demonstrably won't achieve good coverage in practice is frowned upon. Anthropic's process is enormously lossy, maintainers are struggling to process the reports they do get, and lots of software is probably not being covered or has organizational bottlenecks preventing it from being fixed at any useful rate. Also, I don't think that cyberattacks in practice usually involve flashy zero-days or extremely clever-sounding vulnerabilities, rather than boring misconfigurations, human error or unanticipated interactions between minor problems.

We should instead design systems which will hold up better even with many broken parts. Based on admittedly brief web searches, there is not a detailed plan for this, and most AI-driven effort is focused on finding vulnerabilities, or more speculative, technically shinier, longer-term formal verification. Here are some ideas I think are worth trying, which would benefit from cheap software through AI labour:...
items.author: osmarks
items.summary: The post assesses the aftermath of AI-driven vulnerability discovery efforts like Glasswing, arguing that while open-weights models now match scary hacking capabilities predicted months ago, systemic compromise has not materialized due to exploitation friction. It contends that patch-via-report pipelines are unsustainable and lossy, citing findings such as 948 local privilege escalation exploits found by OpenAI in Linux.
items.reasoning: A substantive, evidence-anchored commentary on AI cybersecurity strategy at a topical moment (referencing recent capability milestones and disclosed exploit counts); it offers a concrete critique of current coordinated-vulnerability pipelines and proposes rethinking defensive processes, though it is opinion rather than formal research.

items.content_html:
When Claude Mythos was announced, many people said that we had about six months before open-weights AIs could hack everything, using advanced exploitation and vulnerability-finding capabilities. This timeline for capabilities was correct, and open-weights models have about the same scary capabilities as Mythos did. However, things are not as bad as "everything connected to the internet is probably hacked", and even PHP2Shell seems to not have had especially bad consequences. I think we remain relatively unhacked because exploitation is still difficult and annoying and there's general "inertia", but the situation is likely not sustainable.

Glasswing and similar projects were meant to patch important software, but left large gaps. OpenAI found 948 local privilege escalation exploits in a Linux environment recently. This does not suggest a mature, secured software environment.

In security, doubling down on the same process/design (identifying vulnerabilities and submitting them to maintainers to fix) when it demonstrably won't achieve good coverage in practice is frowned upon. Anthropic's process is enormously lossy, maintainers are struggling to process the reports they do get, and lots of software is probably not being covered or has organizational bottlenecks preventing it from being fixed at any useful rate. Also, I don't think that cyberattacks in practice usually involve flashy zero-days or extremely clever-sounding vulnerabilities, rather than boring misconfigurations, human error or unanticipated interactions between minor problems.

We should instead design systems which will hold up better even with many broken parts. Based on admittedly brief web searches, there is not a detailed plan for this, and most AI-driven effort is focused on finding vulnerabilities, or more speculative, technically shinier, longer-term formal verification. Here are some ideas I think are worth trying, which would benefit from cheap software through AI labour:...

items.title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
items.content:
This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's.

This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period.

You can adjust various axes of this proposal:

- Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition.
- What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints.
- When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed.

One concrete target that I like is: “No checkpoint may be used internally for purposes beyond safety testing, until at least X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor.”

This is one specific implementation of internal deployment lags, an idea that the AI Futures Project (AIFP) briefly discusses in How to pace the US frontier as “AI R&D can only be conducted or assisted by AIs that were trained at least 9 months ago”.

## What does this look like when implemented?

Let’s run through a scenario to pin down the details of this proposal. The places where it could go wrong are in the open questions at the end.

- A legislative body sets a minimum waiting period of X calendar days (starting at 10 and possibly ratcheting up to 90). No checkpoint in a covered model family may be used internally, beyond safety testing, until X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor. Continuing to train a checkpoint’s own weights does not count as internal use. The alternative is for the wait to also block the training of checkpoint N+1, and not just the internal use of checkpoint N. I didn’t go with this because it incentivizes developers to pull out fewer checkpoints for testing, and because delaying training results in an algorithmic overhang.
- More capable models start exhibiting problems that are harder to surface in short periods (e.g. swarms, long-horizon, memory), so X should possibly increase over time.
- A model family becomes covered as soon as any of its checkpoints (pre-, mid- or post-trained) is substantially more capable than the last model to complete its wait. If the developer initially claims that the model is not covered but later finds that it is, they will be subject to some penalty (to be determined). There is also an absolute floor on capabilities, so that this doesn’t apply to lots of benign models.
- In an emergency, the auditor can authorize one named checkpoint to be used early, only for responding to a specific incident (e.g. a harmful model is already causing damage, and the developer has just trained a patched model that could counter it). The standards/legislative body confirms or revokes this within [X days].
- The developer continually pulls checkpoints throughout the training process. They first send an auditor a hash, a short fingerprint of the exact weights; then, they carry out safety testing for X days before deploying a checkpoint broadly internally without the below rules. All work has to be fully transparent to auditors.
- Options for how the X days are structured: Staged testing Stage 1, first part of X: pre-registered evals and named testers in an isolated environment. Stage 2, second part of X: broad monitored internal use, but the model can’t launch jobs, merge code, write to training data, or touch prod. Parallel, hidden runs: whenever someone at the developer uses a cleared model, the new checkpoint gets the same task in a separate sandboxed copy of the environment. Its outputs go only to monitors and the safety team, never back to the person who asked.

## Open questions

The rule itself

- Should we also allow capability testing? What about ML R&D tasks? One way to game this is to register thousands of tasks from your open R&D backlog, and call running them a capability eval. The outputs are real research (e.g. a faster kernel), and even if you ban using them, people still have to read the transcripts to grade them, so they learn what worked. Pre-registering evals doesn’t help, since it fixes the task list in advance but doesn’t check whether the tasks are live problems. You might end up needing a compute cap.
- Should we give exemptions for doing safety research? This is an important crux to ask alignment researchers about. Without an exemption, safety research is done with a model that is X days behind, but a blanket exemption lets capabilities work pose as safety work.
- Should a safety fix (e.g. more post-training, or redoing RL from an earlier checkpoint) restart the X-day wait? It would be bad if it did, as Avi Brach-Neufeld points out here. A developer that finds an issue on day 8 of testing loses more time than one that finds it on day 2, so the rule penalizes finding and fixing problems during the wait. This is probably tolerable at small X, but gets worse as X increases. If safety fixes don’t restart the clock, however, developers could just call capabilities training “safety”.
- What is the principle behind how much X increases?
- How large is the risk that an emergency clause would be abused?
- Concerning behaviours aren’t necessarily caught during pre-deployment testing windows, and are often caught through subsequent monitored internal use. How much are we willing to trade off the value of catching some misaligned behaviours via monitoring internal deployments, vs. being able to pace internal R&D?

Which models are covered

- How is “substantially more capable” defined: effective compute, or something like the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI)?
- How would an auditor check that the developer has faithfully stuck to the “more capable” definition?
- How do you avoid bringing classifiers built using a frontier model into scope?
- Can a developer keep using earlier checkpoints from a family after it becomes covered?
- A developer could train a second model family and keep it just under the “substantially more capable” line, so it’s never covered. Researchers could then use that family right away, while use of the main family is on hold. This only gets them so far, since coverage is measured against the last model to complete its wait, and an uncovered family never completes one, so the second family can only be ahead by the “substantially more capable” margin. This becomes a bigger problem if the capability measure itself can be gamed.

Gaming the wait

- How can we stop a developer from using a checkpoint for acceleratory AI R&D work during the wait, by labeling that work as an allowed activity (i.e. any AI R&D task whose output gets used for anything other than testing that checkpoint)? How can we cleanly separate out safety testing from other activities? A developer could give a new model a real task during training, such as writing faster training code, and then use that code to train other models before the new model has completed the X-day wait. A developer could make every researcher an A/B tester, so that they use the new model for normal work and rate its answers, and the developer calls this training. Similarly, a developer could have an RL environment that is just how well the model does actual work inside the company.
- In stage 1 of staged testing, you run the risk that named testers run large agent swarms for capabilities work, in which case the only difference is that there are fewer humans in the loop. This is probably somewhat mitigated by pre-registering evals, but it’s difficult to still allow AWT.
- In stage 2, you can still copy paste model outputs into training data, or into code and research plans. A developer could also store outputs from the wait and use them the day the checkpoint clears, without breaking any rule. Should there be a blanket ban on training on outputs from the wait, and how would anyone check?
- In stage 2, how will you detect if the model is launching jobs, merging code, writing to training data, or touching prod?
- Developers can game the wait by making lots of models and testing all of them at once, so that the testing period ends up being an AI R&D period. For example, with a 30-day wait, a developer could pull out a checkpoint every day and “test” them all, so that researchers always have a day-old model. Possible mitigations are to cap the number of checkpoints that can be tested concurrently, cap total compute across the entire testing period, or pre-register the kind of testing you want to do during the period.
- If each developer could write its own definition of “safety testing”, a developer could call any monitored employee use testing and move faster. Others would then face pressure to do the same, until the rule no longer binds anyone. A shared template would help, but it depends on the auditor being competent and independent.

Parallel, hidden runs

- There’s no human interacting with the new model, so you miss problems that only show up in back-and-forth with a person. A situationally aware model might also notice it’s in a sandbox and behave differently. Is this okay?
- How big of a problem is leak risk from reviewers back to capabilities researchers?

Verification

- How can you mitigate the risk that the developer simply does not send the hash of a given checkpoint to the auditor? Potentially: In the near term: the auditor spot-checks that the weights running on internal endpoints match filed hashes. One complication is that a hash of the exact weights changes with any conversion (e.g. quantization, sharding, or a change of number format), so the weights being served would often not match the filed checkpoint byte for byte. You would need either a standard way of serializing the weights, or a hash of the version that is actually served. In the longer run: hardware attestation.

## Could this be used as a speed dial?

The wait gives developers and auditors more time for safety testing. X could also be used as a speed dial, which a standards/legislative body could turn up or down if it wanted to modulate the pace of AI progress.

I think that this only works as a speed dial if this proposal delays internal R&D loops; delaying external deployment would mainly have second order effects like:

- Each launch shifts the start of new revenue back by a short period. These delays don’t stack across launches, since every launch is shifted back by the same amount. This could still in principle strain a given developer’s ability to pay for compute contracts, but the impact might be small, since I expect that you are mostly shifting when new revenue starts instead of losing it entirely.
- Some reduction of race dynamics, though I expect the effect size to be quite small.

It’s unclear whether this causes a one-time delay in when the most capable model can be used internally, or a lasting change in the pace of AI progress. This depends on how much the newest model speeds up R&D compared with a model that’s X days older. I have a hunch that, if implemented well, this proposal would have a larger impact on the pace of recursive self-improvement (RSI) itself than on the onset of RSI.

Much of the value of this proposal will depend on how effectively you can specify what counts as “safety testing”, given that the most useful safety testing often looks like real use. A narrower definition limits how much acceleratory AI R&D work gets through during the wait, but it cuts against giving safety researchers signal of misalignment that only show up in broad, realistic use.

## What are the benefits and drawbacks of this proposal?

Benefits include:

- As a speed dial, this should get stronger as things speed up, as the gap between the newest model and the last cleared model gets bigger, whereas a compute cap might stop binding if most of the progress is coming from algorithms.
- Developers would be incentivized to hand the checkpoint to an auditor as soon as possible so that they can deploy more quickly (assuming that they can’t use unfiled checkpoints without being detected).
- It doesn’t result in an algorithmic overhang, because you still allow training, and presumably any new compute multipliers you find are put into the newest model that you are training. The exception is if a developer can secretly stock up capabilities outputs during the wait, e.g. by storing work from hidden parallel runs or ML R&D evals.

Drawbacks include:

- Developers get a lot of signal on misalignment by internally deploying a model. You don’t get less misalignment signal for a given model, since it will be broadly deployed eventually, but you delay the timeline on which a safety issue can be fixed. Today a problem seen in real use can feed into the next model’s training almost straight away; under this proposal, a model will get X more days of training before an issue is detected. Mitigations: the parallel hidden runs idea; a norm that when real use of the cleared model turns up a problem, you test all the waiting checkpoints for it straight away.
- Safety research done with the model is X days behind.
- Unlike proposals that limit the most capable model you have at a given time (like compute caps), this limits the most capable model you can use. The risk incurred by foreign competitors stealing model weights is therefore comparatively higher.
- It’s hard to verify how a checkpoint was used, so you may rely very heavily on auditor judgement.
- This proposal may not work with continual learning, if there were a breakthrough.

Discuss

items.title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
items.content: arXiv:2611.14846v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

items.title: Advancing Weighted Partial MaxSAT Solving via Differentiable GPU Guidance
items.content: arXiv:2611.15091v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present a GPU-CPU hybrid framework for Weighted Partial MaxSAT (WPMAX-SAT) that complements state-of-the-art CPU solvers with differentiable GPU optimization. The GPU stage directly optimizes instance-specific categorical decision parameters without a training dataset or a pretrained predictive model. The central challenge in extending differentiable optimization to WPMAX-SAT is the hard/soft clause asymmetry: hard clauses represent inviolable feasibility constraints while soft clauses carry weights. We introduce a hierarchical differentiable loss that prioritizes hard clause satisfaction before optimizing the weighted soft objective, ensuring that GPU gradient descent leans towards the constraint structure of WPMAX-SAT. Our framework transforms the GPU-optimized variable logits to high-confidence assignments and transfers them to CPU solvers via two complementary modes: partial guidance, which injects the most confident perturbed partial variable assignments as soft clauses into $N$ parallel solver instances, and phase initialization, which guides the CDCL solver's internal branching polarity with the full GPU assignment as a warm start to preserve the problem's originality.
