items.title: QVS-LIVO RiskMap: Health- and Information-Aware View Selection for Multi-Camera LIVO and Off-Road Risk Mapping
items.content: arXiv:2611.16205v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-camera observations in off-road environments vary significantly in reliability, posing challenges when complementing degraded geometric constraints. Motivated by this, we propose Quality-aware View Selection Lidar-Vision Odometry Risk Mapping (QVS-LIVO RiskMap), which decouples visual processing for state estimation from that for semantic mapping. The front end evaluates camera observations through read-only pretracking on a shared lidar-inertial posterior, combining observation health with geometric complementarity. Channel health memory and switching hysteresis govern selection of at most one eligible view for direct photometric correction. The posterior is retained when no view is eligible or the correction fails acceptance. The mapping back end integrates semantic observations from all available views in a shared world grid. Vehicle-scale geometry constrains semantic risk corrections, while spatial and temporal evidence supports risk confirmation. The system also produces a local bird's-eye-view (BEV) risk map and a global 2.5D semantic-terrain risk map with obstacle instance voxels. On two field sequences, QVS-LIVO achieved horizontal root mean square errors of 0.910 m and 1.664 m. It reduced error by 43.3% relative to FAST-LIO2 on the degraded long-route sequence. Across 12 controlled camera-fault configurations involving dropout, black frames and 60 ms timestamp shifts, it maintained complete trajectories with errors of 1.54-2.23 m. When deployed onboard an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the system generates local and global maps at 9.94 Hz and 2.00 Hz, respectively, with a median local mapping latency of 32.4 ms. These runtime results demonstrate the real-time feasibility of selective visual state updates alongside multi-view semantic mapping under challenging off-road conditions. The code and related resources are available at: https://github.com/zihanPan-HIT/QVS-LIVO.
items.author: Zihan Pan, Jinghan Wang, Hang Li, Feng Cheng, Tianchen Liu, Gaoliang Peng
items.summary: QVS-LIVO RiskMap decouples visual processing for state estimation from semantic mapping in multi-camera off-road settings, selecting at most one eligible camera view for direct photometric correction based on observation health and geometric complementarity evaluated against a shared lidar-inertial posterior. Channel health memory and switching hysteresis stabilize selection, and the system produces off-road risk maps. It targets robust perception in degraded environments where camera reliability varies strongly.
items.reasoning: Technically sophisticated SLAM-perception fusion for a genuinely hard setting (degraded off-road sensing), but the contribution is an incremental advance on LIVO-style systems for a specialized audience.

items.title: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field
items.content: arXiv:2611.16652v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce CABOT, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an active computing medium. In the classical Look-Compute-Move (LCM) model every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid once per robot. CABOT strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the grid holds a state from a finite set Q, the states evolve synchronously under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the Look operation returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 1, without multiplicity detection and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |Q|, rather than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required. On an inert floor (|Q| = 1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected, configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row, fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and indicate the range of the model.
items.author: Yonghwan Kim, Gil-Tak Kong, Un-Sook Choi
items.summary: CABOT is a theoretical computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the environment itself computes: the grid floor is a cellular automaton whose cell states evolve by a local rule and are visible to robots during the Look operation, shifting capability increases from the robots to the environment. The paper contrasts this with the classical Look-Compute-Move model where power is added to robots individually.
items.reasoning: A novel and clean theoretical reframing of distributed robot computation by strengthening the environment instead of the robots; intellectually interesting for the theory of distributed systems, though it is a model abstraction with unclear near-term practical relevance.

items.title: Fr\'echet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression
items.content: arXiv:2611.16209v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We propose Fr\'echet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fr\'echet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fr\'echet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.
items.author: Jiaye Chen, Rui Qiu, Zhou Yu
items.summary: The paper proposes Frechet oblique forests for regression where predictors and responses live in metric spaces, using an Alexandrov inner-product score for directional splits and pairwise response distances to avoid repeated Frechet mean computations. It establishes consistency and polynomial risk bounds and demonstrates performance on matrices, distributions, and spherical data.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.16209v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose Fr\'echet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fr\'echet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fr\'echet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.

items.title: FLEX-LBP: Learning Local Binary Patterns with Exact Binary Inference for Texture Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.17302v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Local Binary Patterns (LBP) remain among the most widely used texture descriptors, from industrial inspection to medical imaging. Yet their radius, sampling angles, color transform and thresholds are fixed by hand for each dataset. We present FLEX-LBP, which learns these parameters by backpropagation while every forward pass computes exact binary codes and hard histogram counts. A straight-through estimator acts only in the backward pass, so the deployed descriptor is an interpretable hard-binary LBP with 90 learnable parameters and unchanged inference cost. In a controlled ablation on six color texture benchmarks, the component worth learning is dataset-dependent. One configuration, applied unchanged everywhere, learns the geometry and thresholds with the color transform frozen. It improves the nearest-neighbor accuracy of the identical fixed descriptor by 3.55 points on average over five seeds, significantly on five of six benchmarks and never significantly worse. With a linear discriminant readout, it gains 0.9 points; the fully learned descriptor gains 2.7 and has the highest mean. FLEX-LBP is more accurate than five classical LBP-family descriptors, PCANet and a neural LBP on five of six benchmarks. Its mean nearest-neighbor accuracy exceeds that of frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 features (23.5 million parameters). On the Kather colorectal cancer histology benchmark, the fully learned descriptor reaches 93.8%, significantly above the best classical descriptor (Completed LBP, 92.8%). The learned radii adapt in directions that recur across seeds. Noise drowns single-pixel comparisons and illuminant change flips inter-channel ones; median sampling or gray-world normalization restores 96-97%. The code is available as a drop-in PyTorch layer at https://github.com/medalimoussa/FLEX-LBP.

items.title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
items.content: arXiv:2611.16414v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.

items.title: A Modular Framework for ESG Prediction through Domain-Specific Language Modeling and Graph Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.16831v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) scores are increasingly used to evaluate corporate sustainability, supporting investment decisions, ensuring regulatory compliance and assessing risk. However, current ESG evaluations largely rely on proprietary methodologies that often produce inconsistent ratings. This motivates the development of data-driven prediction frameworks. In this paper, we present ESGPred, a modular framework for predicting ESG scores by combining domain-specific language modeling with graph-based learning over a network that models the relationships among the companies being evaluated. In addition to presenting the rationale behind ESGPred and detailing its ESG score prediction process, we show that ESGPred can effectively predict both overall ESG ratings and their individual Environmental, Social, and Governance components. We evaluated ESGPred using a dataset of 5,266 sustainability reports published by 2,134 publicly listed companies between 2020 and 2023. In this evaluation, we used ESG ratings provided by LSEG Data & Analytics as ground truth. Our experimental results demonstrated that integrating graph-based relational learning improves prediction performance over purely text-based baselines.

items.title: Care, Human Enfeeblement, and the Existential Implications of AGI
items.content: arXiv:2611.14520v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Stuart Russell has named "human enfeeblement" as a long-term societal risk of advanced AI. This paper gives a new interpretation of the enfeeblement danger by interpreting it in light of recent work by Brian Christian, Alison Gopnik, and David Spivak on care and caregiving, and connecting it with the ontological design tradition of Terry Winograd and Fernando Flores. The enfeeblement that threatens is not merely a matter of cognitive off-loading and loss of knowledge, but a form of disengagement with the world which I explain in terms of an erosion of our capacities to care. This paper articulates a conception of care as a constellation of cultivable skills that involve us in the world and with each other, while making life worth living. Designing AI to support our capacities to care addresses the worry recently raised by Demis Hassabis and others regarding the questions of "meaning and purpose" that are looming in a post-AGI world.

items.title: Finite-Cadence Refresh Equilibria for Streaming Prior-Anchored Ridge: A Closed-Form Forgetting Window and Spectral Correction
items.content: arXiv:2611.14586v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = \rho / (\mu_i + \rho)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $\Delta_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $\Psi(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $\omega^* = (4\nu^2 \Sigma / c')^{1/3}$, $c' = \sigma^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho)$, and the plug-in strength $\rho^* = \sigma^2 / (n\delta^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $\rho_{\mathrm{eff}} = \rho (e^{\zeta q} - 1) / (\zeta q)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.

items.summary: A theoretical analysis of recursive ridge estimators on drifting data streams, deriving a closed-form spectral decomposition for the forgetting trade-off in prior-anchored ridge regression when the anchor is refreshed every k steps. It characterizes a finite-cadence equilibrium with an explicit lag and variance-reduction factor, and gives optimal refresh cadence and plug-in scheduling.

items.title: Multiple-Choice Secretary Problem with Predictions
items.content: arXiv:2611.14651v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study the multiple-choice secretary problem, in which candidates arrive in uniformly random order and the goal is to select at most $k$ candidates to maximize their total value. We consider a setting where predictions of individual candidate values are available before any candidate arrives. Fujii and Yoshida's Learned Kleinberg algorithm achieves competitive loss $O(\min\{\log k/\sqrt{k},\eps\})$, where $k$ is the selection capacity and $\eps$ is the maximum multiplicative prediction error. We remove the logarithmic factor through a sharper analysis of the same switching algorithm with a retuned threshold. The resulting competitive ratio is at least $\max\{0,1-\min\{32/\sqrt{k},4\eps\}\}$. In particular, exact predictions ($\eps=0$) achieve the offline optimum on every arrival order.
items.author: Jing Yuan, Qi Cai, Xin Gao, Shaojie Tang
items.summary: Studies the multiple-choice secretary problem where value predictions are available before candidates arrive, improving on a known learning-augmented algorithm by removing a logarithmic factor through sharper analysis and a retuned threshold. The result yields a competitive ratio depending on selection capacity and maximum prediction error, with exact predictions approaching optimal selection.
items.reasoning: A clean theoretical contribution to learning-augmented algorithms with a well-motivated guarantees improvement, but it refines an existing switching algorithm rather than introducing a new framework, so novelty and impact are solid yet incremental.

items.title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
items.content: arXiv:2611.15250v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.

items.title: WaveFlow-UIE: A Single-Pipeline Wavelet-Domain Flow Model for Efficient Underwater Image Restoration
items.content: arXiv:2611.15457v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Underwater image restoration remains challenging because color distortion, scattering, and detail loss affect low- and high-frequency image components differently. Recent diffusion-based methods have shown strong restoration quality, but often rely on multi-stage pipelines and costly iterative refinement. We present WaveFlow-UIE, a single-pipeline wavelet-domain flow model that directly learns to transform degraded underwater wavelet representations into clean ones. Our method applies a discrete wavelet transform, estimates lightweight physics-inspired degradation cues including transmission and ambient light, and conditions a velocity network trained with flow matching in wavelet space. The training objective combines flow-matching, frequency-weighted reconstruction, perceptual, color-consistency, and physics-consistency losses. Across UIEB, LSUI, UFO-120, and EUVP, WaveFlow-UIE achieves a strong quality-efficiency tradeoff, with especially competitive results on perceptual metrics. Relative to a strong wavelet-based diffusion baseline, the proposed model substantially reduces inference cost while maintaining or improving restoration quality on several paired benchmarks. We show that reducing the inference process from five flow steps to a single step preserves nearly all of the restoration quality while providing an additional speedup of about $4\times$ on UIEB at $256\times256$ resolution. This single-step result suggests that a single-pass wavelet-domain model is an effective alternative to heavier diffusion-style refinement.

items.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
items.content: arXiv:2611.16057v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

items.title: Subsurface schematisation from sparse CPT data using the tabular foundation model TabPFN
items.content: arXiv:2611.16088v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Subsurface schematisation supports geotechnical decisions but remains challenging because sparse site-investigation data leave substantial gaps in information about ground conditions. This study explores TabPFN, a foundation model pretrained on general synthetic tabular data, for this task. Using only grid coordinates and soil behaviour type index observations from sparse cone penetration tests (CPTs), we first reconstruct two-dimensional sections without geotechnical fine-tuning or predefined layer boundaries. We evaluate the approach on synthetic sections and at two field sites in the Netherlands, comparing it with SchemaGAN, a conditional generative adversarial network trained on synthetic geotechnical sections, and with reference interpolation methods. In the baseline comparisons, TabPFN achieved mean errors close to SchemaGAN's on synthetic sections and lower mean errors at both field sites. On synthetic sections, TabPFN's mean absolute error decreased at each tested increase in CPT count, and, under the baseline input setting, its pointwise prediction intervals had mean coverage close to nominal levels. Subsequent fine-tuning on the synthetic sections used to train SchemaGAN improved synthetic test accuracy but increased mean errors at both field sites. These findings indicate that general-purpose tabular foundation models offer a promising route for updating subsurface predictions from sparse and evolving site-investigation data without retraining.

items.title: Where in the Input Does a One-Pass Decision Encoder Look?
items.content: arXiv:2611.16477v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question about a text in one pass: the question, the options (each with a name and a description) and the text form one sequence of at most 512 tokens, the window, in the English release. A longer text is silently cut at the end, and we measure what that costs. Test documents place a held-out row's text, the evidence, at a chosen token offset among distractor text; 177 items, five tasks, three checkpoints (released, short-row fine-tune, long-document fine-tune), four window sizes and 93,275 scored requests. When the evidence lies beyond the window, accuracy falls to 26.4% for the released checkpoint (27.2% for both fine-tunes), near the 27.0% of guessing and below the 35.6% of always giving the commonest label. Confidence gives no warning (AUROC 0.50 to 0.55 for telling cut from read requests; 0.5 = chance), and the runtime's truncation flag also fires on requests whose evidence was visible. The released checkpoint reads visible evidence badly once text precedes it: 38.5% pooled against 60% when the evidence comes first, so a larger window alone gains +6.2 points. Fine-tuning on long documents adds +27.6 points on visible evidence over the short-row fine-tune (95% interval +22.3 to +33.1) and nothing on cut evidence. That is an in-family result: training rows and test documents share generator and question types, and the main filler is of the training kind. With encyclopedic filler never seen in training the gain is +13.2 (+9.9 to +16.6), with rows of other tasks as filler -2.0. Among training-free rearrangements a 312-token window scan helps most (+11.9 points over the default for the released checkpoint) at six to eleven forward passes. Documents are synthetic, labels are LLM-made and one backbone is studied, so these diagnose this model, not long documents in general.
items.author: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Allan Kevin T
items.summary: This paper analyzes Laya, a small one-pass multiple-choice question answering model limited to a 512-token window, measuring the accuracy cost when evidence falls outside the window. Using 177 controlled test items with evidence placed at chosen offsets across five tasks, three checkpoints, and four window sizes (93,275 scored requests), the authors find accuracy collapses to roughly 26-27 percent when evidence is beyond the window, near chance. The work offers a careful methodological study of positional limitations in fixed-window decision encoders.
items.reasoning: A rigorous, well-controlled empirical study with an unusually detailed experimental grid, shedding light on windowing limitations in small encoders. However, it concerns a niche small model rather than frontier systems, and the findings are largely predictable (out-of-window evidence degrades performance), limiting broader significance.

items.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.16718v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.

items.title: Profile-Based Auditing of Domestic Violence Survey Selection Across South Asia
items.content: arXiv:2611.15106v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Domestic violence (DV) data in the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) are collected through a specialized module whose household-level sampling and privacy requirements create a distinct observation process. We ask whether demographic, socioeconomic, and household characteristics form reproducible population profiles and whether these profiles contain information about selection into the DV module across South Asia. Using DHS Individual Recode data for 796,374 women aged 15-49 across Afghanistan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, and Pakistan, we harmonize 61 numeric and 8 categorical features, reduce the profile space with PCA, and identify six interpretable profiles. We then evaluate 22 machine-learning models under primary-sampling-unit-aware holdout validation. The best model, HistGradientBoosting, achieves ROC-AUC 0.9167 and PR-AUC 0.9612, versus 0.8475 and 0.9203 for a design-only baseline. Adding woman-level characteristics yields the largest incremental gain, while explicit interaction terms add little out-of-sample performance. Country-specific analyses reveal substantial heterogeneity, and leave-one-country-out evaluation shows that transferability of the incremental profile signal is limited. These results demonstrate that interpretable ML can audit differential coverage in sensitive survey modules beyond the formal sampling design.

items.title: Serving-Aligned Entire-Space Conversion Modeling via Click-Through Rate Knowledge Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2611.15137v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recommendation systems may use predicted click-through conversion rate (pCTCVR), the product of predicted click-through rate (pCTR) and post-click conversion rate (pCVR), to guide ranking decisions. Many pCVR models build on the Entire Space Multi-Task Model (ESMM), which jointly trains pCVR and auxiliary pCTR towers using pCTR and pCTCVR losses, but deploys only the pCVR tower. At serving time, this tower may be paired with a separately trained pCTR model, creating a training-serving mismatch in pCTCVR when its predictions differ from those of the auxiliary pCTR tower. In this paper, we use knowledge distillation (KD) from logged serving pCTR scores to supervise ESMM's auxiliary pCTR tower and improve training-serving pCTCVR alignment. We denote variants by KD-$\alpha$, where $\alpha$ controls the hard-label loss weight. On the Ali-CCP dataset, KD-0.3, the best variant on serving pCTCVR, increases ROC-AUC not only for serving pCTCVR but also for pCVR by 2.1% and 1.6%, respectively, and PR-AUC by 9.9% and 8.8%, respectively, relative to the ESMM baseline. We also test negative downsampling with 5% nonclick retention. Downsampled KD-0.3 increases mean AUC for serving pCTCVR and pCVR by 1.2% and 0.9%, respectively, -and PR-AUC by 8.5% and 4.5%, respectively, relative to downsampled ESMM.

items.summary: Identifies a training-serving mismatch in ESMM-style conversion modeling where the deployed pCVR tower is paired with a separately trained serving pCTR model that differs from the auxiliary tower. It distills logged serving pCTR scores into the auxiliary tower to align pCTCVR at serving time, improving ranking decisions.
items.reasoning: A crisp identification of a real production mismatch with a simple, deployable distillation fix; directly relevant to industrial recommendation systems. Industrial-academic authorship adds credibility, but the technique is narrow and incremental within established ESMM lines.

items.title: Protected Unbiased Sparsification: A Sharp Loewner Curve
items.content: arXiv:2611.15247v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Random sparsification replaces a probability vector by a random vector with few nonzero entries. We ask for unbiasedness, exact preservation of prescribed linear statistics, and a covariance guarantee for every downstream linear response. Let $p$ have $k$ positive coordinates, let $A$ specify the protected statistics, and let $d\le k-2$ be their effective rank. For every $d+1\le m\le k$, we construct an unbiased random probability vector $Q$ with at most $m$ nonzero coordinates, $AQ=Ap$ on every realization, and $\operatorname{Cov}(Q)\preceq h C_{p\mid A}$, where $h=(k-m)/((m-d)(k-d-1))$ and $C_{p\mid A}$ is the categorical covariance after optimal linear adjustment for the protected statistics. This coefficient is sharp uniformly over instances, even among biased estimators when error is measured by its second moment. A residual covariance bridge extends the concurrent unprotected curve to arbitrary pathwise linear protection. We also characterize instance-optimal constants for partitions with uniform weights within classes and derive bounds for peaked weights. For rational inputs, an exact Las Vegas sampler attains the curve within a factor $1+\epsilon$ in expected polynomial time. A separate fast block-pivotal sampler preserves block masses and is no worse in covariance order than independent sampling within blocks. Experiments illustrate the theory on synthetic weights and language-model attention. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct decoding, the fast sampler preserves block masses, while comparisons with VarOpt remain statistically inconclusive and top-$m$ truncation scores highest on RULER.

items.summary: Studies random sparsification of probability vectors subject to unbiasedness, exact preservation of protected linear statistics, and covariance guarantees, constructing schemes with a provably sharp covariance coefficient via a Loewner-order analysis. The result gives optimal variance bounds as a function of support size and effective rank of protected statistics.

items.title: Observations Drift, Structures Remain: Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment for Electromagnetic Signals
items.content: arXiv:2611.15566v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Electromagnetic signal modeling is increasingly moving toward self-supervised pretraining on heterogeneous I/Q observations. However, an observed waveform is jointly shaped by signal generation, propagation environments, and acquisition processes, which mix reusable structural regularities with observation-specific variations. Existing methods usually pursue unified pretraining with reconstruction objectives on mixed observations. This heterogeneity creates two key mismatches for reconstruction pretraining: (1) appearance mismatch, induced by propagation-dependent waveform variations; and (2) temporal mismatch, induced by acquisition-dependent sampling coordinates. These mismatches make observation-specific appearances and sampling coordinates easier to reconstruct than stable signal structures, inducing observational shortcuts. We identify this failure mode as observation-biased pretraining. To address this, we propose Structural Pretraining with Time Alignment for heterogeneous EM signals. It mitigates temporal mismatch with RoPE-fs, which maps token positions to sampling-rate-normalized physical-time positions, and reduces reliance on appearance shortcuts by replacing waveform reconstruction with masked prediction of discrete structural units. These units are organized into atomic structural units and emergent structural units that capture variable-length compositional patterns beyond fixed patch boundaries. Across diverse EM benchmarks, our method improves both full-supervision and few-shot adaptation over existing EM pretraining baselines, showing that the learned representations better preserve structural consistency when observations drift in waveform appearance and temporal scale.

items.title: WELP : Weighted Ensemble in the LooP for committor learning
items.content: arXiv:2611.15963v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Understanding how complex molecular systems transition between metastable states is a central challenge in computational chemistry and biophysics. A key tool for characterizing these transitions is the committor function: the probability that a trajectory initiated from a given configuration reaches one state before another. Because the committor encodes both the progress and the mechanism of a transition, it is an ideal collective variable (CV). Learning it, however, requires sampling the rare transitions it describes. We address this circular dependency with a ``WE-in-the-loop'' framework that couples committor learning with weighted ensemble (WE), an enhanced sampling method that uses a CV to drive transition dynamics. Our framework alternates between the two: WE simulation generates transition data for training a neural network committor with a self-consistent loss, and the learned committor then serves as an improved CV for subsequent WE simulation. Across a two-channel 2D system, alanine dipeptide, and chignolin, our framework consistently outperforms greedy baselines, highlighting the importance of principled exploration. We also curate a public benchmark of empirically determined committor values for alanine dipeptide. Together, the framework and benchmark provide a new method for studying rare transitions in high-dimensional molecular systems and a standard for evaluating committor learning methods.

items.summary: The paper couples committor function learning with weighted ensemble enhanced sampling in a WE-in-the-loop framework, alternating between refining the committor as a collective variable and using it to drive rare-transition sampling for molecular systems. This addresses the circular dependency of needing to sample the transitions the committor describes.
items.reasoning: A clever loop-based integration of ML and enhanced sampling with value for computational chemistry and biophysics; novelty is real but scoped to molecular simulation applications.

We also curate a public benchmark of empirically determined committor values for alanine dipeptide. Together, the framework and benchmark provide a new method for studying rare transitions in high-dimensional molecular systems and a standard for evaluating committor learning methods.

items.title: Subject-Held-Out Evaluation of Deep Ground Reaction Force Estimators Across Two Laboratories: Leakage and Cross-Laboratory Transfer
items.content: arXiv:2611.15966v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Deep networks that estimate ground reaction forces and centers of pressure from motion-capture markers are validated within one laboratory, in a seldom-stated coordinate frame, and sometimes with trial-level splits that put the same person in the training and the test set. We measured what each practice costs, and whether such models transfer between laboratories. Three sequence models (convolutional, convolutional-recurrent, and convolutional-transformer) were evaluated on two independent datasets, locomotion (6 subjects) and occupational patient handling (10 subjects), under one pipeline, one tuning procedure, three seeds, and four protocols: trial-level split, leave-one-subject-out, pooled two-laboratory training with matched held-out subjects, and cross-laboratory transfer. At a fixed configuration, trial-level splits overstated the subject-held-out coefficient of determination by +0.040 to +0.194; on occupational data the overstatement exceeded every difference between architectures. With subjects held out, the three models reached values between 0.583 and 0.804; the leader differed between datasets, and gaps lay within subject-to-subject variability. Pooling the laboratories changed neither dataset on matched subjects. Transfer between laboratories was below chance in both directions, including the vertical force, which no in-plane rotation can affect. Leaving force targets in the plate frame while inputs were heading-aligned cost 0.57 of locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance, enough to make that force look hardest; a Newton's-law correlation detected the mismatch before training. Split protocol and target frame changed reported accuracy more than architecture did. Learned force estimators should be validated with subjects held out, checked for frame consistency before training, and tested across laboratories before deployment claims are made.

items.title: MS-rPPG: Multi-spectral State Space Model for Remote Photoplethysmography in Driver Monitoring Systems
items.content: arXiv:2606.21115v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is a camera-based technique for measuring physiological signals, particularly cardiac activity. From the remotely measured signals, heart rate can be estimated, which is crucial for health monitoring. In this study, we investigate a driver health monitoring system based on remote heart rate estimation. However, driving environments represent uncontrolled settings where videos are subject to varying illumination conditions and frequent head movements. We introduce MS-rPPG, a multi-spectral framework that combines RGB with near-infrared (NIR) face video to alleviate rPPG estimation under challenging driving conditions. To combine the complementary features from two spectral videos, we propose a cross-spectral linear modulation (CSLM) strategy based on frequency-domain analysis. Moreover, we introduce MS-Mamba, a novel state space model designed to effectively model long-range temporal dependencies while jointly capturing cross-channel interactions between multi-spectral features. We collected a real-world dataset called MS-Drive, which was recorded from 50 participants while driving the vehicle. The proposed method was evaluated on the MR-NIRP Car dataset and MS-Drive datasets. The experimental results indicate that MS-rPPG shows better robustness and heart rate estimation accuracy than previous methods, highlighting its promise for driver health monitoring. The codes are available at github.com/ziiho08/MS-rPPG.

items.summary: MS-rPPG combines RGB and near-infrared face video via a cross-spectral state space model to estimate heart rate robustly under challenging driving conditions with variable illumination and head movement. It targets driver health monitoring where standard rPPG degrades.

items.title: Clustering trajectories of modelled estimates: an uncertainty-aware framework, with an application to global cardiovascular disease burden, 1990 to 2023
items.content: arXiv:2611.14529v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Modelled health estimates such as those of the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study are increasingly used in secondary analyses designed for observed data. However, trajectory clustering typically ignores published uncertainty, selects the number of clusters using criteria blind to it, and assigns countries to groups with unwarranted certainty. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that separates trajectory level from shape, quantifies membership probabilities by perturbing estimates within their uncertainty intervals, selects clusters based on stability under uncertainty, and examines the roles of development, region, and measurement quality. Applied to age-standardised cardiovascular disease DALY rates for 201 countries from 1990-2023 (GBD 2023), the framework identified two stable trajectory types, whereas the gap statistic selected three. The additional cluster was poorly supported (median membership probability 0.70) and disappeared once uncertainty was considered. The retained clusters had similar burdens in 1990 but diverged markedly over time: a stalled-improvement group of 78 countries (median change $-8\%$, 40 of them in sub-Saharan Africa) and a sustained-decline group of 92 countries ($-52\%$). Thirty-one countries remained unclassified because their memberships were uncertain. Results were reproduced using mortality rates, a 2000-2023 analysis window, and bootstrap resampling. Among countries with the narrowest uncertainty intervals, a third well-supported trajectory emerged in former Soviet and Eastern European countries. These findings show that uncertainty affects both the number and composition of trajectory clusters. Ignoring it risks over-interpreting unstable groups and overstating confidence in country classifications. Incorporating published uncertainty and measurement quality should become standard practice when clustering modelled health estimates.

items.title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
items.content: arXiv:2611.14540v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.

items.summary: The paper applies graph kernels (Katz kernel) to mechanistic signaling network models of patients to stratify breast cancer cohorts by comparing pathway structures rather than mutations alone. This enables identification of clinically meaningful subgroups in precision oncology.
items.reasoning: Nice integration of graph kernels with mechanistic signaling networks for a clinically meaningful task, but application-limited and the kernel technique is established.

items.title: On-Edge Acoustic Continual Anomaly Detection: A Cross-Platform Comparative Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.15465v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Acoustic Anomaly Detection (AAD) serves as a non-contact approach for machine condition monitoring, yet much of the existing research is evaluated offline and rarely addresses embedded hardware constraints or microphone variations under operational drift. This paper presents a comparative evaluation of on-edge continual AAD across two embedded platforms the ESP32-S3 (with an external I2S digital microphone) and the Arduino Nicla Vision (with an onboard Pulse Density Modulation (PDM) microphone) using a shared detection model. The model utilizes a lightweight ShallowNet encoder and contrastive prototype learning to map spectrograms into a 32-dimensional embedding space. Both boards run an identical TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) encoder, performing on-device prototype learning updated via an exponential moving average. A cloud pipeline orchestrated through Firebase and MQTT enables remote data collection and retraining. Evaluated via a controlled speaker-replay protocol using standardized Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE) Challenge Task 2 machine sounds, the ESP32-S3 achieved 82.35% to 95.00% accuracy across five machine types, while the Nicla Vision achieved 79.41% to 95.00%. The two platforms demonstrated comparable performance, confirming that the lightweight prototypical architecture transfers reliably across distinct hardware and sensor tiers.

items.summary: This comparative study deploys continual acoustic anomaly detection for machine condition monitoring on two embedded platforms (ESP32-S3 and Arduino Nicla Vision) using a lightweight ShallowNet encoder with contrastive prototype learning and TensorFlow Lite Micro. items.title: Reliable Near-Field Source Enumeration and Positioning Informed by Two-Stage MUSIC
items.content: arXiv:2611.15722v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Accurate and reliable near-field multi-source localization is essential for location-aware processing in future wireless systems. However, coherent multipath propagation complicates the direct recovery of line-of-sight (LoS) source positions, while existing estimation methods generally lack explicit control of the risk of source underestimation and positioning uncertainty. In this paper, we investigate reliable source enumeration and positioning in near-field coherent multipath environments. Specifically, we develop a conformal risk control (CRC) based source enumeration scheme that calibrates the penalty coefficient of an eigenvalue-based criterion to control the expected miss-detection ratio at a prescribed level. We further propose MUSIC-Net, a model-based deep learning framework informed by two-stage MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC), which learns the LoS-related subspace and surrogate distances through subspace-distance-based training, thereby enabling direct source positioning without estimating non-line-of-sight (NLoS) path parameters or performing subsequent path association. To quantify the uncertainty of the estimated positions, we develop a split conformal prediction (SCP) based calibration method that constructs angle-range predicted regions with finite-sample simultaneous coverage guarantees. Numerical results show that the proposed framework effectively controls the risk of source underestimation, while providing improved positioning accuracy with tighter predicted regions than benchmarks given the same target coverage levels.

items.summary: This signal-processing paper develops conformal-risk-control-based source enumeration and MUSIC-informed positioning for near-field coherent multipath environments, calibrating penalty coefficients to bound miss-detection risk. The approach explicitly controls source-underestimation and positioning uncertainty for future location-aware wireless systems.

items.title: Random Exploration is Random
items.content: arXiv:2611.17011v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Decision making often requires balancing exploitation of familiar options with exploration of uncertain alternatives. One strategy for exploration is random exploration, in which choices become more variable and less tied to the option that currently appears best. However, it remains unclear whether this variability reflects genuine stochasticity or instead a deterministic structure that traditional cognitive models fail to capture. We examined this question using the Horizon Task in an aggregated dataset of 1,392 participants completing over 1,270,695 trials. In this task, exploration becomes more valuable when participants have more future choices, and choice variability increases under longer horizons. We tested whether more expressive neural network models could recover deterministic structure from this additional variability. Although neural networks provided better overall fits to behavior than the traditional model, long-horizon choices remained consistently less predictable than short-horizon choices. These findings show that limited model expressiveness cannot fully account for the increased variability associated with random exploration, suggesting random exploration truly is substantially random.

items.summary: Using the Horizon Task with 1,392 participants and over 1.27 million trials, the authors test whether human random exploration reflects genuine stochasticity or deterministic structure that standard cognitive models miss. They find that more expressive computational models fail to beat simple random exploration in capturing choice variability, suggesting human exploratory variability is largely noise-like.
items.reasoning: Large-scale, well-powered cognitive science study with a memorable null-style result; methodologically strong and relevant to exploration research, but its impact is more on cognitive modeling than machine learning methodology.

items.title: Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering
items.content: arXiv:2611.17226v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Graph-based collaborative filtering learns user and item representations by propagating embeddings over a user--item interaction graph. We investigate a modular, sheaf-inspired scoring extension placed on top of a three-layer LightGCN backbone. The motivation comes from cellular sheaves, where local vector spaces are related by linear restriction maps; here, this idea motivates structured, pair-dependent transformations of user and item embeddings rather than a change to graph propagation. We compare the identity inner-product scorer, diagonal, rank-one low-rank, and full matrix residual scorers, and a parameter-matched residual MLP baseline (\texttt{mlp\_full}) on Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018. We report ranking quality and catalog coverage at cutoffs 10 and 20. The selected structured variants show modest, dataset-dependent changes in ranking quality and sometimes substantial changes in coverage. Our method is inspired by sheaf geometry but does not construct a cellular sheaf or implement sheaf-Laplacian diffusion; the experiments therefore do not establish a causal benefit from sheaf geometry itself.

It compares these variants against parameter-matched MLP baselines on four standard recommendation benchmarks.

items.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
items.content: arXiv:2611.17246v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

items.title: IsharaBART: An efficient BART-Based Framework for Low-Resource Bangla Sign Language Translation
items.content: arXiv:2611.16359v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Millions of Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) users lack reliable automatic translation tools. Existing systems are limited by data scarcity, unidirectional design, and computationally expensive architectures that are not suitable for low-resource deployment. We introduce IsharaBART, a bidirectional generative framework for gloss-sentence translation in BdSL. IsharaBART uses Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers (BART)-based conditional language modeling with denoising learning objectives. We developed a parallel dataset of 1,000 professionally annotated gloss-sentence pairs, balanced across tenses and structures. We expanded the dataset to 4,831 pairs through four augmentation techniques: rule-based tense transformations, masked token substitutions, back-translation, and one-shot prompting. A compact denoising sequence-to-sequence model was pre-trained from scratch on monolingual Bangla text from six different corpora, then fine-tuned on the annotated and augmented datasets. We compare IsharaBART against four larger baseline models under identical conditions, where it achieves comparable or superior bidirectional performance. On the gloss-to-sentence (G2S) task, it attains Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU-4) score up to 51.7, and on the sentence-to-gloss (S2G) task, it achieves 61.40, outperforming multilingual models despite having fewer than 10% of the parameters. items.title: How Far Can Frozen Vision-Language Models Go on Event Data? A Training-Free Study on EventBench
items.content: arXiv:2611.15756v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.

items.title: Actuation and Control of Passive Tendon-Driven Soft Extensions Through Rigid Manipulator Motion
items.content: arXiv:2611.15386v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Industrial manipulators offer reach and precision but can damage nearby structures in confined spaces. Soft robots provide compliant contact but typically have limited reach. Rigid-soft systems combine their advantages, although they often require dedicated actuation and control hardware. We propose actuating a passive tendon-driven soft extension through manipulator joint motion. As the robot moves, the exterior spans of tendons anchored to upstream links change, altering tendon tension and deforming the extension. Inspection through narrow apertures, for example, constrains the motion of the end effector (EE). We develop a controller that regulates the soft tip while preserving such EE constraints. A differential model separates rigid transport from soft deformation, combining analytic arm and tendon kinematics with a locally identified span-to-deformation map. We also derive a local upper bound on the number of independent deformation directions transmitted by the tendons under the EE constraint, and conditions for the exponential convergence of the tip error. A quadratic program with control barrier functions imposes obstacle clearance, fulcrum limits, and model-validity conditions. Simulations and real experiments show tip and shape regulation under free, position-constrained, and fulcrum-constrained EE motion.
items.author: Ignacio Cuiral-Zueco, Gonzalo L\'opez-Nicol\'as, Youcef Mezouar
items.summary: The paper proposes actuating a passive tendon-driven soft extension using only the motion of a rigid manipulator, avoiding dedicated actuation hardware, and develops a controller that regulates the soft tip while respecting end-effector constraints such as fitting through narrow apertures. This rigid-soft combination targets inspection tasks where industrial reach and precision must coexist with compliant contact. It is a clever systems contribution bridging soft robotics and industrial manipulation.

items.title: SPARC: RoboCup Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition with Initial Datasets, Software, and Simulation Environments
items.content: arXiv:2611.15443v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The RoboCup Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition (SPARC) is a new competition under development of the RoboCup Rescue Robot League that uses the Unitree A2-W as a common robot platform. SPARC aims to make research on artificial intelligence for autonomous rescue robots accessible to a broader research community, including groups without expertise in developing and maintaining custom robot hardware. By providing a capable standard platform and established benchmark environments, researchers can focus on autonomous navigation, perception, manipulation, and embodied AI for challenging disaster-response scenarios. This paper introduces the SPARC competition, its benchmark environment, and the Unitree A2-W standard platform. Furthermore, we present the first open SPARC datasets collected during the IEEE ICRA 2026 Legged Robot Challenges and RoboCup Rescue 2026, release an open-source software stack for autonomous navigation, and provide initial simulation assets representing RoboCup Rescue test environments. Together, these resources aim to lower the barrier to entry for autonomous rescue robotics and facilitate reproducible research and collaborative development on a common hardware platform.

Standardized platforms have historically accelerated research communities, so this could do the same for disaster-response robotics.

items.title: Robot-Induced Bias in Movement Smoothness Metrics for Rehabilitation: Quantification and Correction in Simulation
items.content: arXiv:2611.15743v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robot mechanics can bias kinematic measures of recovery and limit comparisons across rehabilitation devices. We developed a closed-loop human-robot simulation calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics. Paired runs held motor-control parameters and movement plans fixed to quantify bias in seven metrics relative to a low-impedance reference, normalized using external repeatability benchmarks. Within a subset informed by published device specifications, median log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) bias was 0.93 and 1.79 benchmark units for stroke and healthy profiles, respectively. Sobol analysis identified Coulomb friction and apparent mass as leading contributors; LDLJ bias persisted across 11 robustness variants. LDLJ bias increased as simulated movements became less fragmented. If recovery similarly reduces fragmentation, this effect could partly mask improvement in measured smoothness. Correction combining identified robot dynamics and observed metrics with gradient-boosted trees reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.77 to 0.10 for LDLJ and from 0.24 to 0.08 for spectral arc length (SPARC) in the device-informed subset of a random 20% hold-out. Median smoothness residuals remained at or below 0.15 benchmark units across four separately held-out parameter regions. Under an alternative controller, LDLJ error decreased from 1.60 to 0.17 without retraining, although transfer varied across metrics. These simulation results support mechanical characterization and movement-dependent correction toward more comparable robotic assessments, motivating validation in patients.

items.summary: The paper shows that robot mechanics can systematically bias kinematic recovery metrics such as log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) used in rehabilitation, potentially invalidating cross-device comparisons. This is an important methodological warning for the rehabilitation robotics field.

items.title: Prediction-Error-Tightened MPC for Socially Compliant Crowd Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2611.15781v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autonomous navigation of mobile robots in crowded environments, while preserving pedestrians' psychological comfort, requires distinguishing pedestrians from other obstacles, predicting their future motion, and accounting for uncertainty in the predicted trajectories of both pedestrians and the robot. This work extends a previous MPC framework by integrating obstacle and pedestrian detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online prediction-error estimation directly within the collision-avoidance mechanism. To reduce collision-avoidance complexity in crowded scenarios, nearby obstacles are aggregated, thereby reducing the number of collision-avoidance constraints. Simulation studies evaluate the prediction-error margins and the computational benefits of semantics-aware aggregation. In a paired 300-seed closed-loop comparison with a moving generic obstacle, Markov residual tightening reduces the fraction of runs with physical contact from $10.0\%$ to $1.33\%$, at a mean travel-time cost of $0.68$ s. In a separate crowd-navigation semantic ablation, the offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap occupies $2.11\%$ of observed time with pedestrian-aware handling versus $22.84\%$ with generic-obstacle handling.

items.title: Safe and Efficient Navigation Considering Texting Pedestrians via Attention-Aware Cost-map Tuning
items.content: arXiv:2611.16725v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Smartphone-distracted pedestrians deviate from social norms unpredictably and cannot be relied upon to yield to approaching robots -- a safety challenge that existing navigation methods are poorly equipped to handle, since they treat all pedestrians uniformly regardless of attention state. We propose an attention-aware navigation framework that classifies each pedestrian as attentive or distracted in real-time using 3D skeletal features and a Random Forest classifier, then dynamically widens cost-map safety margins around distracted individuals to drive proactive avoidance. A within-subjects user study with 12 participants across 252 trials demonstrates significant improvements in perceived smoothness (p = 0.003) and predictability (p = 0.034) over both a LiDAR-only baseline and a trajectory-prediction-only method, without any increase in travel time. Notably, trajectory prediction alone does not improve subjective navigation quality unless coupled with attention-state-aware cost adjustment -- confirming that appropriately responding to who is in front of the robot can matter more than trajectory smoothness alone.

items.title: Ephemeral agents escape the Arrow Information Paradox
items.content:
The Arrow information paradox (AIP) says there's no ideal way for a potential buyer to determine the value (to them) of some private information a seller is offering to sell them, without actually receiving the information, thus jumping the gun on the potential trade.

The paradox happens because a sale of information is:

- Irreversible: the information can't be "returned" like a physical good, once the cat's out of the bag
- Indivisible: there's no sense in which "half a secret" can be half as valuable as the whole secret

In other words, if you're considering buying a huge amount of wine but you don't know the quality, you can sample a random bottle of the wine, and if the connoisseur who works for you says it's good you buy the whole lot. But if the thing you're considering buying is One Big Important Secret, you couldn't do something like this (at least in the pre-LLM era).

Of course, the way this has been dealt with in practice is NDAs. And patents I guess. But these only go so far, since they depend on a government to enforce the NDAs, and there have been exceptions where people broke NDAs for arguably justified reasons, e.g. whistleblowers. So in some cases the seller would still prefer to enforce the privacy by technical rather than legal means.

Why, fundamentally, has the AIP held? It's because (until recently) there has been no evaluator able to both:

- Understand the secret information and make qualitative judgements about its value, in the buyer's specific context
- Credibly forget everything about the secret information (or alternatively just vanish, removing the need for "forgetting")

Human evaluators can understand and exercise judgement but can't forget; cryptography (zero-knowledge proofs, confidential computing, etc.) can forget but can't judge....

items.summary: The post argues that ephemeral AI agents, which can evaluate private information and then vanish without retaining or disclosing it, offer a novel resolution to the Arrow information paradox by making information appraisal possible without jumping the gun on the trade. This could enable new market mechanisms for selling secrets without NDAs or patents.
items.reasoning: A clever and original application of a classic economics puzzle to LLM-mediated trust and information markets; conceptually interesting for mechanism design around AI agents, though purely conceptual with no formalization or implementation.

This could enable new market mechanisms for selling secrets without NDAs or patents.

items.title: There is no such thing as cosmophagous AI
items.content:
Cosmophagous AI (my name for AI that races desperately at near-light speeds to grab that last galaxy, that last star, that last planet before it forever recedes over the cosmological horizon) is sometimes invoked as a counterargument to the idea that even an ASI that is mostly indifferent to our fate would keep us around if the cost of doing so were sufficiently low.

For example, Ryan Greenblatt makes the following point in Notes on fatalities from AI takeover:

[T]he costs of keeping physical humans alive are extremely low, probably it only slows the industrial expansion by a small amount (and this slowdown is probably the dominant effect from a resource perspective), probably by less than 1 month and very likely less than 1 year. Delaying this long costs a pretty tiny fraction of long-run cosmic resources, probably well less than one billionth of the resources that will ultimately be accessible to the AIs in aggregate.

Thus, extremely small amounts of motivation to keep humans alive could suffice for avoiding large fractions of humans dying due to industrial expansion (depending on the exact preferences of the AI).

Writing in the comment section, Tanner Cook counters:

Framing the cost of a delay as "a billionth" of expected return, then reasoning that because a billionth is a small fraction it is a negligible cost feels like sloppy reasoning.

So let's put actual numbers to it. A delay of a month represents the loss of about 26 billion stars and their respective planets. Suddenly the assumption that preserving humans is worth losing 26 billion solar systems seems a lot less sure. A delay of a day costs 850 million solar systems.

In this post, I argue that our observational evidence and, indeed, our very existence is a strong argument against the existence of cosmophagous AI.

# Our bubble in space...

items.summary: A conceptual x-risk argument contesting the cosmophagous AI scenario (racing at near-light speed to grab cosmic resources before they recede over the cosmological horizon), which is sometimes invoked to argue an indifferent ASI would still kill humans. The author engages with Ryan Greenblatt's cost estimates for keeping humans alive and Tanner Cook's counterarguments to show the scenario is not physically coherent as stated.
items.reasoning: A substantive contribution to long-term x-risk theorizing that directly engages named researchers' arguments and physical constraints. It is purely conceptual with no empirical content, and the stakes of the disagreement are speculative, but it sharpens an argument used in fatality analyses.

So let's put actual numbers to it. A delay of a month represents the loss of about 26 billion stars and their respective planets. Suddenly the assumption that preserving humans is worth losing 26 billion solar systems seems a lot less sure. A delay of a day costs 850 million solar systems.

In this post, I argue that our observational evidence and, indeed, our very existence is a strong argument against the existence of cosmophagous AI.

# Our bubble in space...

items.title: FDT and the sacrificial volunteer's dilemma
items.content:
Consider the "twin sacrificial volunteer's dilemma":[1]

1000 identical agents have the same deterministic decision-making process and the same observations, and can't communicate with each other. They can decide to either do nothing, or pay $1 to volunteer. If at least one agent volunteers, everyone who didn't volunteer gets $1 million[2]. Volunteers never receive anything. All of this is common knowledge.

Payoff matrix for clarity:

You don't volunteer

You volunteer

Nobody else volunteers

$0

-$1

Someone else volunteers

$1M

-$1

Because the agents all make decisions the same way, there are only two possible outcomes (in bold in the table): everybody volunteers (everybody gets -$1) or nobody volunteers (everybody gets $0). Not volunteering is the dominant strategy, and all reasonable decision theories don't volunteer.

(In this situation the agents can't implement a policy like "volunteer with a small chance", since they are deterministic and don't have access to randomness).[3]

## Giving agents serial numbers

Now imagine the same situation, but instead of every agent having the same observations, every agent has a serial number from 1-1000 and is told their serial number (and this is common knowledge). This serial number doesn't change anything about the payoffs. I call this the "numbered sacrificial volunteer's dilemma", and here the symmetry is broken so it's possible for some agents to volunteer and others to not. Does this change things? CDT and EDT agents still don't volunteer for almost the same reasons as before. Functional decision theory is more complicated. (This scenario is somewhat similar to this one from the UDT1.1 description.)...

items.summary: The post analyzes a twin sacrificial volunteer's dilemma among 1000 identical deterministic agents, showing that not volunteering is dominant and all reasonable decision theories decline, then extends the analysis to agents with serial numbers to explore how functional decision theory handles asymmetries in the volunteering decision.
items.reasoning: A clear, well-constructed decision-theory puzzle with payoff analysis and a natural generalization, useful for the FDT research program. It is conceptual game-theory work without empirical content and its practical implications for AI systems are indirect, but it advances a niche technical debate competently.
