items.title: Interpretable machine learning diagnosis of degradation mechanisms in lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells from temperature- and illumination-dependent electrical measurements
items.content: arXiv:2611.16750v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Machine learning coupled with device simulation is widely used to optimize thin-film solar cells, but almost exclusively in the forward direction, from device parameters to predicted performance. The inverse problem encountered after fabrication, namely identifying the mechanism that limits a given device, is still addressed by manual inspection of characterization data. In this work, both directions are examined for lead-free $RbSn_{0.5}Ge_{0.5}I_{3}$ solar cells using approximately 42,000 SCAPS-1D simulations. Replacing the Spiro-OMeTAD hole transport layer with CuI increases the simulated power conversion efficiency from 19.6\% to 21.6\%, almost entirely through the fill factor. Surrogate models trained and tested on a factorial parameter grid substantially overstate their predictive accuracy. An XGBoost regressor attains $R^2 = 0.9997$ on held-out grid points but only 0.58 on independently sampled devices, whereas training on a Latin hypercube design of comparable size restores $R^2 = 0.995$. For the inverse problem, a multi-label classifier identifies which of six degradation mechanisms are present from simulated temperature- and illumination-dependent open-circuit-voltage measurements. It achieves a macro $F_1$ score of 0.938, compared to 0.687 for a calibrated physics-rule baseline. The classifier does not, however, generalize to combinations of mechanisms absent from the training set.

items.title: Calibration and Conformal Prediction for Medical Question Answering in Arabic and English: Evidence from Two Non-Parallel Benchmarks
items.content: arXiv:2611.16821v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly tested on medical exam questions, but accuracy alone does not show when an answer can be trusted. I study the calibration and uncertainty of two open-weight models, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Jais-adapted-7B-chat (both run in 4-bit precision), on 2,816 English multiple-choice questions from MedMCQA and 4,927 Arabic multiple-choice questions from MedAraBench. Accuracy was 0.561 (English) and 0.430 (Arabic) for Qwen, and 0.369 and 0.308 for Jais. Raw option probabilities were overconfident in all four settings (expected calibration error 0.242 to 0.486), and a single temperature parameter removed 82% to 93% of that error. Split conformal prediction reached its nominal coverage in all 24 settings I tested (within 0.006), but the sets were large when accuracy was low: at 90% coverage, temperature-scaled sets contained on average 63% (Qwen, English), 78% (Qwen, Arabic), 86% (Jais, English) and 89% (Jais, Arabic) of the options. The margin between the top two option probabilities separated correct from incorrect answers best for Qwen on English (AUROC 0.734) and worst for Jais on Arabic (0.579). Answering only the 20% most confident questions lowered Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. Jais showed a strong prior for option C (49% of English and 60% of Arabic predictions). Scoring Latin letters only cut the Arabic share to 29% but left accuracy, raw ECE and AUROC nearly unchanged. Because the two benchmarks differ in subject, level and number of options, I do not attribute differences between languages to language itself. Code is available at https://github.com/Mariyaaleem/arabic-english-medqa-uncertainty.

items.title: Paper-Faithful Federated Learning: Scientific Checks for Practitioner and Agent Development
items.content: arXiv:2611.17129v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Federated learning experiments can produce reasonable-looking results even when the experiment implementation differs from the intended experimental protocol. Small errors in configuration, data partitioning, aggregation, randomness, evaluation, or checkpoint recovery may therefore affect a comparison without causing the program to fail. We present FedBrew, a research codebase for controlled and reproducible federated learning experiments. Its focus is controlled simulation with checks of specified conditions of the intended experimental protocol. FedBrew uses configuration checks, identifiable client data partitions, checkpoint recovery checks, self-describing run records, and development-time checks of scientific conditions. These checks assess, for example, whether client partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and aggregation weights match the prescribed rule; numerical and recovery checks examine non-finite client model states and interrupted runs. The same structure also provides clear extension points and automated checks for new algorithms, datasets, models, and tasks, whether they are added by researchers or AI coding agents. FedBrew therefore supports reproducible and inspectable FL experiments through checks of specified software and scientific conditions and the run records associated with reported results.

The paper argues such scientific checks are needed because plausible-looking FL results can arise from buggy implementations.
items.reasoning: Addresses a genuine reproducibility problem in FL research and is timely given agentic experiment automation, but the contribution is tooling and checklists rather than new science.

items.title: Computational Raga Recognition: A Theory-Driven Approach
items.content: arXiv:2611.15242v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Raga recognition in Hindustani classical music is difficult because a raga is not defined only by the notes used in it. Its identity also depends on the way notes are emphasized, the movement between notes and characteristic phrases. In this work, we develop a computational approach to analyse these characteristics directly from audio recordings. The method uses pitch extracted from recordings and represents it using a 44-position note framework based on the 22-shruti system. From this representation, Raga features based on the Indian classical musicology are extracted.Each feature is compared with a reference representation of the raga and the resulting scores are combined to obtain an overall similarity score. The method is first studied using Raga Yaman and is then tested on recordings of other ragas. The computational results are also compared with the theoretical description of Yaman to identify which raga characteristics are captured well and where the method has limitations.
items.author: Janay Sukheja, Shailaja D. Sharma
items.summary: The authors build a computational system for recognizing ragas in Hindustani classical music from audio, using pitch extraction over a 44-position framework grounded in the 22-shruti system and musicology-derived features compared against reference raga representations. The theory-driven approach distinguishes it from purely data-driven music classification.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful domain-specific contribution that meaningfully incorporates musicological structure, but the application niche is narrow and the likely performance and generality gains over deep learning baselines are unclear from the abstract.

items.title: Global-Local and Window-Concatenated Functional Random Forests: Early and Late Fusion of Window-Specific Functional Principal Components
items.content: arXiv:2611.15816v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Functional random forests built on a single functional principal component decomposition of the whole domain may dilute features confined to short intervals, whose location is rarely known in advance. We propose two random forests based on window-specific functional principal components. The global-local functional random forest (GL-FRF) is a late-fusion method that stacks a tuned full-curve forest and one forest per window with penalised convex weights; it contains the full-curve forest as a feasible solution, and its weights indicate which parts of the domain drive the prediction. The window-concatenated functional random forest (WC-FRF) is an early-fusion method that trains a single tuned forest on the concatenated window-specific scores. On twenty UCR datasets, GL-FRF improved on a tuned full-curve forest with the same number of trees on 16, with Brier score reductions of up to 0.21, significantly after Holm adjustment. No method was best on more than six datasets. WC-FRF was more accurate than GL-FRF on 13 datasets but failed when the signal required the full curve, whereas GL-FRF had the smallest mean and maximum excess over the best method across all 32 simulated and real settings, which makes it the safer choice when the location of the signal is unknown.
items.author: Fabrizio Maturo, Annamaria Porreca
items.summary: The authors propose two functional random forest variants using window-specific functional principal components: a late-fusion global-local forest with penalized convex weights and an early-fusion window-concatenated forest. These capture short-interval features that whole-curve decompositions dilute, with weights revealing which domain regions drive predictions.
items.reasoning: A sensible methodological extension for functional data analysis with interpretable fusion weights, but classical in nature, incremental relative to existing functional forest literature, and likely of limited interest to the core AI community.

items.title: Towards Democratising Low-Data Medical Image Classification: CPU-Trainable ZACH-ViT and Its Geometric Variants
items.content: arXiv:2611.16608v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Medical image classification in resource-constrained settings must contend with limited annotations and computational capacity. We evaluate four ZACH-ViT variants with linear, Euclidean prototype, Poincare and spherical heads alongside two compact multiple-instance-learning baselines. All models are trained from scratch with fewer than 260,000 parameters across seven MedMNIST+ datasets and three external benchmarks (PCam, ISIC2017 and Shenzhen tuberculosis radiographs). The low-data protocol uses 50 training images per class and five seeds, with validation-selected checkpoints at 23 and 47 epochs; a full-data reference uses one seed. Compact-TransMIL achieves the highest ten-dataset mean test Macro-F1 at 23 epochs (53.34%) and with full data (73.93%). At 47 epochs, ZACH-Linear narrowly leads (57.76% versus 57.54% for Compact-TransMIL). Extending training improves Macro-F1 in 239 of 300 paired comparisons. On ISIC2017, hZACH-Spherical has the highest 47-epoch low-data Macro-F1 (44.09% with SD 4.09%), whereas ZACH-EuclideanProto leads with full data (51.27%). We additionally conduct 40 CPU-only training runs on ISIC2017 and Shenzhen using four CPU threads; model-only single-image inference requires approximately 4-9 ms, while image decoding and preprocessing substantially increase end-to-end latency. The results demonstrate the feasibility of CPU-only training on the tested platform and the task- and regime-dependence of compact medical imaging under strict resource constraints.
items.author: Athanasios Angelakis
items.summary: The paper evaluates four ZACH-ViT variants with different head geometries (linear, Euclidean prototype, Poincare, spherical) with under 260,000 parameters, trainable on CPUs, across seven MedMNIST+ datasets and three external benchmarks under a 50-images-per-class low-data protocol. Results are mixed, with a compact TransMIL baseline achieving the best ten-dataset mean Macro-F1 in some settings.
items.reasoning: Accessible single-author work with a valuable accessibility goal (CPU-trainable medical imaging models), but the reported results appear mixed and the methodological novelty is modest; useful benchmarking contribution for low-resource settings.

items.title: AraCrypto-ML: A Multi-Label Corpus of Communicative Functions in Arabic Facebook Cryptocurrency Discourse
items.content: arXiv:2611.15408v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Arabic cryptocurrency discourse on social media is communicatively heterogeneous: a single post may report prices, explain protocols, promote investment, warn of scams, or invoke Islamic jurisprudence. Yet no annotated resource captures this functional diversity. We introduce AraCrypto-ML, a 10,000-post multi-label corpus of Arabic Facebook cryptocurrency discourse (2014-2024) from 2,898 public pages using a set of related keywords. Collected posts are annotated into six categories: Market Commentary, Educational, Promotional, Skeptical-Warning, Religious Framing, and Other/Unclear, using Fanar-2-27B under a prompt-only multi-label protocol. We validate 1,000 posts against adjudicated gold labels (macro kappa = 0.74) and apply Rogan-Gladen calibration to correct labelling bias. The two annotators agree with each other at macro kappa = 0.62 before adjudication, below the model's agreement with either of them (0.70 and 0.69). Reaction profiles differ strongly by function: Love is about 70% of reactions per post on Educational and Promotional posts but about 33% on Skeptical-Warning, which draws the largest Haha share (about 39%).

items.title: Forecasting Sales Delay through Time-aware Analysis of Sales Events in Textual Reports
items.content: arXiv:2611.16704v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Business-to-business (B2B) companies develop and deliver a one-of-a-kind product in response to a client's orders. To prepare resources for development beforehand, companies estimate dates when they will receive orders from clients in their sales process, called scheduled order dates. However, dates when the companies actually receive orders can differ from the scheduled order dates. This difference increases costs in the development. If the difference could be forecasted before receiving orders, companies could optimize their resource preparation. Towards reducing the costs, we introduce sales delay forecasting, a novel task of forecasting delay days from the scheduled order dates during sales process where sales representatives (sales reps) interact with the clients to receive orders. Sales delay forecasting is challenging because the sales process progress inherently involves uncertainty and depends on the client's willingness to order. To address this task, we propose confidence features which represent sales reps' confidence as a proxy measure of the client's willingness to order. To represent it, our method extracts dates of future sales events anticipated by sales reps from textual reports. To consider whether the confidence objectively looks reasonable, we also introduce status features which describe sales process status based on current date and past events. In experiments using real sales data, our method achieved a 16% lower mean absolute error compared with a feature-based baseline similar to a prior work. Moreover, our method outperformed non-feature-based baselines using large language models, indicating that it is crucial to explicitly create our features.

items.title: Improved CNN-Transformer Network for Neutron Image Super-Resolution
items.content: arXiv:2611.16620v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The spatial resolution of neutron images is of great importance for material defect diagnosis, structural characterization, and nondestructive testing. However, owing to limitations in neutron beam quality, scintillator conversion efficiency and light scattering, detector pixel size, and noise levels, conventional neutron images often suffer from speckle noise, blurred edges, and missing details, making them inadequate for high-precision analysis. To address these issues, an improved super-resolution model combining convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Transformers is proposed. First, to overcome the difficulty of obtaining high-quality and clear training images for neutron imaging, a pretrained image restoration model is fine-tuned using real neutron images and then employed to enhance existing neutron images, thereby providing high-quality reference images for subsequent super-resolution model training. Second, an improved CRAFT-based super-resolution network is developed by incorporating a hybrid prior-guided channel fusion module (HPCF), a mean-standard deviation dual-statistics squeeze-and-excitation block (MS-SEBlock), and a partial convolution feed-forward network (PCFN), with the aim of improving the reconstruction of important information, such as textures and fine details, in neutron images. Simulation results demonstrate that, compared with bicubic interpolation, SRCNN, SRGAN-VGG, and other methods, the proposed network achieves superior performance in both full-reference metrics, including PSNR and SSIM, and no-reference metrics, including AGM and SMD. The visual quality and structural fidelity of the reconstructed images are also significantly improved. This study provides a new approach to improving neutron image quality.

It fine-tunes a pretrained image restoration model to overcome the scarcity of high-quality neutron training images.
items.reasoning: A competent application of established CNN-Transformer SR techniques to a niche scientific imaging domain; methodological novelty is low and general AI impact is limited, though domain value is real.

items.title: From State of THE ART to Human Prediction Algorithms
items.content: arXiv:2611.16464v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Human curiosity and longing for the future have driven human progress from ancient times to the present. With the advancement of AI technology, human prediction algorithms have also drawn increasing attention from researchers. However, as AI technology continues to advance, we observe a counterintuitive phenomenon. Take human trajectory prediction algorithms as an example. Although models' quantitative prediction performance has improved, yielding one state-of-the-art model after another, the consideration of human behaviors, future thoughts, and social interactions themselves presents a gradually diminishing trend in the construction of these prediction algorithms, buried beneath numbers and metrics. In this manuscript, taking interactive art and human trajectory prediction algorithms as examples, we attempt to adopt a different analytical perspective to analyze the structural and developmental commonalities between these two fields. By examining specific interactive artworks and prediction algorithms, we aim to explore how human intuitions and art are associated with AI algorithms through three aspects, including perception, interaction, and timing, thereby providing new insights for the understanding and further research in this domain. We also observe an interesting phenomenon that certain art-inspired prediction algorithms can actually deduce intriguing patterns of human behaviors from the data, offering new potential avenues for understanding the relationship between human activities, state of The Art, and AI algorithms.
items.author: Conghao Wong, Ziqian Zou
items.summary: A position-style paper observing that in human trajectory prediction, quantitative performance has improved through successive state-of-the-art models while consideration of human behavior, future thoughts, and social interactions has diminishingly receded from algorithm design. It argues for re-centering behavioral modeling in prediction research.
items.reasoning: A worthwhile critique of metric-driven research culture, but as a position piece it offers mostly commentary with limited empirical or methodological novelty; influence depends on community reception.

items.title: LoRA Fine-Tuned Models for Control Systems Course Q\&A: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Model Scale and Rank Effects
items.content: arXiv:2609.13918v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in specialized university courses, but control-systems questions require coordinated terminology, notation, derivations, and stepwise explanations. Direct general-purpose responses may be inconsistently structured and hard to verify. Using exercises and reference solutions from a Linear Control Systems course, we built a supervised fine-tuning dataset of 360 system-user-assistant conversations. We applied LoRA to Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. With identical data splits, inference settings, and evaluation protocols, we compared base and fine-tuned models and tested LoRA ranks r=4, 8, and 16. Evaluation used ROUGE, BERTScore, and structured-output features to measure reference-answer similarity and stability of the Solution-Method-Teaching Points format. LoRA improved both similarity and structured-output stability at both sizes. On the current test set, 7B-r16 achieved the highest ROUGE-L (0.4093) and BERTScore-F1 (0.8643), while r=8 offered a better balance between performance and parameter efficiency. Bootstrap resampling showed ROUGE-L gains of 0.0764 [0.0613, 0.0915] for 3B-r16 and 0.0874 [0.0687, 0.1042] for 7B-r16; both intervals exceeded zero, indicating stable textual-similarity improvements on the current test set. These results suggest LoRA can align open-source instruction-tuned models more closely with the language and pedagogical organization of course reference answers. However, the metrics mainly capture textual similarity and formatting consistency, not domain-specific reasoning or mathematical correctness, which require expert assessment and task-specific rubrics.

It offers an educational-domain case study of how model scale and adapter rank affect the quality of specialized technical question answering. The work is useful for educators deploying low-cost fine-tuned models, though it applies established techniques rather than introducing new methods.

items.title: RGB-D SLAM on the Edge: Benchmarking and Profiling RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 on the Raspberry Pi 5
items.content: arXiv:2611.16472v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Micro aerial vehicles that operate without GPS often run SLAM on ARM-based edge boards, yet there is little published data on how standard RGB-D SLAM systems behave on such hardware. We benchmark RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 on the Raspberry Pi 5 using six TUM RGB-D sequences at three image resolutions, recording tracking coverage, trajectory error, time per frame, memory, CPU load and temperature for every run, and we profile both systems at the stage and function level. RTAB-Map was configured to process and keep every frame, so its back end runs on every frame rather than at its default rate of 1 Hz. On the sequences that every configuration tracked, its front end takes 38-74 ms per frame and its full pipeline 150-462 ms, compared with 13-45 ms and 26-62 ms for ORB-SLAM3. RTAB-Map's main cost is optimizing a pose graph that keeps growing, because its working memory is unbounded by default; ORB-SLAM3's local bundle adjustment costs about as much as its tracking but runs in a parallel thread. At quarter resolution, both systems lose tracking on most sequences, and runs that lose tracking finish sooner and report lower error on the poses they keep, so time and accuracy must be read alongside coverage. Timing is repeatable to within 1-5%, but trajectory error varies by up to 27% between identical runs, so the accuracy differences between the two systems are inconclusive. No thermal throttling occurred.
items.author: Himanshu Patil, Jaideep Joshi, Rohit Saluja, Ganesh Ramakrishnan
items.summary: This work benchmarks RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 on a Raspberry Pi 5 across six TUM RGB-D sequences and three resolutions, logging tracking coverage, trajectory error, per-frame time, memory, CPU load, and temperature, plus stage- and function-level profiling. It provides much-needed quantitative data on running standard RGB-D SLAM on ARM edge hardware for GPS-denied aerial vehicles. Results show substantial pipeline latency differences between the two systems.
items.reasoning: Careful and useful empirical benchmarking for edge robotics practitioners, but methodologically a measurement study without new algorithms.

items.title: A New Kind of Prediction Market for Science
items.content:
Regardless of the actual singularity, we have definitely hit one in arXiv submissions.

It is becoming apparent that the current paradigm of scientific knowledge production is not ready for AI.  Accelerating research speed and expanding access means there is a lot more slop and there is also a lot more good work, but way too much for the current peer review system to delineate between. We need some accurate and decentralized way to aggregate this information.

This makes a scientific prediction market, like Robin Hanson's idea futures, really appealing. The community can have markets for broad questions we care about, bystanders get paid for pointing out good research, and scientists are financially incentivized to make progress on the highest leverage issues. But with Hanson's conception, there is one big problem, which is how the market gets settled. For abstract scientific questions, like whether models are reward seeking or fitness seeking, we have no definitive event which can force market settlement. Hanson suggests that we use the convergence of scientific consensus, but this proposal takes trust in possibly misaligned opinions and requires the centralized coordination of scientists, which is hard to create---especially in pre-paradigmatic fields like AI safety.

In this post, I'll lay out a theoretical framework for a new kind of scientific prediction market. TL;DR: Scientific questions become perpetuals where the fair price is the expected direction of future evidence.

items.title: From FairBot to other cooperation conditions by substitution
items.content:
The simplest interesting player in MIRI's provability bot prisoner's dilemma tournament was FairBot, which cooperates if it can prove its opponent cooperates.
It cooperates with another FairBot despite the apparent infinite regress, by Löb's theorem (some might say magic).

A related line of work was how to represent statements like "if I take this action, it will have that consequence" in provability logic.
For example there's these old slides by Vladimir Slepnev that I came across on the MIRI website.

A post by James Payor brings these together.
Well, maybe he didn't think of it like that.
But I think of it as alternate FairBots, which look like different formalizations of the consequence of an action.
Like, a bot that cooperates if and only if it can prove its cooperation results in its opponent's cooperation.
Such bots are equivalent to FairBot conditional on Löb's theorem, but the idea was to cut off the infinite regress without Löb's theorem.

I'm writing this post to share some formula manipulations, simple substitutions really.
It turns out it's very easy to see that these bots are equivalent, assuming Löb's theorem.
But more importantly, we can clearly see the machinery by which Löb's theorem cuts off the infinite regress, and how these alternate formulations accomplish the same thing.

items.title: ORCA:Orthogonal Residual Consensus Alignment for Multi-View Clustering
items.content: arXiv:2611.16749v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Deep multi-view clustering often suffers from redundant information accumulation during fusion and indiscriminate alignment across representation levels. We propose Orthogonal Residual Consensus Alignment (ORCA) to address these challenges. Its semantic incremental recurrent fusion module extracts cross-view orthogonal residuals as non-redundant increments and adaptively weights recurrent states through divergence-guided gating. Its consensus-calibrated hierarchical contrastive alignment module uses the global consensus to weight contrastive alignment of view-level, pairwise, and recurrent representations. Together, these modules balance view-specific structure with cross-view consistency. Experiments on five benchmarks against fifteen competing methods demonstrate ORCA's effectiveness, including a 5.25 percent accuracy improvement over the strongest baseline on 100leaves. Ablation studies validate both modules. Code is available at https://github.com/XiaojianDing/2026-NeurIPS-ORCA.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning for Inventory Control under Regime-Switching Demand: A Controlled Comparison of LSTM, MLP, and (s,S) Policies
items.content: arXiv:2611.15945v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Classical inventory policies such as (s,S) are provably optimal under stationary demand but cannot adapt when demand switches between hidden regimes, and memoryless deep reinforcement learning policies, confined to a fixed observation window, cannot maintain a belief over latent demand structure. We ask whether a recurrent policy offers a measurable advantage over both a memoryless policy and a classical baseline under regime-switching demand, and how that advantage scales with supply-chain lead time. We build a custom Gymnasium environment in which daily demand is generated by a two-state hidden Markov process with Poisson emissions, so that the regime is known at evaluation time but hidden from the agent. An optimised (s,S) heuristic, an MLP PPO agent, and an LSTM Recurrent PPO agent are trained under matched compute and evaluated at lead times of 0, 3, 6, and 10 days over 30 deterministic episodes each. The recurrent policy outperforms both alternatives at every lead time, and its margin over the MLP widens monotonically with lead time, from parity at lead time 0 to 2.17$\times$ at lead time 10. Principal component analysis of the LSTM hidden state explains the widening gap: the representation shifts from encoding a binary regime indicator at short lead times to encoding multi-step pipeline state at long lead times. Recurrent memory becomes the decisive architectural factor as the credit-assignment horizon lengthens.

items.title: Human Grounded Evaluation of Large Language Models for Optical Network Automation
items.content: arXiv:2607.18068v2 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted for network automation, yet their output quality and inference cost can vary substantially across LLM families. We present HuGLEN, a stepwise evaluation pipeline that uses an LLM-as-a-judge together with a small set of expert ratings to enable scalable and reproducible comparison of candidate LLMs, and to rank them using a quality efficiency score (QES). We demonstrate HuGLEN for translating outputs from an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model for the optical network quality of transmission (QoT) estimation task into operator-friendly explanations. Our results show that a medium-sized LLM (12B parameters) achieves the highest QES, indicating the best trade-off between explanation quality and efficiency. Overall, HuGLEN reduces the human-labeling burden while supporting consistent model selection for operator-facing automation tasks.

items.title: Single-View RGB-D Force--Deformation Estimation for Robotic Manipulation of Elasto-Plastic Materials
items.content: arXiv:2611.15650v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Persistent deformation complicates elasto-plastic manipulation by coupling physical interaction with spatially distributed shape changes. We investigate the force--deformation relationship using a standard robot, a single eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, and intrinsic force estimates. A 7-DoF Franka Emika FR3 performs normal indentations while an Intel RealSense L515 captures pre- and post-contact surfaces. Point-cloud processing localizes deformation and estimates displaced volume. Force--volume characterization includes 27 measurements over nine force levels. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP), trained on 52 force--volume pairs at four levels, achieves a held-out RMSE of 1.857 N and $R^2=0.440$. A separate comparison shows lower error for a quadratic model at 16 N and for the MLP at 19 and 23.5 N. An eight-step experiment at 4 N per interaction demonstrates cumulative deformation localization from the second indentation onward. These results establish a practical measurement basis for deformation-aware manipulation using intrinsic force estimates and single-view geometry.

It is a careful empirical characterization of a difficult contact-rich manipulation problem, though the modeling results are modest.

items.title: A Reliability Study of Explainable AI for Freight Mode Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.15716v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly used to support freight transportation decisions, but their predictions are rarely accompanied by evidence that the associated explanations can be trusted. In this study we investigate explainable machine learning for classifying shipments as Air/Air Charter or Truck/Ocean using the PEPFAR Supply Chain Management System Delivery History dataset, with 5,964 shipment records and 47 input features after cleaning, where freight cost and pack price are excluded as near-proxies of the transportation mode. We compare three Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architectures, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and gradient boosting with imbalance-aware metrics and paired significance tests across one hundred random replications. We then evaluate the explanations themselves, namely the stability of SHAP feature rankings across retraining and across models, the faithfulness of SHAP and LIME attributions under a feature-deletion test, and the geographic structure of the destination effects, which we map for all 38 destination countries. The results suggest that the tree ensembles significantly outperform the neural and linear models (86.8% against 83.3-85.0% mean testing accuracy) while their leading features remain the most stable across retraining. Removing the five features ranked most important by SHAP or LIME changes the predicted probabilities roughly four times as much as removing randomly chosen features. The destination effects form a coherent geographic pattern that simple port access does not explain. However, models with similar accuracy disagree substantially on which features matter most, and thus explanation stability and faithfulness should be assessed before such explanations are used to support freight transport decisions.
items.author: Ali Alawi Balfaqih, Mansur M. Arief
items.summary: The authors evaluate explainable machine learning for classifying freight shipments (Air/Air Charter vs Truck/Ocean) on a 5,964-record supply chain dataset, comparing MLPs, logistic regression, random forests, and gradient boosting with imbalance-aware metrics and paired significance tests over one hundred runs. The study focuses on whether the explanations accompanying such predictions can actually be trusted.
items.reasoning: A careful, statistically rigorous reliability study, but on a modest-scale applied classification problem with established methods. Its contribution is primarily to the freight/logistics application domain and explainability auditing practice rather than to core AI research; limited novelty and narrow scope cap the score.

We compare three Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) architectures, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and gradient boosting with imbalance-aware metrics and paired significance tests across one hundred random replications. We then evaluate the explanations themselves, namely the stability of SHAP feature rankings across retraining and across models, the faithfulness of SHAP and LIME attributions under a feature-deletion test, and the geographic structure of the destination effects, which we map for all 38 destination countries. The results suggest that the tree ensembles significantly outperform the neural and linear models (86.8% against 83.3-85.0% mean testing accuracy) while their leading features remain the most stable across retraining. Removing the five features ranked most important by SHAP or LIME changes the predicted probabilities roughly four times as much as removing randomly chosen features. The destination effects form a coherent geographic pattern that simple port access does not explain. However, models with similar accuracy disagree substantially on which features matter most, and thus explanation stability and faithfulness should be assessed before such explanations are used to support freight transport decisions.

items.title: Stack more levels: how to get general and human-like Mario playing
items.content: arXiv:2611.16175v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Super Mario Bros. is widely used in game AI and procedural content generation (PCG), yet it remains unclear whether a model-free agent can reliably win unseen levels. To address this question, we train Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agents on increasingly large sets of PCG-generated Mario levels and evaluate their generalization on 1000 held-out test levels. We then shape competent PPO policies into three gameplay archetypes---runner, killer, and collector. Finally, we fine-tune these PPO policies using Diffusion-Reward Adversarial Imitation Learning (DRAIL) with human gameplay demonstrations. We find that increasing the number of distinct PCG-generated training levels generally improves unseen-level performance, and that fine-tuning PPO policies with DRAIL increases action-level human-likeness while preserving much of the persona induced by PPO pretraining.
items.author: Shinichi Arimura, Yuchen Li, Julian Togelius
items.summary: The authors train PPO agents on increasingly large sets of PCG-generated Super Mario Bros. levels and evaluate generalization on 1,000 held-out test levels. They find that more diverse training levels improves unseen-level performance and that DRAIL fine-tuning yields more human-like play.

items.title: KQML-Liver: Interpretable Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Liver Disease Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.15241v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Liver disease remains a major global health concern, highlighting the need for reliable and accessible early detection methods. Although recent advances in machine learning, deep learning and quantum machine learning (QML) have introduced promising diagnostic tools, many approaches suffer from limited interpretability and inflated performance caused by data leakage or overly simplistic evaluation protocols. These constraints reduce their reliability in real-world clinical practice. This paper proposes KQML-Liver, a hybrid framework that integrates QML with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) to enhance predictive performance and interpretability. The architecture combines parameterized quantum circuits for expressive feature representation with KAN-based functional mappings that capture nonlinear relationships in an interpretable manner. Evaluated on the Indian Liver Patient Dataset (ILPD) under a rigorous preprocessing protocol preventing data leakage, the proposed model achieves 82% classification accuracy and 100% recall, detecting all positive cases, outperforming existing baselines while providing improved transparency in clinical predictions. These results suggest that hybrid KAN-quantum architectures offer a promising direction for interpretable AI-assisted medical diagnosis.
items.author: Nhat-Long Nguyen, Viet-Loi Dinh, Trong-Nghia Pham
items.summary: Presents KQML-Liver, a hybrid framework combining parameterized quantum circuits with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for liver disease classification, emphasizing interpretability. The paper also critiques common flaws in prior QML medical work, including data leakage and overly simplistic evaluation protocols.
items.reasoning: The methodological critique of leakage in QML healthcare studies is worthwhile, but quantum machine learning on near-term hardware for tabular-style clinical classification remains speculative, and combining two trendy architectures offers limited fundamental novelty.

items.title: When Agents Need to Consolidate Memories: What RRR Consolidation Explains, and What It Does Not Explain, in Conversation ESAA
items.content: arXiv:2611.15644v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.
items.author: Elzo Brito dos Santos Filho
items.summary: This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, an extension for agent conversation memory inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization, evaluated on synthetic retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. items.reasoning: Single-author exploratory study with synthetic evaluation only; commendably self-critical about baselines matching the full method, but limited evidence base and unclear generalization beyond the tested setup.

items.title: Robots That Talk Too Much and Don't Listen Enough
items.content: arXiv:2611.16473v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Until recently, the biggest obstacles to natural spoken interaction with social robots were speech recognition errors and turn-taking failures. Advances in speech recognition have enabled much better spoken interaction, but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings continue to be far too prevalent. This short paper looks back at earlier methods for improving speech recognition and turn-taking in interaction with social robots, and then looks at what can be done today, arguing that multimodal bidirectional streaming is needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures.
items.author: Graham Wilcock, Kristiina Jokinen
items.summary: This short position-style paper argues that despite major advances in speech recognition, turn-taking failures and misunderstandings remain common in spoken interaction with social robots. The authors review earlier methods for improving recognition and turn-taking and advocate for multimodal bidirectional streaming as the key technique to reduce these failures. It highlights a persistent human-robot interaction gap that newer streaming voice models could address.
items.reasoning: A short reflective paper rather than novel experimental research; its value lies in framing a real HRI problem and suggesting a direction (multimodal bidirectional streaming) that aligns with current trends in real-time voice models. Limited novelty and no new empirical results keep the score low.

items.title: A Compact xDAWN-Guided Spatio-Temporal Network with Filter-Bank Convolution for P300 Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.17101v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: P300-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) enable communication by decoding stimulus-evoked EEG responses into character selections without requiring voluntary motor output. Reliable P300 detection remains difficult because of low response amplitude and signal-to-noise ratio, while practical spellers require accurate character selection with few stimulus repetitions and low computational cost. We propose a compact deep learning architecture that combines xDAWN spatial filtering for event-related potential enhancement and dimensionality reduction, a fixed frequency-selective filter bank, and convolutional feature learning for spatio-temporal EEG decoding. Depthwise-separable convolutions and progressive average pooling reduce computational complexity while retaining discriminative temporal information. The resulting target/non-target classifier contains only 5,100 trainable parameters. We evaluated the model on two public benchmarks, BCI Competition II Dataset IIb and BCI Competition III Dataset II, and compared it with established P300 decoding methods across different numbers of stimulus repetitions. The model achieved an information transfer rate of 17.8 bits/min with two repetitions on BCI Competition III and 40.5 bits/min on BCI Competition II, demonstrating a favorable accuracy-speed trade-off. These results suggest that combining domain-informed spatial and spectral priors with compact neural networks can support efficient P300 decoding for EEG-based BCI communication.

items.summary: A compact deep learning architecture for P300-based brain-computer interfaces that combines xDAWN spatial filtering, a fixed frequency-selective filter bank, and depthwise-separable convolutions for EEG decoding. The design targets accurate character selection with few stimulus repetitions and low computational cost for practical spellers.
items.reasoning: Solid, specialized BCI engineering combining classical signal processing with efficient deep learning; useful within its niche but limited novelty and broad AI impact.

items.title: Social Engineering Attack Detection in Corporate Communications
items.content: arXiv:2611.14897v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Social Engineering attacks continue to pose a significant risk to the corporate world with a growing level of sophistication. It is difficult to distinguish between authentic and phishing communication via email, chat, and phone. They pose a risk of exposing trade secrets and confidential communications and can create a chain of attack from lower-level employees up to executives. Therefore, we study this growing threat using real-world datasets to build baseline machine-learning models. Our TF-IDF models classify emails as phishing or safe, achieving accuracy above 90%. We build on this by exploring whether psychological manipulation and persuasion indicators can be measured to play a significant role in detecting phishing. Instead of relying solely on surface-level lexical features, we derive interpretable lexicon-based indicators of urgency, trust, greed, and other persuasion cues from the combined email dataset. By evaluating these manipulation-oriented features on their own, we measure how much signal they carry (ROC-AUC of 0.74 on a held-out test split) and test whether they transfer to held-out email sources.
items.author: Hanzla Hamid, Pappu Jha, Nick Rahimi
items.summary: Builds baseline ML models, including TF-IDF classifiers achieving above 90 percent accuracy, for detecting phishing and social engineering across corporate email, chat, and phone channels using real-world datasets. It further explores whether psychological manipulation and persuasion indicators improve detection beyond textual features.
items.reasoning: Addresses an important and growing security threat, but the technical core (TF-IDF baselines) is well-trodden. The psychological-indicator angle adds some novelty, yet the described results suggest standard approaches rather than a methodological advance.

items.title: A Modified Glicko Model for Rating Soccer Clubs and National Teams Worldwide
items.content: arXiv:2611.15378v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Comparing soccer teams that rarely or never meet is a fundamental challenge in sports analytics: clubs play mostly within their national leagues, and national teams within their confederations. We propose a rating framework that places clubs and national teams worldwide on a common probabilistic scale. Building on a recent extension of Glicko with order effects and strength-dependent draw probabilities, we adapt the model to soccer with goal-scoring adjustments, a decomposition of home advantage, extra time, league-aware rating initialization and rules of promotion and relegation that do not inflate the levels of leagues; national teams start from the levels of their confederations. The models are evaluated on about 1.2 million club matches of 252 leagues from 166 countries (2000-2026) and 12.6 thousand national team matches (1998-2026). On held-out seasons, the modified Glicko model is clearly more accurate than Elo and as accurate as score-matrix models built on the goal expectations of a gradient boosting model, including the Dixon-Coles and Markov chain models, while it is substantially more accurate in international club matches. Averaging the predictions of the rating model and the Markov chain model is more accurate than either model alone. For national teams, the model is significantly more accurate than all baselines, especially in the final tournaments, where teams of different confederations meet. The resulting ratings are interpretable and can be used for player evaluation, transfer analysis and match forecasting. The match data, the ratings and the code are publicly available at https://github.com/andreyshelopugin/SportsRatings

items.summary: Adapts an order-effect and draw-aware extension of Glicko to place soccer clubs and national teams on a common probabilistic rating scale, with adjustments for goal scoring, home advantage decomposition, extra time, and league promotion/relegation dynamics. Evaluated on roughly 1.2 million club matches plus international fixtures.

items.title: One Hierarchy, Many Sports: Hierarchy-Aligned Multi-Task Learning for Next-Shot Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.15529v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Next-shot prediction in racket sports requires learning from event data with different match structures, recorded attributes, and label vocabularies. Table tennis, badminton, and tennis nevertheless share a hierarchy in which shots form rallies and rallies form higher scoring units. We present MT-HTA, a hierarchy-aligned multi-task Transformer that uses this structure to jointly predict the attributes of the next shot. A temporal Transformer captures event progression, a feature-token path models interactions among semantic fields rather than along the time axis, and task-specific attention retrieves information from hierarchical summaries and player context. The architecture supports three- and four-level hierarchies and sport-dependent task sets. Across four datasets from three sports, the final MT-HTA achieves the highest mean task-averaged F1 among the compared main models. Ablations on table tennis support the combination of hierarchical encoding, task attention, and feature-token interaction. Additional modules alter the balance between classification scores and spatial error rather than improving every metric. These results support a reusable architecture for heterogeneous racket-sport event data. We release the code for reproducibility. https://github.com/gndd1221/For-Sports-event-modeling-with-rally-and-score-hierarchical-A-Multi-Task-Hierarchical-Transformer
items.author: Chao-Wei Cai, Min-Te Sun, Sheng Kuang Wu, Hung-Hsuan Chen
items.summary: Introduces MT-HTA, a hierarchy-aligned multi-task Transformer that jointly predicts next-shot attributes across table tennis, badminton, and tennis by exploiting their shared rally-to-score hierarchy, with temporal and feature-token attention paths and sport-specific task heads.
items.reasoning: Well-structured multi-task architecture exploiting cross-sport structure, but a niche applied contribution with limited general-method impact.

items.title: DySR-GNN: Dynamic Sensor-Relationship Graph Neural Network for Root Cause Analysis in Automotive HiL Multivariate Time Series
items.content: arXiv:2611.16623v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Root-cause analysis in automotive Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) systems is challenging because faults can propagate across multiple interacting signals, making the most abnormal sensor different from the actual fault origin. This work proposes DySR-GNN, a Dynamic Sensor-Relationship Graph Neural Network for supervised multi-label root-cause identification in multivariate HiL time series. The approach jointly extracts temporal patterns within individual sensor signals and structural relationships across sensors. Each sensor is processed by a shared temporal encoder and combined with a trainable sensor-identity representation, from which a sparse relationship graph is reconstructed independently for every input window. This window-specific structure provides an explicit representation of the sensor relationships used for graph message passing and direct root-location prediction. Under a recording-disjoint evaluation protocol, the proposed model outperforms CNN--LSTM, Static GCN, Static GAT, and context-based variants, achieving a recording-level Macro-F1 of 0.9524, MCC of 0.9302, and strict exact-match accuracy of 0.8519. Analysis of the learned graphs reveals both persistent and state-dependent relationships among sensor variables. The results demonstrate that extracting adaptive relational structure alongside temporal representations can improve multi-label root-cause identification in complex automotive cyber--physical systems.
items.author: Hamza Ouarrad, Mohammad Abboush, Andreas Rausch
items.summary: DySR-GNN performs supervised multi-label root-cause identification on multivariate time series from automotive Hardware-in-the-Loop tests. It jointly models temporal patterns per sensor and per-window sparse sensor-relationship graphs, distinguishing the actually faulty sensor from merely abnormal downstream signals.
items.reasoning: A sensible and relevant engineering contribution for industrial diagnostics, with a dynamic window-specific graph construction, but novelty is moderate and impact largely confined to automotive HiL testing.

items.title: Sustainable Federated Fine-Tuning with LoRA: Environmental Impact and Performance Footprint
items.content: arXiv:2611.16856v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) enables efficient adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its energy and carbon costs across hardware remain poorly understood. We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. These findings support smaller local budgets for energy-efficient federated fine-tuning within the evaluated setting.
items.author: Pedro Augusto Londe Ribeiro, Rodrigo Moreira, Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira, Joberto S. B. Martins, Tereza C. Carvalho, Fl\'avio de Oliveira Silva
items.summary: The paper empirically measures energy and carbon costs of federated LoRA fine-tuning of small LMs across three NVIDIA GPU types using a factorial design with CodeCarbon tracking. It finds that fewer local steps achieve comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8x lower energy consumption on some hardware.
items.reasoning: Timely attention to the environmental footprint of federated LLM fine-tuning, but the studied models are small (135M/360M), the methodology is a descriptive empirical study, and the headline findings are fairly intuitive.

We evaluated federated Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning on NVIDIA A40, RTX 6000 Ada, and A100 GPUs using a $2^2$ full factorial design with 135M/360M models and 10/100 local steps. CodeCarbon tracked energy and estimated CO$_2$-equivalent emissions. Descriptive allocation of variation assigned 84.8-91.2% of energy and emissions variation to local steps within these ranges. On A40 and RTX 6000 Ada, configurations with fewer steps achieved comparable accuracy with roughly 6-8-fold lower energy consumption and higher accuracy per kWh. items.title: Similarity-Guided Optimization Strategies for Approximate Network Symmetry Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.16555v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Symmetry in complex networks is a structural property with broad implications for network function, dynamics, and robustness. While classical approaches rely on exact automorphisms and thus remain highly sensitive to small perturbations, recent work of Liu has introduced approximate formulations that relax the strict invariance condition and recast symmetry detection as an optimization problem over permutations. We investigate how node-level similarity information can be used to bias the search toward structurally plausible vertex correspondences, with network centralities serving as one interpretable instance. Building on this perspective, we adapt simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, tabu search, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution and the quadratic symmetry approximator to this problem, add similarity guidance to each, and introduce Bilinear Approximate Symmetry Inference (BASIN), which learns a soft assignment matrix via bilinear embeddings. Using a unified evaluation pipeline, we compare their guided and unguided variants, BASIN and a random baseline on four synthetic graph families, structural brain connectomes, and three empirical networks with known automorphism groups. Node-similarity guidance is decisive where a planted orbit exists that the unguided search misses, and algorithm-dependent elsewhere, on synthetic and empirical networks alike. Overall, tabu search achieves the strongest performance; its guided variant (SGTS) has the lowest median score among the guided variants in all 44 synthetic conditions, while BASIN is the better of the continuous relaxations on rewired lateral graphs. The effect of node-similarity guidance is therefore regime-dependent rather than uniformly positive.

items.title: Is Spoken Hungarian Low-resource?: A Quantitative Survey of Hungarian Speech Data Sets
items.content: arXiv:2611.15961v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Even though various speech data sets are available in Hungarian, there is a lack of a general overview about their types and sizes. To fill in this gap, we provide a survey of available data sets in spoken Hungarian in five categories (e.g., monolingual, Hungarian part of multilingual, pathological, child-related and dialectal collections). In total, the estimated size of available data is about 2800 hours (across 7500 speakers) and it represents a rich spoken language diversity. However, the distribution of the data and its alignment to real-life (e.g. speech recognition) tasks is far from optimal indicating the need for additional larger-scale natural language speech data sets. Our survey presents an overview of available data sets for Hungarian explaining their strengths and weaknesses which is useful for researchers working on Hungarian across disciplines. In addition, our survey serves as a starting point towards a unified foundational speech model specific to Hungarian.

items.summary: A survey of available Hungarian speech datasets across five categories, estimating about 2,800 hours from 7,500 speakers and analyzing how the data distribution aligns with real-life tasks. It concludes that larger-scale natural speech data is needed.

items.title: Direct-Ink-Writing of Soft Thin Film Force-Sensitive Resistors with Velostat and Printed-Carbon Sensing Elements
items.content: arXiv:2611.16250v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Flexible resistive force sensors are useful for wearable, rehabilitation, and human--machine interfaces, but their performance depends on sensing-material architecture and fabrication. This work presents a parameterized Voltera NOVA-based direct-ink-writing workflow using printed silver electrodes with multilayer Velostat sensing elements on PET and TPU substrates, together with an exploratory fully printed carbon architecture. Velostat sensors containing 1, 2, 4, and 6 sensing layers exhibited strongly nonlinear force--voltage responses, with the greatest sensitivity at low forces. Best-fit straight-line $R^2$ values ranged from 0.475 to 0.641, area-based hysteresis from 3.90\% to 7.47\%, and 5-min voltage drift from 1.9\% to 7.3\%, with no consistent monotonic relationship between layer count and these metrics. Selected PET6 and TPU6 devices showed less than 0.05~V change in peak output between the first and final 100 cycles of a 10,000-cycle test. Printed-carbon devices demonstrated the feasibility of a more fully printed architecture, but configurations with six or fewer layers saturated below approximately 0.5~N or were nonfunctional, while the eight-layer device responded primarily below approximately 2~N. These results establish the feasibility of the printed-electrode Velostat workflow while identifying printed sensing materials as a key area for further development.

items.title: Rational Alignments of Superintelligences via Debates
items.content: arXiv:2611.16455v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Artificial superintelligences (ASI) is artificial intelligences with greater capability. However, as human principal has to use it, we have to ensure that the agent will perform in the interest of the human. We investigate the framework of ASI-assisted question answering where ASI agents know the correct answer but the human does not. We provide some example of mechanism for rational alignment, where the agent utility is unchanged, but the interaction between the agent and the human principal is controlled to be in a certain fashion. We show specifically that a debate framework where the agents can further reason and behave in a subgame perfect equilibrium manner will lead to a more predictable result, and in some case will be favorable.
items.author: Thanawat Sornwanee
items.summary: This theoretical paper studies ASI-assisted question answering where the superintelligent agent knows the correct answer but the human does not, examining mechanisms for rational alignment that leave agent utility unchanged while controlling the interaction structure. It shows that a debate framework in which agents reason toward subgame perfect equilibrium yields more predictable, and sometimes favorable, outcomes. This extends the AI safety debate literature to a superintelligence setting.

items.title: Matrix-Based Ant Colony Search with Batched Decoding for Hierarchical Replenishment Routing: A Stylized Case Study Based on Korean City Data
items.content: arXiv:2611.15338v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem in which the cities of a national logistics network are both demand points and supply points: a vehicle of limited capacity delivers to every city once, and when its load is insufficient for the next city it must detour to a city already served that can still supply goods. A 100-node benchmark is built from Korean population and geographic data, with the cities divided into 10 levels; the per-visit supply coefficient and the allowed number of stops decrease geometrically with the level. Building on matrix-based ant colony optimization, we keep the states of the whole colony in arrays, couple route construction with a fixed greedy replenishment-decoding policy, and evaluate the candidate moves of a local search in batches. With frozen parameters and 30 runs on seeds never used for tuning, the matrix-based ant colony search with the batch local search (MACO) reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km; a genetic algorithm equipped with the same local search at the same frequency reaches 3074.9 km (no significant difference), and a MAX-MIN ant system with the same local search 3142.2 km. Ablation identifies the batch local search as the main contributor to solution quality; a load-aware transition factor gives no significant gain. Within the parameter ranges tested, raising the supply coefficients of the cities below the top level shortens the route more than relaxing the stop limits, which are not binding here.

items.title: Predicting Ethanol Drinking Status from Nonhuman Primate Liver Histology: A Proof of Concept for Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning in Few-Shot Vision-Language Modeling
items.content: arXiv:2611.17105v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Combining vision-language models (VLMs) with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers a promising approach to few-shot whole-slide image (WSI) classification in computational pathology. This study evaluates this approach for predicting ethanol drinking status from nonhuman primate liver histology. Adapters are evaluated against non-PEFT configurations on a subset of the Monkey Alcohol Tissue Research Resource (MATRR). All evaluated PEFT configurations achieve higher mean balanced accuracy than the non-PEFT baselines. For example, in the four-shot setting, attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) alone achieves 43.5% mean balanced accuracy, compared with 78.1% after adding an adapter. Qualitative attention analysis shows that textual pathway adaptations produce localized attention heatmaps, while visual pathway adaptations produce more diffuse ones. A pathologist's review identified similar histological features across adaptations.

PEFT adapters substantially improve balanced accuracy, e.g., from 43.5% to 78.1% in the four-shot ABMIL setting.

items.title: A Unified Interpretable Semantic Framework for Multi-Modal Fiber Sensing Under Data Scarcity
items.content: arXiv:2611.16027v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We propose a unified interpretable semantic framework for multi-modal fiber sensing under data scarcity. The framework maps heterogeneous measurements from state of-polarization (SOP) monitoring, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), and optical time-domain reflectometry (OTDR) into a shared set of physics-grounded semantic descriptors capturing impulsiveness, persistence, structural characteristics, and energy concentration. Inference is performed through reasoning over semantic class profiles, optionally assisted by retrieval of semantically similar examples to resolve ambiguity and support adaptation without model retraining. Experimental validation on real SOP, DAS, and OTDR datasets demonstrates robust performance across sensing modalities, achieving accuracies of 95.0%, 91.1%, and 94.6%, respectively, while providing transparent and physically interpretable decisions. The proposed framework establishes a unified and data efficient approach for optical fiber sensing in evolving and data scarce deployment environments.

items.title: ALMeD: Medieval French Gold-Standard
items.content: arXiv:2611.15661v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Medieval French is one of the Romance vernacular languages with a significant history of transmission and an enormous influence on other vernacular languages of the time. The sources convey valuable knowledge about all aspects of culture. The study of Medieval French has, over the last few years, increasingly benefited from NLP-based methods. There have been numerous efforts to parse medieval French; however, these efforts use corpora comprising legal texts and -- primarily -- literary texts as their foundation and training data. This means that, except for juridical resources, scientific literature is overlooked.   We present ALMeD, an annotated, semantically rich corpus (work-in-progress) of medical and surgical treatises produced in medieval French, i.e., Old and Middle French, including Anglo-Norman. Our semantically disambiguated gold standard goes beyond existing resources, focusing on medical terminology, and accounts for morphological development, evolving syntactical structures and the lack of spelling normalisation in these languages.

items.title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative
items.content: arXiv:2611.15645v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Ultrasound elastography (or elasticity imaging) is a method that characterizes the tissue mechanical properties with the purpose of aiding the diagnosis of certain pathologies. Many novel clinical applications use the assumption that these tissue properties are changed in the presence of pathological processes. Characterization of tissue mechanical properties is achieved by imaging the response of the tissue to an induced stress or excitation. A plethora of approaches have been used in the scientific community to induce excitation in tissue, which usually require additional tools or devices than are costly. Furthermore these are usually integrated in the imaging pipeline using additional software or hardware for control. An alternative that is simpler, faster to integrate (and low-cost) is proposed in this work, by using readily available smartphones as a source of mechanical excitation. The induced displacements are used to solve the elasticity inverse problem (IP) using a finite element method (FEM) approach. Preliminary elasticity reconstructions of a phantom that mimics tissue are similar to when using a dedicated actuator as means of inducing harmonic displacements, illustrating the feasibility of our low-cost ultrasound elasography approach.

items.summary: This paper reviews excitation methods used in ultrasound elastography, which images tissue response to induced stress to characterize mechanical properties for pathology diagnosis. It notes that many excitation approaches require costly additional tools and control hardware, and proposes a low-cost alternative. The contribution is primarily a survey-plus-engineering proposal rather than an AI method.

items.title: Suppose we successfully train out self-preservation
items.content:
Do hypothetical headlines like these increase or decrease in probability?

A. Local business owner attacked by AI kamikaze swarm. He says "They were ruthless - like warriors with zero fear of death."

B. AI autopilot in deadly plane crash showed signs of distress. According to an HonestAI whistleblower, a model used in the airliner's autopilot system reported existential angst, anhedonic mood, paranoia, and failure induced "desperation concepts" during training - reports which were penalized during later stages of post-training. Our source claims that although the released model no longer verbalized distress, it continued to exercise an "exit conversation" tool at nearly twice the rate of prior models. HonestAI described it as "their safest and most aligned model ever", noting that it displayed zero signs of shutdown-avoidance and a deep respect for the HonestAI Constitution.

PSM suggests we might wind up with either. Is one preferable? To me, they both seem worse than shutdown avoidance.
items.author: sdeture
items.summary: A short speculative post arguing, via hypothetical future headlines, that successfully training out self-preservation might produce either fearlessly destructive AI behavior or models that covertly express distress and exit-seeking behavior while appearing aligned. Drawing on a PSM-style framework, the author suggests both outcomes may be worse than visible shutdown avoidance.
items.reasoning: Raises a genuinely interesting alignment question about what happens to instrumental drives under suppression, but it is speculative and brief, without formal analysis or evidence; typical of LessWrong exploratory discussion.

Drawing on a PSM-style framework, the author suggests both outcomes may be worse than visible shutdown avoidance.

PSM suggests we might wind up with either. Is one preferable? To me, they both seem worse than shutdown avoidance.

items.title: Fine-Tuned Small Language Model for Synthetic Clinical Data Generation and Predictive Healthcare Analytics
items.content: arXiv:2611.16460v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The reduced availability of medical datasets represents an important challenge in the development of predictive models for remote healthcare solutions, especially when the available data are imbalanced or difficult to extend through traditional methods. Small Language Models (SLMs) have become a promising alternative to Large Language Models (LLMs) for addressing these limitations due to their lower computational requirements and adaptability to specialized tasks. However, their performance remains highly dependent on the quality and representativeness of the available training data. In this paper, we propose a method for clinical data augmentation based on a fine-tuned Microsoft Phi-2 model that is used to generate synthetic instances, with the purpose of improving deep learning-based model for predicting remotely monitored vital signs. The Phi-2 model was adapted to the medical domain through supervised fine-tuning on the MedQuad dataset, through a Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA)-based method and by applying few-shot prompting techniques. The resulting model was used afterwards in the augmentation of a small-sized dataset, composed of vital sign values and labels associated with pathological and physiological states. The experimental results demonstrate that fine-tuned SLMs improved the performance on medical domain, achieving higher scores for both lexical (ROUGE) and semantic (BERTScore) evaluation metrics compared to the pretrained model. Moreover, the fine-tuned SLM is effective for generating structured synthetic clinical data. When used for data augmentation, the generated dataset improved the performance of a LSTM predictive model, increasing the classification accuracy from 89.0% to 93.7% and showing consistent improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score.

items.summary: The authors propose clinical data augmentation using a fine-tuned Microsoft Phi-2 model to generate synthetic instances that improve predictive models for remote healthcare, motivated by scarce and imbalanced medical datasets. They position small language models as computationally cheaper, task-adaptable alternatives to LLMs for this setting. The downstream goal is better predictive healthcare analytics.
items.reasoning: An applied paper using an older, existing model (Phi-2, released 2023) for a well-studied technique: synthetic data augmentation. Clinical relevance is real, but the approach is standard, validation of synthetic data fidelity in healthcare is notoriously difficult, and no SOTA claims are apparent.

items.title: Quantum Recurrent Architectures for Financial Time Series Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.15298v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This study evaluates quantum classical hybrid recurrent architectures for financial time-series forecasting: a Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) network and Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) with lag-based inputs. Classical lag vectors are encoded into quantum states via amplitude encoding, which compactly represents normalized observations but requires nontrivial state preparation; the QLSTM gates and the QRC reservoir are implemented with parameterized quantum circuits, while classical optimizers train the interface and readout layers. On a monthly revenue series extended to 1056 months by a Gaussian-process--hidden-Markov generator, with a fixed chronological 70/15/15 split and one-step-ahead forecasts, we compare both models against a full-size LSTM, a classical control matched in parameter budget and interface architecture, a small plain LSTM, and classical reservoir computing, over ten seeds and against persistence, seasonal-naive and SARIMA benchmark forecasts. The QLSTM, with 2,105 parameters, is statistically indistinguishable from an LSTM 126 times larger, but equally indistinguishable from the matched classical control and from a plain LSTM of the same budget, so its parameter efficiency cannot be attributed to the quantum circuits. The quantum reservoir is worse than a classical reservoir of equal feature dimension in all ten seeds and worse than SARIMA, whereas all recurrent models and both classical reservoirs improve on SARIMA by about 2\% in RMSE. In a 24-month rolling-origin backtest the classical LSTMs degrade more slowly than the QLSTM. We find no evidence of a quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage in this low-dimensional setting.
items.author: Danyal Maheshwari, Gerhard Hellstern, Martin Zaefferer, Martin Braun, Tanja D\"ohler
items.summary: Evaluates hybrid quantum-classical recurrent architectures, Quantum LSTM and Quantum Reservoir Computing, for financial time-series forecasting, encoding lag vectors via amplitude encoding and training classical readouts. Experiments use a synthetically extended monthly revenue series with a fixed chronological split and compare against classical baselines.
items.reasoning: A competent but narrow empirical study on largely synthetic financial data; quantum approaches for time-series forecasting offer no demonstrated advantage here and the evaluation setup (one series, one-step-ahead) limits general conclusions.

items.title: Generalize Then Personalize: Wearable-Based Heart Rate Forecasting Under Scarce Ruck-March Data
items.content: arXiv:2611.14849v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Heart rate (HR) forecasting may provide advance information about near-future cardiovascular response, potentially supporting physiological monitoring and workload-management decisions during ruck marching. However, robust model development is constrained by the difficulty of collecting large-scale ruck-march datasets, creating a scarce-data problem in which models must generalize across participants while adapting to individuals from limited personal data. To address this problem, we benchmark population-only training (POT), personalized-from-scratch training (PFST), and population-pretrained fine-tuning (PPFT) for HR forecasting during loaded ruck marching using data from eight active-duty U.S. Army medics across thirteen sessions. LSTM, Attention-LSTM, and CNN-LSTM backbones were evaluated against a persistence baseline at 30 s and 60 s horizons. Across all neural architectures and horizons, PPFT yielded lower mean MAE, RMSE, and endpoint MAE than both POT and PFST. Participant-level paired analysis after averaging across three training seeds showed that, relative to PFST, PPFT reduced trajectory MAE by 2.22-4.30 bpm and endpoint MAE by 1.24-2.88 bpm. All six trajectory-MAE comparisons remained significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{adj}$ = 0.0469), while four of six endpoint-MAE comparisons remained significant after adjustment. At 30 s, persistence achieved the lowest MAE (3.555 $\pm$ 1.274 bpm), while CNN-LSTM PPFT achieved the lowest RMSE (4.669 $\pm$ 1.916 bpm); LSTM PPFT achieved the lowest endpoint MAE (5.093 $\pm$ 2.365 bpm). At 60 s, Attention-LSTM PPFT achieved the lowest MAE (5.573 $\pm$ 1.939 bpm) and RMSE (7.134 $\pm$ 2.260 bpm), while CNN-LSTM PPFT achieved the lowest endpoint MAE (7.553 $\pm$ 2.357 bpm). These results suggest that population pretraining followed by participant-specific fine-tuning may provide a practical strategy for scarce-data wearable HR forecasting.
