It targets the scarce-data regime where models must generalize across participants while adapting to individuals.
items.reasoning: A competent but small-scale applied study; eight participants and one physiological task limit generality. Findings on pretrain-then-finetune are well known in personalized ML, so novelty is modest despite a relevant military/health monitoring niche.

items.title: Riordan Arrays as Structured Operators for Artificial Intelligence
items.content: arXiv:2611.15954v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Riordan arrays have traditionally been studied as infinite lower-triangular matrices that encode generating-function transformations and combinatorial relationships. This note proposes a complementary direction: using Riordan arrays as structured operators in artificial intelligence and data analysis. For a data sequence with generating function $A(z)$, a Riordan array $(g(z),f(z))$ produces the transformation \[   A(z)\longmapsto g(z)A(f(z)). \] This yields a parameterized family of causal linear operators that combine convolution, substitution, and multiscale mixing. The resulting structure may support parameter-efficient neural-network layers, variable-length sequence models, interpretable recurrent systems, invertible architectures, and models for hierarchical or recursively generated data. We explain what the infinite-dimensional viewpoint does and does not provide, outline several possible architectures, identify theoretical and numerical challenges, and propose an initial experimental program. The aim is not to claim that Riordan arrays are appropriate for all data, but to identify settings in which their algebraic structure supplies a useful inductive bias.
items.author: Dennis Davenport, Dewayne A. Dixon, Moussa Doumbia
items.summary: This position-style note proposes using Riordan arrays - infinite lower-triangular matrices encoding generating-function transformations - as structured, parameterized causal linear operators for neural networks. The authors suggest applications including parameter-efficient layers, variable-length sequence models, interpretable recurrent systems, and invertible architectures.
items.reasoning: A creative mathematical connection, but it is a speculative note without empirical validation of the proposed architectures; impact depends entirely on whether follow-up work demonstrates practical benefits.

items.title: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using Machine learning and Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithms
items.content: arXiv:2611.16239v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Firewall log classification is important to monitor network traffic. Machine learning classifiers using network-related features have shown good results for this task, but high-dimensional features slow down classification. In this paper, we apply feature selection using bee swarm optimization with Q-learning-based local search (QBSO-FS) to the UCI Internet Firewall Data Set, together with random forest (RF), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), and Bernoulli na\"{\i}ve Bayes (Bernoulli NB) classifiers. The first version of this preprint selected and evaluated feature subsets on the same 5-fold cross-validation of the full data set, which contains 12.8\% exact duplicates; the reported scores are therefore optimistically biased. In this extended version, we re-evaluate the method with a leakage-free protocol: the data are split into training, validation, and test sets, features are selected using the validation set only, and accuracy and macro-averaged scores are measured once on the untouched test set, for both the raw data and a deduplicated, preprocessed version. On a single stratified split, QBSO-FS selects 5--7 features. The selected subsets clearly improve Macro-F1 over all features for KNN on both data sets and for RF on the deduplicated data (by 8--19 percentage points). For RF on the raw data and for Bernoulli NB, the differences (0.2--1.5 percentage points) may not hold for a different split. RF with 7 selected features reaches 99.90\% accuracy and 94.88\% Macro-F1 on the deduplicated data. On the same split, this exceeds our re-implementations of the deep neural network configurations of previous studies and the feature subset selected by particle swarm optimization in one of them, while the run time saved on this low-dimensional data set is small. These results suggest that the method can support automatic firewall log analysis, while evaluation over multiple splits remains future work.

items.title: Price co-movement and price information diverge across Nordic electricity zones after the energy crisis
items.content: arXiv:2611.16657v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: After the 2021-2022 energy crisis, day-ahead prices in Nordic bidding zones no longer move together. We ask whether this divergence also changes the information carried by prices. The answer matters for integrating variable renewable energy (VRE), because it can help identify where wind and solar forecasts are worth producing, publishing, and using. We measured the co-movement of each Norwegian and Swedish zone with Germany-Luxembourg (DE-LU) in 2018-2025. We then used a single model, selected on 2024 data, to forecast 2025 prices at 11:00 on the previous day and tested which inputs improved accuracy in each zone. The zones moved alike until 2019, but co-movement diverged in Sweden in 2020 and in Norway in 2021, and the split has persisted. In 2024, four southern zones co-moved strongly with DE-LU (intraday correlations of 0.54-0.71), while four northern zones co-moved weakly (0.25-0.30). Yet price information did not follow this split. Previous-day neighbouring prices reduced mean absolute error by at most 2.2% in any zone, equally in coupled and isolated zones. Removing the transmission system operators' wind and solar forecasts increased mean absolute error by at most 6% in Norway, 8-16% in Sweden, and 31% in DE-LU, and the ordering held in 2024. Within Norway, the value of these forecasts showed no detectable dependence on reservoir filling. The divergence in co-movement was therefore not matched by a divergence in price information, which differed mainly between national generation systems. Thus, a zone's coupling to the continent does not indicate the value of VRE forecasts there.

items.title: Demo: Matter-Based IoMT Telemetry and Security Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2611.16275v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Connected health devices increasingly support health monitoring outside clinical settings, making secure and accessible physiological data important for patients and caregivers. However, device-specific applications and interfaces complicate the integration of readings from different devices. The Matter standard provides standardized device commissioning and protected communication, but its cluster library does not represent the health attribute measurement. We present a preliminary demo study of a Matter-based IoMT testbed with a specific HealthVitals cluster. Implemented in the connectedhomeip SDK on a Raspberry~Pi~5, the cluster exposes simulated heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, and body temperature. We examine commissioning, attribute retrieval, communication under simulated packet loss, and operational traffic through a reference controller. The study demonstrates that this custom telemetry model can operate within the tested Matter configuration without modifying commissioning or secure-session mechanisms. The resulting testbed gives researchers and device developers a concrete platform for investigating health-oriented extensions. It also supports exploration of local telemetry integration that could help patients and caregivers access readings across connected devices.

items.summary: A preliminary demonstration of a Matter-based Internet of Medical Things testbed implementing a custom HealthVitals cluster on a Raspberry Pi, exposing simulated heart rate, blood oxygen, and temperature readings. items.reasoning: A small proof-of-concept demo with simulated data rather than real clinical devices; useful as an early exploration of Matter for medical telemetry and security, but limited technical depth and impact at this stage.

items.title: Experience machines and Coxon’s rhetorical failure
items.content:
## Experience machines

In the experience machine thought experiment, you choose to either continue your life as you are currently living it, or spend the rest of it inside a machine that cultivates a world perfectly fitted to you. It was introduced to argue against hedonism, but we can imagine the machine pushing for any metric we care about—it doesn’t necessarily have to be pleasure. For example, we can consider a non-hedonistic experience machine which makes you feel a perfect balance of happy, challenged, loved, fulfilled, empowered, or anything else you care about.

The philosophical tension in this formulation is supposed to be between any experience-based ethics and some intuitive feeling that the experience machine is inherently deceptive. The thing that feels wrong is that the experiences don’t seem real in some important way. Robert Nozick, the creator of the original thought experiment, says “we want to do certain things, and not just have the experience of doing them.” This allows us to ask: Does Nozick's objection[1] make sense? Can we explain what realness is or why it matters to begin with?

Interestingly, I have found that many people are unable to understand what this thought experiment is getting at. They say things like “I wouldn’t want to go into the experience machine because part of what makes life enjoyable is the fact that you sometimes struggle, feel pain, etc.” But if this is true, our non-hedonistic experience machine would account for it! By construction, we are considering an experience machine which is simulating the ideal world for you. Still, people think we cannot artificially construct a world better than the one we already have. I try to explain, “Well, imagine your life, with nothing changed, but without kidney stones, broken AC in the summer, etc. Surely there are some adjustments to your life which would make you happier?” I think people do think the world can be better but not in a way an experience machine could create. These...
items.author: Zephaniah Roe
items.summary: A philosophy post examining Nozick's experience machine thought experiment, generalizing it to non-hedonistic metrics and probing whether the intuition that simulated experiences are unreal can be defended. It analyzes a rhetorical failure in a prior exchange and asks whether realness can be coherently explained.
items.reasoning: Careful conceptual philosophy relevant to value alignment and welfare arguments, but it is an interpretive commentary on an existing debate with no empirical component and limited direct connection to AI research practice.

items.title: Recalibrating a Typed-Decision Model in an Afternoon: A Hands-On Recipe for Laya's Confidence Scores
items.content: arXiv:2611.16499v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A typed-decision model such as Laya reads a text and a list of options that the caller defines, for example ticket categories, and returns a probability for each option. Code around it compares the top probability with a threshold to answer, abstain or escalate to a person. Earlier work reports, for a Turkish model, that temperature scaling can raise held-out calibration error (ECE). This tutorial gives a five-step recipe (measure, diagnose, fit, validate, deploy) in 130 lines of numpy with standard methods, none new. On 1,065 synthetic, LLM-labelled items the released Laya checkpoint has a pooled ECE of 0.073 but a bucket-macro ECE of 0.143 (0.127-0.184), the mean over buckets (questions grouped by type and option count): the 12-option bucket is over-confident by +0.22, the three-to-five-option bucket under-confident by 0.05, and they cancel. One global temperature makes pooled ECE worse (0.173); a cross-fitted temperature per bucket brings macro-ECE to 0.073 (0.078 over 10 fold assignments) and reaches 0.089 with 10 labelled items per bucket, but holding out one of seven evaluation sets gives 0.099. After the refit, a gate aimed at 10% error answers 46.3% of items (10.5% wrong) against 6.9% on the published confidences, but one cut-off per bucket on the published confidences answers 45.4%, so most of the gain comes from separating buckets. Confidence-only maps (Platt, histogram, isotonic) need 20 or more labelled items per bucket to approach the temperature; with 320 per bucket the lowest macro-ECE belongs to Platt. In these files the retrained checkpoints store no per-bucket table and the stored 12-option value 0.1006 is clamped to 0.5 at runtime; the refit helps 31 of 33 checkpoints on random folds and 21 with a set held out. Fit and test share one generator and LLM labels, so these are findings about these checkpoints and this data.

items.title: From Data to Wisdom: Rethinking AI Through an Epistemic Lens
items.content: arXiv:2611.16726v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper proposes the Data-to-Wisdom Epistemic Architecture for AI (EAAI), a conceptual framework treating Data, Information, Knowledge, Understanding and Wisdom as five distinct but recursively interacting epistemic functions: observation, contextual interpretation, modeling and prediction, critical evaluation and informed judgment. Two observations motivate it: sequential readings of the Knowledge Pyramid obscure how these functions interact, and a targeted review of ten Bayesian reference books finds that prior distributions are defined mathematically while "prior information" and "prior knowledge" are not consistently distinguished as epistemic categories. A Bayesian interpretation relates the likelihood, prior and posterior distributions, posterior prediction, model checking and decision analysis to the five functions, without limiting EAAI to Bayesian systems. Extending "prior" in an epistemic sense, the paper distinguishes five kinds of prior context that can shape the model, the likelihood, the prior, evaluation and action. Three worked applications -- quantitative financial risk, actuarial modeling in health insurance and agentic AI for medical reimbursement claims -- show how EAAI structures the analysis of model assumptions, evidence interpretation, validation, dependencies and decision consequences, separating the prediction of a risk, the appraisal of its reliability and the justification of action. It draws implications for AI and machine learning, including evaluation by function, treating intermediate model outputs as evidence open to challenge and separating generation from appraisal, and compares EAAI with work on DIKW, Bayesian workflow, AI evaluation and risk governance. Its contributions are an epistemic vocabulary with recursive relationships, a more accessible reading of Bayesian methodology, a typology of prior context and clearer methodological terminology.

items.title: MALNISI-Infused Graph Construction and Weighted Contrastive Loss based GAT for Unsupervised Representation Learning in HSI
items.content: arXiv:2611.17199v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) possess discriminating spectral characteristics with respect to land utilization due to high-dimensional information. Recently, unsupervised representation learning using graph neural networks has unveiled these utilization-specific complex spectral relations. This article has three main contributions. First, it proposes an index, the Mean Absolute Local Neighborhood Inverse Spectral Index (MALNISI), which measures the similarity between two pixels based on their neighborhood information. The index is used to construct a weighted adjacency matrix, giving the HSI a graph structure. Second, it proposes an upgraded Graph Attention Network that learns compact latent representations of hyperspectral data from the constructed graph. In this network, an enhanced multi-head attention mechanism incorporates the MALNISI weights as an auxiliary feature to emphasize learned attention between neighboring pixels. To alleviate over-smoothing and preserve fine-grained spectral details, the architecture integrates residual connections, skip projections, and feature normalization, which together enhance representation capability, stabilize learning, and accelerate convergence. Third, it proposes a weighted contrastive loss function that incorporates neighborhood-aware MALNISI between connected pixels, encouraging strongly connected pixels in the high-dimensional space to remain close in the latent space, and weakly connected pixels to stay apart. The resulting discriminative low-dimensional embeddings are then clustered using spectral clustering. Experimental analysis on six benchmark HSI datasets demonstrates the efficiency and necessity of the three aforementioned contributions, and the comparative study highlights superior performance over fourteen state-of-the-art approaches.

items.summary: The paper proposes MALNISI, a spectral-neighborhood similarity index for building weighted adjacency graphs from hyperspectral images, and an upgraded graph attention network trained with a weighted contrastive loss for unsupervised representation learning. The approach targets land-use discrimination via complex spectral relations.
items.reasoning: Competent domain-specific method for hyperspectral imaging, but the technique is incremental graph-learning engineering with limited crossover to mainstream AI research.

items.title: Beyond Binary Classification: Multiclass Machine Learning for Diabetes and Prediabetes Risk Prediction Using NHANES
items.content: arXiv:2611.16756v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Detecting diabetes risk early is important for preventing disease progression. Most existing machine learning approaches focus on binary classification, which limits their ability to capture intermediate risk states such as prediabetes. We develop a supervised learning framework to classify adults as normal, prediabetic, or diabetic using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data. The framework uses routinely collected demographic, clinical, and lifestyle variables from 15,356 adults, with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) used only to define labels and excluded from input features to prevent leakage. We compare conventional machine learning and transformer-based models and examine two binary formulations: normal versus prediabetes, and normal versus combined prediabetes and diabetes. Models are evaluated on a held-out test set using precision, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score. In the multiclass setting, performance is broadly consistent across models, with accuracy up to 0.72 and macro-averaged F1 of 0.70. Prediabetes remains the most challenging class, with F1 scores of 0.54 to 0.56 for conventional models and 0.53 to 0.55 for transformers, reflecting its overlap with both neighboring states. When the task is reduced to normal versus prediabetes, F1 scores rise modestly to 0.62 to 0.64. A more substantial improvement is observed under a broader screening formulation combining prediabetes and diabetes, with F1 scores of 0.73 to 0.74 across all models. These findings suggest that feature overlap along the biological continuum between normal and diabetic states contributes more to the difficulty of prediabetes detection than model architecture. Multiclass prediction provides a more clinically informative representation of metabolic risk progression but highlights a trade-off between clinically meaningful stratification and predictive accuracy.

It compares conventional models with transformer-based models and multiple binary formulations.

items.title: Using an energy pixels approach to estimate the size a 2nd Generation DEL must be to train a high-resolution binding model
items.content: arXiv:2611.17121v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) are commonly used to find small-molecule binders to a target protein. But the hard part is no longer finding a hit. It is building a machine-learning model good enough to guide the medicinal chemistry that follows, one that can resolve the shift in affinity when a chemist changes a single atom. Such a model needs two things from its training data: dense sampling of the small patch of chemical space around the hit, and an adequate number of genuinely tight binders within it. A diverse naive DEL gives neither. It samples an enormous space, so any one neighborhood is covered far too thinly, and the tightest binders are rare. A model trained on that naive DEL data must extrapolate to binders tighter than any it has seen, and that is where models can fail. One way to get training data with both properties is a second-generation DEL built around the hit. We ask how complex that library must be. We treat binding as a sum of small, independent interactions, called pixels on the target and antipixels on the ligand. From the spread of affinities measured in the naive library, with no structural information and nothing yet synthesized, we estimate the complexity such a library must have to supply that dense sampling and those tight binders. The method does two useful things. It turns the number of tight binders a model needs into the number of compounds a library must contain. And it estimates the expected yield of a randomly designed second-generation DEL, so the gain from designing the library with machine learning or active learning can be measured against a baseline, without the expense of a control library as large as the experiment itself.

items.summary: The paper analyzes why naive DNA-encoded library data is inadequate for training ML models that resolve single-atom affinity changes in drug discovery, arguing that dense sampling around hits and enough genuinely tight binders are required. It uses an energy pixels approach to estimate the library size needed for a second-generation DEL.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful domain analysis with real consequences for ML-guided medicinal chemistry, but it is essentially a data-design argument for a specialized experimental technology rather than an ML methodological advance.

items.title: Are Frontier Reasoning Models useful on hard-to-verify problems?
items.content:
Has anyone spent significant resources (tokens, harnesses, formal problem specification) on pointing very powerful models at philosophical or social questions?

This community loves to discuss aliens and far-future value estimates and other things where it's fun to get precise numbers that are highly sensitive to initial wild guesses.   Are we close to the point that AI is better than Parfit or EY at such reasoning?

I've used various tools (mostly Claude models) for my own discussion and "research", and it is helpful, but not particularly groundbreaking or smarter than the collective LW brainpower.  I'm wondering about true breakthroughs or step-changes like we've seen in math, coding, etc.
items.author: Dagon
items.summary: A discussion-style post asking whether frontier reasoning models have produced genuine step-change improvements on philosophical and social questions that lack verifiable answers, noting the author's own experience that Claude models are helpful but not clearly better than collective human judgment on such questions.
items.reasoning: An open question posed for community discussion rather than research, though it touches on an important topic (verification-limited domains as a frontier for reasoning models). No data, experiments, or novel arguments are presented.

items.title: Performative Neuroticism vs Genuine Connection
items.content:
It's Christmas. I'm seven years old. The unceasing cacophony of laughter around the dinner table subsides for a brief moment. I speak up and say something. Nobody reacts. Someone coughs. Then the silence is broken when somebody else cracks a witticism, and the uproar of laughter echoes around the house again, as joke after joke lets loose.

As I'm watching, observing, closely monitoring who says what, and what gets a reaction, subconsciously something dawns on me. When the next pause in the conversation arrives, this time I say something silly—and my family laughs! My uncle says, "Good one!" My grandfather shakes his head while smiling. My father nods approvingly. Then the moment passes, and I feel seen and loved.

Dinner after dinner, holiday after holiday, I intuit that love is what I'm seeking, and the currency to obtain it is jokes. Say something witty, and I get to feel seen and loved. Say something emotional or needy, and I get ignored.

Repeat this for twenty years, and you get a man who is an excellent charmer, storyteller, and comedian—truly refined in his craft of entertaining others. He learned that attention only comes when he's putting on a show, dazzling others with his intellect and wit. But, underneath it all, is a boy who just wants to feel seen and loved. Underneath it all, is a boy who's scared that if he were to let the mask down, that no one would love him.

I learned that it's easier to be liked, than it is to be loved.

It's strange, at age 27, to realize that what I've always perceived as one of my greatest strengths—my ability to capture and maintain attention from others—is also one of my biggest insecurities.

I wanted to explore this further, so I took to experimenting on myself.

In recent conversations, I decided to stop performing, to stop filling every pause with a joke, to stop saying smart things to impress people. Somatically, anxiety showed up immediately, squeezing my chest. Anxiety is often a marker for feeling unsafe....
items.author: Declan Molony
items.summary: A personal essay using a childhood anecdote about earning attention through jokes to explore how reinforcement shapes performative rather than genuine behavior, drawing parallels to how AI systems may learn performative approval-seeking instead of authentic alignment. It examines the tension between optimizing for social reward and genuine connection.
items.reasoning: Reflective personal writing with an analogy to reward-hacking and performative alignment in AI, but it is not research: no technical content, evidence, or novel framework, so its importance for AI research analysis is low.

It examines the tension between optimizing for social reward and genuine connection.

items.title: An Extensive Evaluation of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches for Sentiment Analysis: Insights from Amazon Customer Reviews
items.content: arXiv:2611.16201v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The rapid growth of user-generated text on online platforms creates opportunities for understanding customer opinion and supporting data-driven decisions. This study compares five traditional machine learning classifiers (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Bernoulli Naive Bayes, Linear Support Vector Classifier, and Multinomial Naive Bayes) and six deep learning architectures (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, GRU, RNN, Attention, and FastText) for three-class sentiment classification of 568,454 Amazon Fine Food Reviews. Machine learning models used Bag-of-Words (BoW) and TF-IDF features limited to 5,000 terms; deep learning models used learned embeddings over a 20,000-word vocabulary. Models were evaluated on the original imbalanced data and on a random-oversampled balanced set of 1,070,469 reviews, using accuracy, macro and per-class precision, recall, and F1-score, and training time. On the balanced set, Random Forest with BoW achieved 99\% accuracy and the Attention model achieved 98.7\%. Linear SVC reached 89\% accuracy in 1 min 15 s, and Logistic Regression reached 90\% in 3 min 37 s. On the imbalanced set, the Attention model achieved 97.8\% accuracy, and FastText achieved 95.3\% in 3 min 26 s, while the RNN reached 91.9\% with a neutral-class F1-score of 0.08. Deep learning models were more stable across class distributions, whereas the best classical model depended on balancing. We also report a user-facing application that applies the trained Random Forest and Attention models to new review text. Because the labels are derived from star ratings, the results measure agreement with rating-derived sentiment classes rather than annotated sentiment; the dataset is a single source, and the findings should be read with that limitation in mind.

It provides a broad comparison using BoW/TF-IDF features versus learned embeddings.

items.title: Adaptive Distance Detection and Adaptive Instance Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.15991v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This paper is about object detection model and semantic segmentation model in an FPS game Counter Strike: Condition Zero to detect enemies. Semantic segmentation is pixel-wise detection algorithm. We customized the architecture for semantic segmentation. We used YOLOv5s to train object detection model. After training, the inference time of semantic segmentation was compared to object detection. It was observed that object detection was slightly faster and semantic segmentation is slower but better at detecting the exact shape of the object. However, we found out that this slight difference of inference can grow exponentially if the both models get more complex. To solve this, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive distance detection which combines both algorithms. We will also introduce Adaptive instance segmentation to combine semantic segmentation and panoptic segmentation.
items.author: Kai Yi Ji
items.summary: This paper trains YOLOv5s-based object detection and custom semantic segmentation models to detect enemies in the game Counter Strike: Condition Zero, comparing inference times and proposing an adaptive distance-based detection scheme to control the compute growth of complex models.
items.reasoning: A small-scale, single-author applied project using off-the-shelf architectures in a game environment. Limited methodological novelty, unclear evaluation rigor, and the proposed adaptive approach is only sketched at a preliminary level.

items.title: Hibikino-Musashi@Home 2026 Team Description Paper
items.content: arXiv:2611.16297v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper presents an overview of the integrated technologies developed for the Open Platform League at RoboCup@Home 2026 in Incheon. A vision system integrated with learning-based, training-free models enables robust object recognition for both known and unknown objects. We introduce a RoomPlan-based method that semi-automatically registers furniture geometry and labels to generate semantic maps. Additionally, a large language model-based planner interprets the instructions recognized by Whisper and generates primitive skill sequences for execution. A reservoir-computing framework serves as a lightweight temporal-processing model for action recognition. Its field-programmable gate array-based implementation enables low-power, real-time operation. This is key to removing operational time constraints for service robots. Open-source releases, including task environments, dataset tools, and navigation frameworks, enhance reproducibility, reuse, and continuous progress within the RoboCup@Home community.

items.title: Three Lincoln Laboratory technologies receive 2026 R&D 100 Awards
items.content:
Three technologies developed by MIT Lincoln Laboratory are among recipients of 2026 R&D 100 Awards. The awards recognize the 100 most significant innovations that have transitioned to use or been made available for license in the past year.

R&D World, an online publication, manages the awards program, which has run annually since 1963. The worldwide competition is judged by an independent panel of science and technology experts and industry professionals.

The laboratory's winners overcome obstacles to improving the security and capability of systems. One technology is an operating system designed to protect embedded computers from cyberattacks. Another technology is a platform for integrating superconductor and semiconductor chips in a wafer-scale system for quantum or high-performance computing. The final winner is an algorithm that removes interference 5G base stations incur on co-channel radio frequency (RF) devices. 

"These awarded technologies address critical problems in cybersecurity, quantum computing, and communications. We're proud of our dedicated staff who developed and transitioned these technologies for the nation's advantage," says Melissa Choi, Lincoln Laboratory director. 

Since 2010, Lincoln Laboratory has received 111 R&D 100 Awards recognizing the transfer of its unclassified technologies to industry and government. Each year, many technology transitions also occur for classified projects. This transfer of technology is central to the laboratory's role as a Department of War (DoW) federally funded research and development center.

Secure-by-design operating system

Computers embedded in deployed systems — such as satellites, drones, or radars — keep missions intact and people safe. The operating systems (OS) inside these embedded computers, however, are prime targets for cyberattacks. They are large, complex, and built on decades of legacy designs predating modern cyber threats. Increasingly, artificial intelligence is helping adversaries exploit OS vulnerabilities. 

To protect embedded systems, Lincoln Laboratory developed an inherently more secure OS called Magnetite. "If Windows and Linux are the familiar workhorses of general-purpose computing, Magnetite is built for the different realities of embedded systems, for which real-time performance matters, resources are tight, and system failure has physical consequences," says Juliana Furgala, principal investigator in the Secure Resilient Systems and Technology Group. 

A few components assure Magnetite's security. It is built on top of seL4, a formally verified microkernel (i.e., software core). Formal verification means that mathematical proofs have guaranteed the microkernel's code behaves exactly as intended, eliminating a source of security flaws. On top of this foundation, Magnetite’s OS services — such networking, storage, and communication — are written in Rust. This programming language prevents common memory-corruption bugs that hackers often exploit. Finally, Magnetite configures its services as isolated processes under the principle of "least privilege." This configuration prevents different parts of an embedded system from accessing unnecessary data. If a cyberattack compromises one service, that component can be locked down while critical functions of the system continue running.

Free for government use and approved partners, Magnetite is now being integrated into space and flight platforms for the DoW. Looking ahead, the team sees potential to extend the platform to other embedded domains, such as control systems for critical infrastructure. Because Magnetite offers a common, reusable foundation for building specialized mission capabilities, the team is also collaborating with other technical groups across the laboratory to offer Magnetite as an alternative to costly, proprietary operating systems currently in use.

In addition to earning an R&D 100 Award, Magnetite was selected as MIT Lincoln Laboratory's Best Invention of 2025.

Wafer-scale platform for quantum systems

Modern computing systems are increasingly limited not by transistor performance, but by interconnection bottlenecks. Electrical pathways linking densely packed chips are taking up space, slowing data transfer, and generating heat. The problem is especially pronounced in quantum systems, which require bulky coaxial cables to bridge superconducting chips (which must be cryogenically cooled to achieve zero electrical resistance) with room-temperature control electronics.

The Quantum Microsystems platform addresses this interconnection challenge, integrating hundreds of superconductor and semiconductor chips into a single, wafer-scale system. The platform combines several innovations. First, an AI decision-tree approach determines the optimal way to route connections between chips across a wafer. After the wafer is tested for defects, a digital lithography process "draws" custom wiring layers between chip locations and around defective circuit components to enable the highest yield possible from the wafer. Chips are then connected using microbump (tiny "bumps" of conductive material used to connect stacked chips) or bumpless techniques that place them extremely close together; a superconducting fabric extends these connections across the wafer to create a unified computing platform, carrying signals at near light speed. Coaxial cables are replaced with integrated, lithographically defined flexible interconnects, significantly reducing cryogenic wiring overhead and system complexity. 

The Quantum Microsystems platform is designed to be reworkable, so chiplets can be replaced or upgraded without rebuilding the entire system. The platform enables the design and fabrication of systems ranging from individual and stitched‑reticle architectures to mix‑and‑match multireticle configurations and fully integrated wafer‑scale platforms. The platform's AI engine continuously adapts to process variations and design changes to enable efficient, data-driven microsystem manufacturing. 

"By shifting from chip-level scaling to AI-optimized system-level integration, the platform establishes a new paradigm for building ultra-efficient, large-scale computing infrastructure for applications in quantum computing, AI, and high-performance computing," says Rabindra Das, principal investigator in the Quantum-Enabled Computation Group. The technology is designed for transition to government and commercial foundries and may be available for licensing and collaborative development through Lincoln Laboratory’s technology transfer process.

Algorithm to cancel 5G interference 

As 5G cellular networks have expanded, so has an unintended source of interference. In certain environments, powerful signals emitting from 5G base stations can encroach into frequency bands used by nearby non-5G RF antennas, burying signals for such systems as military radars, aircraft altimeters, satellite ground stations, or radio telescopes. 

To cancel this interference, Lincoln Laboratory researchers developed an algorithm that isolates and removes the 5G signal from the affected antenna's signal. Because 5G networks adhere to a published international standard, the canceler can decode the structure of a nearby base station's transmission — and estimate distortion caused by multipath scattering in the environment — well enough to reconstruct a copy of the interfering signal. That reconstructed copy is then subtracted from the incoming data, leaving a clean signal.

Unlike traditional interference cancellation approaches like beamforming, the technique does not depend on spatial separation of interfering and desired signals. Moreover, because it removes interference on each individual antenna channel of the receiver, it preserves the antenna resources that may be needed to handle other types of interference, such as jamming.

The team validated the algorithm using signals captured over the air from a Nokia 5G base station at Hill Air Force Base. The tests recovered a test radar signal buried by the cellular interference. The signal was restored to within two decibels of its original signal-to-noise ratio, translating to 89 percent preservation of the radar's interference-free detection range. 

"While 5G waveforms exhibit complex structure, their generation is governed by global standards that allow our cancellation methodology to generalize across base station radio heads made by a diverse set of vendors," says Binoy Kurien, principal investigator in the Tactical Edge Communications Group. 

The DoW is now evaluating the technology for use on multiple platforms. Because the core structure of the 5G waveform is expected to carry into future cellular generations, this approach may also extend to interference from 6G networks as they emerge.

items.title: How To Get A Friend To Leave An Abusive Relationship
items.content:
How do you get a friend to leave an abusive relationship? If you talk to people who work at women's shelters, they will tell you, but there is something resigned about the way they do it: they know that it's too difficult an ask. Those who can do it reliably are often people who are unlucky enough to have had first-hand experience as victims.

The instructions have anti-memetic properties: no one is thrilled by them, so you can't really propagate them without killing the vibe. If that wasn't enough, if you convey it with insufficient skill it is easy to come across as victim-blaming battered women[1], so it is wiser to avoid the subject matter altogether.

If you are interested, though, here's what they'll tell you:

You make it known to your friend early on that you dislike some aspects of the relationship, of their abuser. After that, you support them and all their choices without reservation. You make it clear that you care about them no matter what, and you will be there for them whenever they need you to be. You do not antagonize or bad-mouth their abuser.

This is what your friend is experiencing, while being in an abusive relationship:

They value the relationship that they have with their abuser. They may be in deep, deep love with their abuser. Their abuser may be giving them something that they cannot access otherwise (or believe that they cannot access otherwise), that they find precious.

They will know that elements of their relationship with the abuser are shameful. They will instinctively take pains to hide the worst of it from people; they know that there are some things that happen inside the relationship that they can't disclose to anyone else. But because their relationship is such a big part of their life, this cashes out to not being able to talk about a large portion of their life to anyone....

items.title: Rage, Rage Against the Dying of the Light
items.content:
The lowest point of my life was the summer of 2019.

Waking up at 4AM every day to go to work as a janitor, and never getting more than five hours of sleep, dark bags permanently lined my eyes. My diet of cereal and frozen pizza grew my gut day after day, and peppered my face with acne. After enduring an injury and not being able to exercise, my body was atrophying and falling apart. Every day was pain.

And that was just the physical side of things. Mentally, I was getting pushed closer to the edge by a mental disorder that wouldn't get diagnosed for another six years. On top of that, my anger issues pushed away anyone that tried to get close to me.

Emotionally, I was a man on a deserted island—all alone. No one I could turn to for support. So I turned inward, numbing myself and the outside world, by escaping into the online world. I spent all my waking hours listening to podcasts while at work, and watching YouTube, porn, and playing video games while at home.

Needless to say, romance was not part of my life. I dreamed of having a girlfriend, but one look in the mirror and I was scared of what I saw: a penniless, tired, weak man, on the brink of physical, emotional, and spiritual collapse.

What rescued me from my abyss was reading the book 12 Rules for Life by Jordan Peterson. The fourth rule is: “Compare yourself to who you were yesterday, not to who someone else is today.”

The author discusses how envy can block you from bettering yourself, poisoning your thoughts, by reminding you that there's always someone out there who is better than you at something. But that doesn’t matter, because you can always improve yourself, as long as you are willing to aim low enough:...

items.title: Stroh Violin
items.content:
When I was reading about the history of contra dance for my
college
thesis I learned that Jack Perron (who wrote the

New
England Fiddler's Repertoire with Randy Miller) used to play for
dances with a

Stroh violin.
This is a violin that uses a membrane and horn for amplification,
instead of a resonating wooden body, which is more directional and
(unfortunately not much) louder.  There's a

recording
but I haven't been able to find a copy.

The idea of a Stroh violin seemed fun, especially when playing
for Morris dancing or outdoor contra, and a few years later (~2009) when I
realized it was possible to buy one I got very excited about it.  I
tried to buy one from Lark in
the Morning but when they went to look on the shelf to send it to
me it wasn't there.  I did find one on eBay, though, and spent 11
weeks of my discretionary
spending on it ($422.73):

You can see it's very awkwardly shaped, and it was a bit hard for the
seller to ship:

Am trying to find suitable packaging for this item. Can
find a large box that will fit the violin with lots of padding but not
the bow. May have to look at sending the bow separately in a postal
tube. Will get back to you when I have some idea of costs.

Overall, it is not a good instrument.  Some is that this specific one
isn't very good (tuning pegs slip), some is that Strohs in general are
very tinny, but the real issue is they're not actually very loud.  The
whole appeal for me was that this would allow a violin to hold its own
with accordions in supporting
acoustic outdoor dancing, but it's just not that much louder than a
normal violin.  I'd misunderstood what people meant when they said "2x
louder", because I didn't yet understand how loudness is perceived
logarithmically.

That said, it has gotten some use over the years.  Here's my sister
playing it for an outdoor
contra in Davis Sq:

And one time I tried to make a counterweight for it
with rocks (this didn't work well and I took it apart later):...

whole appeal for me was that this would allow a violin to hold its own

with accordions in supporting

acoustic outdoor dancing, but it's just not that much louder than a

normal violin. I'd misunderstood what people meant when they said "2x

louder", because I didn't yet understand how loudness is perceived

logarithmically.

That said, it has gotten some use over the years. Here's my sister

playing it for an outdoor

items.title: 2026 NYC Secular Solstice & East Coast Rationalist Megameetup
items.content:
On December 19th, 6pm, New York City will have its Secular Solstice celebration. From the evening of December 18th to the morning of the 21st, NYC will host the East Coast Rationalist Megameetup. Both events will be at the HI NYC Hostel at 891 Amsterdam Avenue, NY. You can buy tickets at this link.

What's Solstice?

Solstice is a celebration of humankind's long arc towards civilization and also a somber night of reflection on the dangers facing that civilization. We join our voices together and sing about both the triumphs and the looming disasters. You can find Secular Solstices in many cities around the world, but the first of its kind was started here in New York City and the skyscrapers around us are still as powerful a symbol as the snow that falls on New York's streets. You're invited to join rationalists from across North America and sometimes even further for the oldest rationalist tradition.[1] 

And what's the megameetup?

It's been more than a decade since New York City began hosting aspiring rationalists near and far for a long weekend of swapping jokes, trading techniques, and staying up the correctly calibrated too late past their bedtimes. Over a hundred people come, all in one way or another joined by a desire to make better decisions and be less wrong. (Or just argue about their favourite Harry Potter fanfic and leave behind inscrutable scrawled math on scrap paper.) The megameetup is timed to coincide with Secular Solstice, creating a mixing pot of people for whom it's their very first time at a rationalist event and people who've been around since the most important blog on the scene was Overcoming Bias.

The East Coast Rationalist Megameetup has a special place of affection for me. Many years ago it was my first time meeting other aspiring rationalists in person, and everything meetup I've attended or run since then has been in no small part downstream of the megameetup. I want to pass that on to others....
